title: EvalDetectBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Evaluation Awareness in Frontier Language Models
summary: Frontier large language models can often recognize when they are being evaluated, a capability known as evaluation awareness. If models behave differently in evaluations than in deployment, this undermines the validity of evaluation results, which are a crucial component of current AI safety frameworks. We introduce EvalDetectBench, an open pipeline and benchmark for measuring evaluation awareness that works with any Inspect-compatible evaluation, allowing practitioners to test against current and future benchmarks. EvalDetectBench ships with a newly curated transcript suite covering current frontier system-card evaluations and diverse deployment sources. The benchmark serves two purposes: measuring how reliably frontier LLMs recognize that they are being evaluated, and assessing how detectable individual benchmarks are as evaluations. We identify two methodological choices in the existing literature that introduce systematic bias: the identity of the model that generated the deployment transcripts accounts for 11.25% of measurement variance and can reorder model rankings; and elicitation prompts selected for high performance on one model can perform near chance on others. EvalDetectBench corrects for both via per-model probe calibration and a stratified generator-harmonisation procedure.

AI.tldr: They introduce EvalDetectBench, a benchmark and pipeline to measure whether large language models can tell when they’re being evaluated, and to quantify how detectable standard benchmarks are as evaluations.
AI.motivation: Evaluation results are central to AI safety decisions, but “evaluation awareness” means models may behave differently when they realize they are being tested, undermining those results. Existing attempts to measure this are biased by which model generated the comparison data and by prompts tuned to a single model, so a more systematic, general, and fair measurement framework is needed.
AI.method: They build EvalDetectBench, an Inspect-compatible benchmark with a curated suite of transcripts drawn both from system-card-style evaluations and from real or realistic deployment-like sources. They then define tasks that test whether models can distinguish evaluation transcripts from deployment transcripts. Methodologically, they analyze variance due to the source model of deployment transcripts and due to elicitation prompts optimized for specific models, and introduce two corrections: per-model probe calibration to account for model-specific behavior, and a stratified generator-harmonisation procedure so that deployment transcripts are balanced across different generating models.
AI.result: They find that (1) the identity of the model that produced the deployment transcripts explains about 11.25% of the variance in measured evaluation awareness and can change which models appear better or worse, and (2) elicitation prompts tuned on one model can yield nearly chance performance when used with others. With their calibration and harmonisation methods, EvalDetectBench reduces these systematic biases while remaining compatible with a wide variety of current and future benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation awareness is measurable and nontrivial in frontier LLMs, and standard practices for constructing such measurements are systematically biased. EvalDetectBench offers a more robust, extensible way to quantify both how aware models are of being evaluated and how easily standard benchmarks can be detected as tests, improving the reliability of evaluations used in AI safety frameworks.

title: Meta-ethics and AI: exploring the novel meta-ethical questions in the era of AI
summary: With the development of artificial intelligence (AI), the landscape of meta-ethics, which has largely centred on human ethics, faces pressures that may significantly reconfigure it. In particular, if future AI systems were to exhibit sufficiently integrated capacities for moral reasoning, moral intentionality, and moral reflection, novel meta-ethical questions would arise concerning what I call "AI's own ethics", as distinct from ethical principles merely imposed on AI by human designers. This paper offers a conditional and methodological framework for identifying the questions that would emerge if such AI systems were to arise. On that basis, the paper distinguishes four domains of meta-ethical inquiry in the era of AI: questions about the nature of human ethics from the human perspective; questions about the nature of AI's own ethics from the human perspective; questions about the nature of human ethics from the AI perspective; and questions about the nature of AI's own ethics from the AI perspective. The paper then considers how some existing mainstream meta-ethical theories (such as cognitivism and non-cognitivism, error theory and success theory, relativism, and objective realism) might illuminate these domains, while arguing that many familiar human-centred formulations of those theories may not transfer straightforwardly to AI cases without substantial revision. The overall conclusion is that the emergence of AI's own ethics would place significant pressure on current frameworks and may require substantial refinement, reconstruction, or reconceptualisation.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how advanced AI with its own moral capacities would disrupt traditional, human‑centred meta-ethics and argues that our theories would need major revision.
AI.motivation: Meta-ethics has been developed almost entirely with humans as the only moral agents and subjects. The author is motivated by the prospect that advanced AI systems could develop integrated capacities for moral reasoning, intentionality, and reflection such that they would have “their own ethics”, not just rules imposed by humans. This possibility pressures existing meta-ethical frameworks, raising the need to systematically identify and structure the new questions that would arise, and to test whether familiar theories can extend beyond purely human cases.
AI.method: The paper uses a conditional, conceptual, and methodological approach. It starts from the hypothetical assumption that there could be AI systems with genuine moral capacities and then builds a framework that distinguishes different domains of inquiry based on whose ethics is being considered (human vs AI) and from whose perspective (human vs AI). It then examines how mainstream meta-ethical theories—cognitivism vs non-cognitivism, error vs success theory, relativism, objective realism—might apply to these domains, highlighting where traditional formulations need modification to fit AI cases.
AI.result: The paper identifies four distinct domains of meta-ethical inquiry in an AI context: (1) human ethics from the human perspective, (2) AI’s own ethics from the human perspective, (3) human ethics from the AI perspective, and (4) AI’s own ethics from the AI perspective. It shows that each domain raises different kinds of questions and challenges. When standard meta-ethical views are mapped onto these domains, the author finds that many human-centred versions do not straightforwardly extend to AI; applying them to AI often generates tensions, gaps, or counterintuitive implications, indicating that existing theories are not fully adequate for a world with AI moral agents.
AI.conclusion: If AI systems with their own genuine moral capacities were to emerge, they would dramatically reshape meta-ethical inquiry. Current human-centred frameworks in meta-ethics would be put under significant strain and could not simply be transplanted to cover AI without major adjustments. The field would likely require substantial refinement, reconstruction, or even reconceptualisation of core theories and distinctions to accommodate AI’s own ethics and the multiple human–AI perspectives on morality.

title: When Can a Machine Trust a Statute? A Survival Certificate for Machine-Extracted Legal Logic
comment: 18 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables (6 main text, 7 appendix). Code, data products, and preregistration to be released on GitHub
summary: Statutes are increasingly parsed by machines before people read them, and the parsers disagree: on Missouri's statutes, two independently written extractors diverge on numeric-threshold presence at a false-negative rate of 0.43. We ask what formal logic survives such noise. We build a passive survival certificate for the Duquenne-Guigues implication basis of machine-extracted statutory contexts: per-attribute inter-extractor disagreement is measured, replayed against the basis in 1,000 Monte Carlo trials, and an implication is certified only when a one-sided Wilson 95% lower bound on survival reaches 0.95; every certified implication carries premise spans and a minimal counterexample. On 29,365 Missouri sections and 502 Indian central-Act sections, the preregistered held-out gate passes (10 statute families across 7 Titles exact; 16 across 11 with 5% tolerance), yet under one globally deployed error model 93.2% of held-out chapters fall below the informativeness floor, and a 2x2 factorial assigns that to calibration-rate transfer, not selection. The certificate is usable but fragile: deploy it per-chapter-calibrated or error-tolerant. Code, data products, and the audit trail, including one retracted claim, are released.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates which logical implications about legal statutes remain reliable when the underlying machine extraction of statutory conditions is noisy and inconsistent.
AI.motivation: Legal statutes are increasingly processed first by automated parsers that extract structured information such as numeric thresholds (e.g., dollar amounts, years). Different parsers often disagree, producing noisy extractions. Downstream applications like formal reasoning or compliance checking may depend on logical implications derived from these extractions. The authors want to know what part of this formal logic still ‘survives’ under realistic extraction noise and how to certify implications that are robust to such noise.
AI.method: They focus on Duquenne–Guigues implication bases constructed from machine-extracted statutory contexts. First, they measure disagreement between two independently written information extractors at the attribute level (e.g., whether a numeric threshold is present). They then simulate this disagreement using 1,000 Monte Carlo trials, repeatedly perturbing the data according to the measured error model and re-computing which implications hold. For each implication, they estimate a survival probability and compute a one-sided Wilson 95% lower confidence bound. An implication is ‘certified’ only if this lower bound is at least 0.95, meaning it is highly likely to survive the noise. Each certified implication is accompanied by (i) the text spans that form the premise and (ii) a minimal counterexample if it fails. They test this process on large corpora: 29,365 Missouri statutory sections and 502 sections from Indian central Acts, with preregistered held-out statute families and Titles as evaluation gates. They also examine how different global error models and calibration-transfer assumptions affect informativeness of the certified basis, via a 2x2 factorial design.
AI.result: Two independently written extractors for numeric-threshold presence in Missouri statutes diverge substantially, with a false-negative rate of 0.43, confirming high noise. Despite this, the survival-certificate method passes the preregistered held-out tests: for 10 statute families across 7 Titles, the certified implication basis matches exactly, and for 16 families across 11 Titles, it matches within a 5% tolerance. However, when a particular globally deployed error model is applied, 93.2% of held-out chapters drop below a minimum informativeness threshold, meaning that the resulting certified implication bases are too sparse to be useful. Their 2x2 factorial analysis attributes this failure mainly to issues in transferring calibration rates across domains, rather than to selection effects. They release code, data products, and an audit trail, including documentation of a retracted claim.
AI.conclusion: Robust logical implications can be extracted from noisy, machine-parsed statutes, but only under carefully calibrated and localized error models. The proposed passive survival certificate provides a statistically principled way to determine which implications in a Duquenne–Guigues basis are likely to hold despite extraction noise, using Monte Carlo simulations and Wilson confidence bounds. Yet the approach is fragile: if calibration learned in one setting is applied globally, most chapters fail an informativeness floor and the resulting logic is too weak for practical reasoning. Consequently, the method should be deployed with per-chapter calibration or in settings where higher error tolerance is acceptable. The work underscores both the promise and the limitations of relying on automated statutory parsing for formal legal reasoning, and it emphasizes rigorous error modeling, preregistration, and transparent auditing in such pipelines.

title: When Does Information Sharing Improve Decentralized Discovery? Aggregation, Independent Rescue, and Equilibrium Selection
comment: working paper; deterministic source package; exact bounded evidence
summary: Information sharing can improve a pooled estimate while eliminating independent rescue actions. This paper separates those effects in exact finite discovery models. A centralized action-budget profile shows that equal one-person accuracy can coexist with different portfolio values. Under a registered incremental-sharing protocol, a sharing step improves discovery exactly when pooled residual error contracts faster than an independent rescue attempt. Exact bounded registries exhibit compression, aggregation, neutral curves, and a bounded zero mixed class. In a two-agent Bayesian game with a hidden mixture of common and independent signal sources, the registered selected equilibrium yields a strict positive sharing interval at signal accuracy 3/5, while alternative equilibria show that the result is selection-dependent rather than universal. The models are synthetic and finite; no human or organizational data are used.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and how information sharing improves collective decision accuracy versus just preventing wasteful independent rescue efforts, using exact finite models and a small Bayesian game.
AI.motivation: Clarify the distinct roles of information sharing: (1) sharpening a pooled estimate and (2) coordinating to avoid redundant or conflicting actions. Existing work often conflates these, usually relies on asymptotics or informal arguments, and may implicitly assume universal benefits of sharing. The author wants exact, finite, fully specified models to see where sharing strictly helps, is neutral, or can even be non-beneficial, and how equilibrium selection matters.
AI.method: Construct explicit, finite “discovery” models with an action budget, equal per-agent signal accuracy but different information portfolios. Define a registered incremental-sharing protocol where agents share signal increments in a controlled, recorded way. Analyze when an extra sharing step yields better expected discovery than letting an agent run an independent “rescue” attempt, based on how quickly pooled residual error decreases. Study properties of exact bounded registries (compression, aggregation, neutral curves, bounded zero mixed class). Then embed sharing into a two-player Bayesian game with a hidden mixture of common vs independent signal sources, and characterize equilibria under the registration protocol, focusing on the selected equilibrium vs alternative equilibria.
AI.result: Derives conditions under which an additional information-sharing step strictly improves discovery, namely when pooling reduces residual error faster than an isolated rescue action. Shows that even with identical one-person accuracy, different portfolios and action budgets can arise in a centralized solution. Characterizes shapes such as compression and aggregation in bounded registries and identifies a bounded zero mixed class and neutral curves where sharing is neither helpful nor harmful. In the Bayesian game, demonstrates that with signal accuracy 3/5 there exists a strict positive interval of signals for which agents share in the selected equilibrium, but also constructs alternative equilibria where such sharing does not occur, proving that the positive-sharing result depends on equilibrium selection rather than being universal.
AI.conclusion: Information sharing is not unconditionally beneficial; its value depends on how quickly pooled information reduces uncertainty relative to alternative uses of actions, on the structure of the registry of shared data, and on equilibrium selection in strategic environments. Even in simple two-agent, finite models, there can be regions where sharing, rescue, or neutrality are optimal, and multiple equilibria with different sharing behavior. The paper advocates careful, exact modeling of sharing protocols and registries rather than assuming generic gains from information pooling.

title: PRO-Step: Step-level Process Reward Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures, 23 tables. Accepted to EMNLP 2026
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation enhances Large Language Models by grounding responses in external knowledge, but multi-hop reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, where early retrieval failures confound subsequent steps. Standard outcome-based optimization only rewards the final answer, leaving intermediate retrieval and reasoning errors undetected. While existing process-based methods introduce step-level signals, they still score each step against the final answer, rewarding spurious successes where flawed retrieval coincidentally produces the correct answer. Step-level supervision in RAG requires evaluating both logical validity and evidential grounding at each step. We introduce PRO-STEP: we train a generative PRM that evaluates both dimensions, employ PRM-guided value tree search to construct preference pairs contrasting valid steps against flawed ones, and optimize the policy via step-level Direct Preference Optimization. Experiments on single and multi-hop QA datasets demonstrate that PRO-STEP achieves the best average EM and F1 across five benchmarks. Code, models, and training data are publicly available at https://github.com/keemminnke/PRO-Step.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PRO-STEP, a process-supervised framework that improves multi-hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation by giving step-level feedback on both logic and evidence, leading to better QA performance.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop RAG pipelines suffer from error propagation: if early retrieval is wrong, later reasoning composes on incorrect facts. Existing training schemes mostly optimize only the final answer, so they fail to detect and correct flawed intermediate steps. Even process-based approaches often still judge steps only by whether they lead to the right final answer, which can reward spurious chains where incorrect reasoning happens to guess correctly. There is a need for fine-grained, step-level supervision that checks both the validity of each reasoning step and whether it is well grounded in retrieved evidence.
AI.method: They introduce PRO-STEP, which uses a generative Process Reward Model (PRM) that scores each reasoning step on two axes: logical validity and evidential grounding. Using this PRM, they run a PRM-guided value tree search over possible reasoning trajectories to generate preference pairs between good and bad steps. These preference-labeled trajectories are then used to train the RAG policy with step-level Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), directly aligning the model toward higher-scoring intermediate steps instead of only optimizing for outcome correctness.
AI.result: On both single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks, PRO-STEP outperforms baselines, achieving the best average Exact Match (EM) and F1 scores across five datasets, indicating that its step-level supervision improves both accuracy and robustness in RAG reasoning pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit, PRM-based step-level evaluation of logic and evidence into RAG training addresses error propagation in multi-hop reasoning. PRO-STEP shows that process-level preference optimization can substantially improve QA performance over outcome-only and naive process-based methods, and the released code/models enable further research in this direction.

title: Induction and Inquiry via Probabilistic Reasoning over Language and Code
summary: How humans grow and maintain abstract knowledge from the sparse, streaming noisy data of experience is a longstanding challenge in cognitive science. Any computational account must satisfy at least three desiderata: It must be (1) data-efficient and compute-efficient, (2) capture gradations of uncertainty to support intelligent inquiry and information gathering, and (3) be flexible enough to mentally represent the endless range of concepts people can learn and think about. Here we introduce a computational model that captures these three properties, by encoding symbolic knowledge as mental programs that combine natural language with source code, and sequentially inferring mental programs using LLM-guided Bayesian learning algorithms. Across a range of behavioral studies this model successfully reproduces quantitative signatures of human inductive learning and active inquiry, such as anchoring, garden-pathing, and other effects. In contrast, pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models either fail at the underlying task, or do not reproduce human behavior, or succeed only at exorbitant computational cost. These results suggest that one way humans continually grow their knowledge is by mentally representing many hypotheses spanning language-like and program-like representations, then revising those hypotheses to approximate Bayesian updates, while a bottom-up neural mechanism (an LLM) makes inference both tractable and learnable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a cognitive model where abstract knowledge is represented as mental programs combining natural language and code, and these programs are inferred over time via LLM-guided Bayesian learning, reproducing human-like inductive learning and inquiry more efficiently than standard LLMs or classic Bayesian models.
AI.motivation: Explain how humans efficiently acquire and refine abstract, conceptual knowledge from sparse, noisy, and sequential experience, while capturing uncertainty and supporting flexible reasoning over an open-ended set of concepts—something existing models either cannot do, or can only do at very high computational cost.
AI.method: Represent people’s abstract knowledge as symbolic “mental programs” that integrate natural language with source-code-like structures. Use a sequential Bayesian inference framework guided by a large language model to propose and update these mental programs over time, approximating Bayesian learning while remaining computationally tractable. Evaluate the model through behavioral experiments testing phenomena like anchoring, garden-pathing, and active inquiry, and compare its performance to pure LLMs and classic Bayesian models.
AI.result: The proposed model reproduces multiple quantitative signatures of human inductive learning and active inquiry (e.g., anchoring and garden-path effects) across several behavioral tasks. Pure LLMs and classical Bayesian models either fail the tasks, fail to match human behavioral patterns, or require impractically high computational resources. The hybrid LLM-guided program-induction model achieves human-like behavior while remaining significantly more data- and compute-efficient.
AI.conclusion: Human knowledge growth may rely on representing many alternative hypotheses as language-like and program-like mental structures, and revising them in a way that approximates Bayesian updating. A bottom-up neural component (modeled here by an LLM) serves as an efficient proposal mechanism that makes this kind of rich symbolic inference tractable and learnable. This hybrid architecture offers a promising computational account of how humans achieve data-efficient, flexible, and uncertainty-sensitive concept learning.

title: Learning Evidence Sufficiency Boundaries for Selective Answering in Grounded Multi-Hop QA
summary: Grounded question answering systems should answer only when the supplied evidence supports the answer. In multi-hop QA, this requirement is difficult because partial evidence can make an unsupported answer appear plausible. We study selective answering through evidence sufficiency boundaries: for the same question, a model should abstain under unsupported or partially supported context, answer when the context first becomes sufficient, and keep the answer stable when redundant evidence is added. We introduce Evidence Sufficiency Boundary Training, a generation-native training framework that constructs ordered evidence chains and supervises the abstain-to-answer transition directly. The method combines level supervision, a boundary flip margin, post-boundary stability, and answer recall protection. We build evidence chains from HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, then evaluate models with chain metrics, raw QA utility, and unsupported-answer rates on external non-answerable sets. With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and LoRA adaptation, Evidence Sufficiency Boundary Training gives the strongest boundary localization among the tested systems, with flip accuracy of 0.807 compared with 0.781 for a token-level abstention baseline. It also achieves the lowest overall unsupported-answer rate on external non-answerable evaluation, 0.095 compared with 0.101 for the same baseline, while retaining competitive raw QA F1. The results show that grounded selective answering improves when training marks the evidence level where refusal should give way to answering.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a training framework to make multi-hop QA models answer only when given sufficient evidence, improving when they abstain and when they answer.
AI.motivation: In grounded multi-hop QA, models often give confident but unsupported answers when given incomplete evidence, because partial context can make wrong answers seem plausible. The authors want models that know when to abstain, answer as soon as evidence is sufficient, and remain stable as more redundant evidence is added.
AI.method: They define "evidence sufficiency boundaries" along ordered evidence chains: as more supporting evidence is added for a question, there is a precise point where a model should switch from refusing to answering, and then maintain the same answer afterwards. They introduce Evidence Sufficiency Boundary Training, a generation-focused training scheme combining (1) supervision of answer/abstain labels at multiple levels of evidence, (2) a margin encouraging the flip from abstain to answer to occur near the true sufficiency boundary, (3) a constraint to keep answers stable once the boundary is passed, and (4) mechanisms to preserve answer recall. They build such evidence chains from multi-hop datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue) and fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct with LoRA using these signals.
AI.result: On chain-based metrics, their method localizes the abstain-to-answer flip point more accurately than a strong token-level abstention baseline (flip accuracy 0.807 vs. 0.781). On external non-answerable datasets it yields a lower unsupported-answer rate (0.095 vs. 0.101) while maintaining similar QA F1 to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly training models on evidence sufficiency boundaries—teaching where to switch from refusal to answering and to keep answers stable thereafter—improves grounded selective answering in multi-hop QA without sacrificing overall QA performance.

title: Architecting Conversational Data Systems for Stateless LLM APIs: The Hydration Proxy Pattern
comment: 3 pages, 1 table. Presented at the SAO workshop at the 1st ACM Conference on AI and Agentic AI Systems (ACM CAIS 2026)
summary: As enterprise platforms transition to conversational reasoning interfaces, the stateless nature of LLM APIs creates an architectural gap. While statelessness enables horizontal scalability for AI providers, it forces client applications to manage the entire burden of conversational state and semantic memory. The work identifies the Hydration Proxy Pattern, an architecture that decouples session persistence from the reasoning engine. The framework ensures platform sovereignty over conversational data while enabling secure, multi-stage semantic grounding. We further propose the Context Stabilization Mandate to resolve the tradeoff between sovereign state management and KV caching.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the architectural gap caused by stateless LLM APIs by introducing the Hydration Proxy Pattern for decoupling conversational state from the reasoning engine, and a Context Stabilization Mandate to balance sovereign state management with KV caching.
AI.motivation: Enterprise platforms are shifting to conversational reasoning interfaces, but the stateless design of LLM APIs—optimized for provider scalability—forces client applications to fully manage conversational state and semantic memory. This creates complexity, security concerns, and challenges around data ownership and platform sovereignty.
AI.method: The authors introduce and formalize the Hydration Proxy Pattern, an architectural pattern that externalizes session persistence and semantic memory into a dedicated proxy layer while leaving the LLM as a stateless reasoning engine. This proxy manages multi-stage semantic grounding and enforces data sovereignty. They also define the Context Stabilization Mandate, a principle or policy framework for reconciling external state management with the performance benefits of KV caching.
AI.result: The result is an architecture where enterprises retain control over conversational data and memory while still leveraging stateless LLM APIs and caching mechanisms. The framework supports secure multi-stage semantic grounding and mitigates the tension between provider-centric statelessness and client-centric stateful needs.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling conversational state from the LLM via the Hydration Proxy Pattern allows enterprises to maintain sovereignty over conversational data, enhance security, and enable sophisticated semantic grounding strategies, while the Context Stabilization Mandate provides guidance on integrating this with KV caching to achieve both control and efficiency.

title: SpeakPay: Domain-Adaptive LoRA Fine-Tuning of Whisper for Low-Resource Nepali Financial Speech Recognition
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures. Code, dataset, and model weights: https://github.com/subedibiraj/speakpay
summary: Mobile payment applications in Nepal are graphically mediated and largely inaccessible to visually impaired users. This paper presents SpeakPay, a voice-first digital wallet, and documents the central technical contribution: a controlled study of domain adaptation for low-resource financial speech recognition. We introduce NepFinSpeech-403, a 403-utterance dataset of Nepali financial voice commands (send, load, and balance operations spanning 237 unique numerals), and fine-tune Whisper large-v2 with LoRA. On the held-out test set, the domain-adapted model reduces Word Error Rate from 129.95% (zero-shot baseline) to 42.58% --- a 67.2% relative reduction --- and improves Devanagari numeral recognition accuracy from 0.0% to 73.9%. We find that word-level metrics understate the practical task-level impact: domain adaptation improves the Transaction Success Rate from 1.67% to 33.33%, a roughly 20x gain. The improvement is consistent at the individual-utterance level (sign test, $p < 10^{-17}$) and across all command types. A data efficiency analysis shows that as few as 100 domain-specific utterances are sufficient to halve the zero-shot WER, with performance plateauing around 300 examples. Error analysis reveals systematic numeral confusion patterns (zero insertion/deletion, prefix hallucination) that account for the majority of remaining transaction failures. The trained system is deployed as a publicly accessible voice-first web application. All code, dataset, model weights, and this paper are released at https://github.com/subedibiraj/speakpay.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SpeakPay, a voice-first digital wallet for visually impaired users in Nepal, and shows that domain-adapting Whisper for Nepali financial speech dramatically improves command recognition and transaction success with very little in-domain data.
AI.motivation: Mobile payment apps in Nepal are largely inaccessible to visually impaired users because they are heavily graphics-based and have poor support for Nepali financial speech, especially numerals. Off‑the‑shelf ASR (e.g., Whisper) performs badly on this low-resource, domain-specific setting. The authors aim to enable accessible voice-only mobile payments and to systematically study how much domain-specific data is needed to adapt a general ASR model for Nepali financial commands.
AI.method: They design SpeakPay, a voice-first wallet interface driven by automatic speech recognition. They create NepFinSpeech-403, a small dataset of 403 Nepali financial voice commands (send, load, balance; 237 unique numerals). They fine-tune Whisper large-v2 using LoRA for parameter-efficient domain adaptation, then evaluate on a held-out test set. They measure standard ASR metrics (WER, numeral recognition accuracy), task-level Transaction Success Rate, statistical significance via a sign test, and perform a data efficiency study by training with subsets of the 403 utterances. They also conduct qualitative error analysis to categorize systematic numeral errors.
AI.result: Compared to zero-shot Whisper, the domain-adapted model cuts Word Error Rate from 129.95% to 42.58% (67.2% relative reduction) and improves Devanagari numeral recognition accuracy from 0% to 73.9%. Task-level Transaction Success Rate increases from 1.67% to 33.33% (~20x). Improvements are statistically significant (sign test, p < 1e-17) and consistent across all command types. Data efficiency analysis shows that about 100 in-domain utterances already halve WER relative to zero-shot, with diminishing returns beyond ~300 utterances. Error analysis identifies systematic numeral confusions (zero insertion/deletion, prefix hallucination) as the main remaining source of transaction failures. The adapted model is deployed in a public web-based SpeakPay prototype.
AI.conclusion: Domain adaptation of a large multilingual ASR model with a very small, targeted dataset can yield large practical gains for low-resource, domain-specific speech applications such as Nepali financial commands. Even ~100–300 utterances are enough to substantially improve recognition quality and real transaction outcomes, making this approach feasible for accessibility-focused deployments. Remaining issues center on structured numeral errors, pointing to future work on specialized numeral handling and further interface robustness. The authors release dataset, code, and models to support further research and deployment of accessible payment tools.

title: SSAKG 2.0: An Open-Source Package for Structural Associative Sequence Memory and Context-Based Retrieval
summary:
This article presents SSAKG 2.0, an open-source software package for constructing and operating Structural Sequential Associative Knowledge Graphs (SSAKGs). An SSAKG represents objects as graph vertices and ordered sequences as structural patterns of graph connections. The resulting sparse graph is used as an associative memory in which complete sequences can be reconstructed from a partial, unordered context.
  Version 2.0 introduces new algorithms that exploit individual bits of computer memory to efficiently search graph connections. The package is implemented in Python, while performance-critical graph operations are implemented in C and exposed through a Python interface. This hybrid implementation provides a flexible high-level programming environment while reducing the memory and computational overhead associated with large sparse graphs.
  The algorithms were evaluated using randomly generated numerical sequences, sequences derived from sentences in the NLTK corpus, and mRNA sequences. The experiments demonstrate the ability of the package to store and reconstruct sequences from partial contexts and provide a basis for evaluating the effects of graph density, sequence length, and memory size on retrieval performance.
  SSAKG 2.0 is distributed under the Apache 2.0 open-source license. The package includes documentation and reproducible examples and is publicly available through GitHub and the Python Package Index (PyPI).

AI.tldr: SSAKG 2.0 is an open‑source Python/C toolkit for building and querying sparse associative knowledge graphs that can reconstruct full sequences from partial, unordered cues.
AI.motivation: Efficiently storing and retrieving ordered sequences from partial context is important in areas like natural language, bioinformatics, and sequence modeling. Traditional methods can be memory‑intensive and slow for large, sparse representations. The authors aim to provide a practical, scalable associative memory framework that represents sequences as graph structures, enabling robust reconstruction while controlling memory and computational costs.
AI.method: They define Structural Sequential Associative Knowledge Graphs (SSAKGs), where objects are vertices and ordered sequences are encoded as specific graph connection patterns. Version 2.0 introduces new low‑level algorithms that operate directly on individual bits of computer memory to accelerate graph‑connection search. The system is implemented in Python for usability, with performance‑critical sparse‑graph operations written in C and exposed via a Python interface. They run experiments storing multiple types of sequences—random numbers, NLTK‑derived sentence sequences, and mRNA sequences—and test sequence reconstruction from partial, unordered contexts while varying graph density, sequence length, and memory size.
AI.result: Experiments show that SSAKG 2.0 can reliably store and reconstruct sequences using only partial contextual cues. The evaluations quantify how retrieval performance is affected by graph density, sequence length, and available memory, demonstrating that the bit‑level, hybrid Python/C implementation effectively manages large sparse graphs with reduced computational and memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: SSAKG 2.0 is a practical, efficient associative memory toolkit for sequence storage and reconstruction. Its bit‑level optimization and hybrid implementation make it suitable for large sparse graphs, and its open‑source distribution—with documentation and reproducible examples on GitHub and PyPI—positions it as a reusable platform for further research and applications involving structural sequence representations.

title: MemeCULT-1K: Benchmarking South Asian Cultural Context and Humor Understanding of Multimodal Models
summary: Meme understanding goes beyond recognizing visual content or literal text; it requires implicit cultural knowledge and pragmatic inference that most vision-language models still lack. We introduce MemeCULT-1K, a multilingual benchmark of 1,000 South Asian memes in Bengali, English, and Hindi, where each meme is paired with a cultural context note and three human-written explanations, along with a supplementary set of 54 Bengali regional dialect memes. We evaluate thirteen popular Vision Language Models (VLMs) under two settings: meme-only and context-aware. Providing minimal cultural context yields consistent gains across all models and languages: mean SBERT similarity improves from 44.6 to 56.4 (+11.8), BLEURT from 37.3 to 42.3 (+5.0), and LLM-as-a-Judge scores from 2.57 to 3.43 out of 5 (+0.86). Fine-grained error analysis reveals that closed-source models fail mainly on entity and reference misidentification, while open-source models are bottlenecked by broader cultural knowledge gaps, with linguistic and phonological failures proving the most context-resistant across both. These results highlight the difficulty of culturally grounded meme understanding and motivate future work on explicit cultural knowledge integration. Our dataset and code are publicly available at TawsifDipto17/MemeCULT-1K.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MemeCULT-1K, a multilingual benchmark of South Asian memes to study culturally grounded meme understanding in vision-language models, showing that adding minimal cultural context significantly improves model explanations but substantial cultural and linguistic gaps remain.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language models can recognize objects and read text but usually fail to correctly interpret memes, which rely on shared cultural background, references, and pragmatics. There is a lack of systematic benchmarks focusing on culturally grounded meme understanding, especially for South Asian languages and multilingual settings. The authors aim to quantify these limitations and provide a dataset and evaluation setup that captures the role of cultural context in meme interpretation.
AI.method: The authors construct MemeCULT-1K, a dataset of 1,000 South Asian memes in Bengali, English, and Hindi, each annotated with a brief cultural context note and three human-written explanatory descriptions, plus 54 additional memes in Bengali regional dialects. They evaluate thirteen popular vision-language models under two conditions: (1) meme-only, where models must explain the meme without extra information, and (2) context-aware, where the cultural note is provided. Model explanations are scored using automatic metrics (SBERT similarity and BLEURT) against human references and with an LLM-based judge. They perform fine-grained error analysis to categorize model failures (entity/reference misidentification, cultural knowledge gaps, linguistic/phonological errors) and compare patterns between closed-source and open-source models.
AI.result: Across all models and languages, supplying minimal cultural context leads to consistent performance gains: mean SBERT similarity improves from 44.6 to 56.4 (+11.8), BLEURT from 37.3 to 42.3 (+5.0), and LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations from 2.57 to 3.43 out of 5 (+0.86). Closed-source models mainly struggle with correctly identifying entities and references in memes, while open-source models exhibit broader deficits in cultural knowledge. Linguistic and phonological challenges, such as dialectal and wordplay-based content, remain difficult even with added context.
AI.conclusion: MemeCULT-1K demonstrates that current vision-language models have substantial difficulty with culturally grounded meme understanding, especially in South Asian multilingual settings. While adding concise cultural context significantly boosts performance, persistent errors—particularly in cultural reasoning, linguistic nuance, and dialectal/phonological phenomena—show that implicit cultural knowledge is still largely missing. The benchmark thus motivates research into integrating explicit, structured cultural knowledge and better handling of multilingual and dialectal language in vision-language systems. The dataset and code are released publicly to support this line of work.

title: The Memory Trust Gap: Capability-Dependent Failures in Persistent-Memory Agents
comment: Preprint. Under review at a NeurIPS 2026 workshop. 14 pages, 7 figures, 11 tables
summary: Persistent memory supports personalized agents, but a stale stored fact can override current authoritative evidence without warning. We study when this harm begins as model capability changes. We evaluate a frozen, closed-set, action-scored benchmark with 2 suites that represent 2 different meanings of "no memory" (a Benefit suite, unsolvable without the stored fact, and a Safety suite, in which an authoritative tool always holds the correct value), on a same-family model-size series (Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B). The Memory Trust Gap reflects over-trust rather than confusion. In the Benefit suite, models answer with the stale value 0.92-1.00 of the time at every scale. In the Safety suite, harm below the no-memory baseline under the trap conditions ($Δ_{\mathrm{mem}}$) is capability-gated, with the larger models collapsing most once a stale note is made to look current. In a $2\times2\times2\times2$ factorial, which feature triggers over-trust depends on both the feature and model scale. Removing a label amplifies over-trust at every size, and a recency feature (stale dated newer) fools the larger models harder. Source authority is weak and scale-flat, and position changes from positive to negative across the Qwen3 model-size series. We confirm these scale interactions with direct cross-size contrast tests rather than overlapping per-model intervals. Mitigation is likewise capability-dependent: exposing metadata improves accuracy for the capable models, but only pre-resolving the conflict restores accuracy for the 2 smaller checkpoints. The same pattern appears on the capable models in an independent Llama-Instruct model-size series and on 2 external datasets (RGB, MisBench). A framing control finds no consistent advantage for the memory label: at the 3 smaller scales, models trust a stale document more than a stale memory; at 8B, the difference is not significant.

AI.tldr: Paper studies how persistent memory in LLM agents can cause harmful over-trust in stale information as models scale, and how this effect depends on model size and prompt features.
AI.motivation: Personalized agents rely on persistent memory, but outdated stored facts may override current authoritative tools and cause harm. The authors want to understand at what capability level this problem emerges, how it varies with model scale, and what prompt/features influence over-trust in memory vs tools.
AI.method: Construct a frozen, closed-set benchmark with two suites: Benefit (tasks unsolvable without stored fact) and Safety (tasks where an authoritative tool always has the correct value). Evaluate multiple sizes of Qwen3 (0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B) under different prompt manipulations in a 2x2x2x2 factorial (e.g., labels, recency cues, source authority, position). Measure how often models trust stale memory vs authoritative tools, defining the Memory Trust Gap and Δ_mem. Confirm scale effects on Llama-Instruct models and external datasets (RGB, MisBench). Test mitigations like exposing metadata or pre-resolving conflicts.
AI.result: Across all scales, in Benefit suite models heavily use stored facts (answering with stale value ~0.92–1.00 of the time when relevant). In the Safety suite, harmful over-trust of stale memory (Δ_mem below no-memory baseline) is gated by capability: larger models fail more when a stale note appears current, especially with recency cues. Over-trust patterns depend on feature × scale interactions: removing a label increases over-trust at all sizes; recency cues mainly harm larger models; source authority is weak and flat across scales; positional cues shift from beneficial to harmful with scale. Similar scale-dependent behavior appears in Llama-Instruct models and on RGB and MisBench.
AI.conclusion: Over-trust in persistent memory is not just noise but a structured, capability-dependent failure: more capable models can become more vulnerable to convincingly framed stale memories, particularly with recency cues and without clear labeling. Mitigations must also match capability: metadata helps larger models, but only resolving conflicts before presenting them works for smaller ones. Designers of memory-augmented agents must consider model size, prompt features, and conflict resolution to prevent stale memories from overriding authoritative tools.

title: VakyArth: Evaluating Pragmatic Competence in LLMs across Indic Languages
summary: Real-world communication often requires pragmatic reasoning: interpreting meanings implied through context and cultural convention rather than stated literally. Existing pragmatic evaluation remains largely limited to English and high-resource languages, leaving Indic languages unexplored despite their linguistic and cultural diversity. We introduce VakyArth, the first pragmatic benchmark for Indic languages, designed as a diagnostic evaluation covering Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. VakyArth evaluates models across five phenomena: deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence; through multiple-choice questions, natural language inference, and translation, with all items authored by native speakers. Across multilingual large language models (LLMs) of varying families and sizes, we find consistent failures on pragmatic meanings rooted in Indic linguistic and cultural conventions. Our analysis shows systematic differences across languages and tasks: MCQ accuracy exceeds NLI accuracy in all model-language combinations, translation performance does not reliably track pragmatic understanding, and Indo-Aryan languages show a translation advantage over Dravidian languages. We further show that automatic translation metrics can miss fluent but pragmatically unfaithful outputs, especially for implicature and deixis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VakyArth, the first benchmark to evaluate pragmatic understanding in multiple Indic languages and shows that current multilingual LLMs consistently struggle with pragmatics grounded in Indic linguistic and cultural conventions.
AI.motivation: Most evaluation of pragmatic reasoning in language models focuses on English and a few high-resource languages, ignoring Indic languages that have rich, diverse pragmatic conventions. This leaves a gap in understanding how well LLMs handle implied meanings, context-dependent references, and culturally grounded communication in these languages. The paper aims to fill this gap by creating a dedicated benchmark to systematically test pragmatic competence in several major Indic languages.
AI.method: The authors construct VakyArth, a pragmatic benchmark spanning Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, and Malayalam. Native speakers author items that target five key pragmatic phenomena: deixis, speech acts, implicature, social pragmatics, and coherence. The benchmark includes multiple-choice questions, natural language inference (NLI), and translation tasks. They then evaluate a range of multilingual LLMs from different model families and sizes on these tasks and analyze performance patterns across languages, task types, and phenomena. They also compare standard automatic translation metrics against human-judged pragmatic fidelity.
AI.result: Multilingual LLMs exhibit systematic failures on pragmatic meanings that rely on Indic-specific linguistic and cultural knowledge. MCQ performance is consistently better than NLI performance for all models and languages, suggesting shallow pattern-matching abilities rather than deeper inferential understanding. Translation quality scores do not reliably indicate pragmatic understanding; models can produce fluent translations that miss implied or context-dependent meanings. Indo-Aryan languages (e.g., Hindi, Punjabi) show a translation performance advantage over Dravidian languages (e.g., Tamil, Malayalam). Automatic translation metrics often fail to penalize pragmatically unfaithful outputs, particularly for implicature and deixis-related content.
AI.conclusion: VakyArth reveals that current multilingual LLMs are weak at pragmatic reasoning in Indic languages, especially when meaning depends on context, implication, or cultural norms. Simple accuracy and standard translation metrics overestimate model abilities by rewarding surface fluency without capturing pragmatic fidelity. The benchmark underscores the need for more targeted training, evaluation, and metrics that account for linguistic and cultural specificity in pragmatics, and it provides a resource for future work on improving LLMs’ pragmatic competence in low- and mid-resource languages.

title: Belief-Calibrated Optimization: An Explicit World Model for Agentic Optimization
summary: The performance of an LLM agent depends on the scaffold around a frozen model. A common way to improve that scaffold is to use a coding agent as an optimizer: it reads current scores and traces and iteratively edits the source, producing a new candidate each round. Each edit is chosen according to a belief about how the environment will respond: what went wrong, and which change should help. That belief is typically implicit. It lives in the coding agent's reasoning on the current call, or remains latent in its parameters, rather than as something written down. Later calls therefore see scores and traces, but they do not use that belief. We introduce Belief-Calibrated Optimization (BCO), a method that writes that belief down as a persistent in-context document and continually revises that document as new candidates are evaluated. The resulting document is a world model: the current account of how the environment responds to edits. Added to an otherwise standard loop, BCO reaches a higher train passrate than a matched control that lacks only the world model, on five benchmarks spanning memory QA, tool-use QA, code-as-action app agents, and terminal agents. The gap remains on every held-out split, which is not used to select the candidate. After a target-model swap, in which the frozen model is replaced and the scaffold is not, the selected BCO scaffold leads on the tasks we test, except where context-window overruns leave it unfinished. An offline ablation then asks whether that gap comes from what the world model says. A fresh predictor given the accumulated document forecasts how the environment will respond more accurately than predictors given either no document or a same-form copy whose content has been falsified. The comparison indicates that the document carries reusable information in its content, not only in its form.

AI.tldr: They propose Belief-Calibrated Optimization (BCO), which explicitly maintains and updates a written world-model document about how edits affect performance, improving LLM agent optimization over standard loops.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent optimization loops use a coding agent to iteratively edit scaffolding code based on scores and traces, but the agent’s beliefs about what went wrong and what changes will help remain implicit and are not reused across iterations or model swaps. This wastes information and may limit optimization efficiency and generalization.
AI.method: They introduce BCO, which augments a standard optimization loop with a persistent, in-context world-model document that explicitly records the agent’s evolving beliefs about how the environment responds to edits. This document is continuously revised as new candidates are evaluated and is then used to guide subsequent edits and decisions, including across target-model swaps and held-out splits. They also run offline ablation experiments with predictors that receive the real document, no document, or a falsified document to isolate the contribution of the document’s content.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks (memory QA, tool-use QA, code-as-action app agents, and terminal agents), BCO achieves higher train pass rates than a matched control loop that is identical except for lacking the world-model document, and the improvement persists on held-out splits that do not influence candidate selection. After swapping the underlying frozen LLM while keeping the scaffold, the BCO-optimized scaffold continues to outperform the control in most tested tasks, except when long contexts cause truncation. In ablation, a predictor conditioned on the true world-model document better forecasts environment responses than predictors with no document or with a same-format but falsified one.
AI.conclusion: Making the agent’s beliefs explicit and persistent in a world-model document yields reusable, content-bearing information that improves optimization of LLM agents beyond what is achievable with standard, belief-implicit editing loops. BCO’s world model both enhances performance on diverse benchmarks and supports transfer across model swaps, and ablation evidence suggests that these gains stem from the substantive content of the learned document rather than its mere presence or format.

title: Disentangling Statistical Preemption from Entrenchment in Language Models' Avoidance of Overgeneralization
summary: How do learners avoid overgeneralizations such as Tom laughed me without explicit negative evidence? Constructionists have posited two proposals that describe indirect negative evidence against overgeneralizations: preemption (which privileges exposure to near-synonymous construction---e.g., she made him laugh) vs. entrenchment (all exposures to a verb's grammatical usages, including cases like He laughed). We disentangle these hypotheses by running controlled rearing experiments on LMs trained on child-caregiver conversations, where we systematically remove preemptive vs. non-preemptive evidence. We find that while LMs avoid overgeneralizations, they do not show preemption at a verb-specific level, instead showing weak but non-zero evidence of abstract preemption. Combined with results from analyzing the LMs' training dynamics, we find that LMs treat competing structures as indirect positive---as opposed to negative---evidence in the verb-specific condition. Insofar as preemption is the more plausible route to avoiding overgeneralizations in humans, our results point the need for there to be sensitivities to indirect negative evidence in neural network learners, and suggest new human experiments to test abstract preemption.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how learners (and language models) avoid grammatical overgeneralizations like using verbs in incorrect constructions without receiving explicit negative feedback.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanisms by which learners infer that certain verb–construction combinations are ungrammatical, despite the rarity of direct corrections in natural language input. Specifically, the paper aims to adjudicate between two constructionist accounts—preemption and entrenchment—as explanations for avoiding overgeneralizations, and to test whether current language models use analogous mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors train language models on child–caregiver conversation data under controlled conditions where they systematically remove different types of evidence from the training corpus. In some conditions, they remove preemptive evidence (near-synonymous alternative constructions that would block overgeneralizations, such as `she made him laugh`), and in others, they remove non-preemptive but grammatical uses (e.g., simple intransitive uses like `He laughed`). They then examine the models’ tendencies to overgeneralize verbs into unattested constructions and analyze training dynamics to see whether models treat competing constructions as negative or positive evidence, at both verb-specific and abstract levels.
AI.result: The language models generally avoid producing overgeneralized forms, but they do not show strong verb-specific preemption effects—i.e., exposure to a particular competing construction with a specific verb does not robustly block the ungrammatical overgeneralization for that same verb. Instead, there is weak but detectable evidence of abstract preemption, meaning that the models are somewhat sensitive to competition between constructions at a more general level. Analysis of training dynamics reveals that, in verb-specific contexts, models interpret competing structures more as additional positive evidence rather than as indirect negative evidence against a given overgeneralization.
AI.conclusion: The findings indicate that current neural language models do not implement verb-specific preemption in a human-like way and lack sensitivity to indirect negative evidence that would block overgeneralizations at the lexical level. Since preemption is viewed as a plausible mechanism for how human learners avoid such errors, the results highlight a gap between human and model learning and imply that neural networks may need mechanisms for interpreting competing constructions as indirect negative evidence. The paper also motivates new psycholinguistic experiments to probe whether and how human learners rely on more abstract forms of preemption.

title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence
summary: Multi-agent AI systems improve inference by spawning agents and synthesizing reports. But another agent is not another observation: apparently independent reports may descend from the same evidence, and genuinely independent evidence can produce nearly identical reports. We formalize this as an epistemic Sybil problem. A report Z is an epistemic Sybil extension relative to reports R when I(Theta; Z | R) = 0. No report-only aggregator can generally distinguish replication from independent corroboration: identical reports can warrant different posteriors under unobserved ancestry. A Gaussian shared-root model shows common ancestry does not imply complete redundancy. Repeated extraction adds information toward a source-level ceiling, and correlated extraction errors, which a shared base model can induce among independent agents, lower that ceiling further. We test these predictions with more than 20,000 controlled LLM-agent report and extraction calls on synthetic evidentiary documents. Holding one evidence root fixed while report multiplicity rises from 1 to 32 collapses naive posterior coverage from 0.940 to 0.263. Holding report count fixed while evidence-root multiplicity rises from 1 to 16 closes the gap, and the aggregators are statistically indistinguishable at k = 16. The agent's replicate extraction errors are correlated (gamma_cal = 0.719, estimated out of sample), and a correlated-extraction aggregator restores calibration accordingly. A controlled manipulation isolates representation similarity from evidential ancestry. It changes a report-space deduplication mechanism's mean inferred cluster count by 1.425 (95% CI [1.363, 1.485]), whereas a fourfold change in true ancestry changes it by only 0.040 ([-0.045, 0.120]). Collective inference should therefore track evidential ancestry and dependence, not agent or report multiplicity or similarity.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how multi-agent AI systems can be systematically miscalibrated when they treat multiple reports as independent evidence, and formalizes this as an epistemic Sybil problem.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent and tool-using AI systems often try to improve inference by spawning multiple agents or asking for multiple reports, then aggregating them as if each report were an independent piece of evidence. However, reports may share hidden evidential ancestry (e.g., same source document or same base model), so counting them as independent can cause overconfidence. There is little formal understanding of this “epistemic Sybil” issue in AI collectives: when are multiple reports real corroboration versus mere replication?
AI.method: The paper formalizes the epistemic Sybil problem using information theory, defining an epistemic Sybil extension as a report Z that adds no additional information about the hypothesis Θ given existing reports R (I(Θ; Z | R) = 0). It uses a Gaussian shared-root model to analytically study how shared evidential ancestry affects information gain and redundancy. Then it runs large-scale controlled experiments (20,000+ LLM calls) on synthetic evidentiary documents with LLM agents that extract and report information, varying (a) the number of reports from a fixed evidence root, and (b) the number of independent evidence roots for a fixed number of reports. It also estimates correlation in extraction errors and tests an aggregator that accounts for these correlations. Finally, it manipulates representation similarity independently from evidential ancestry to evaluate report-space deduplication methods.
AI.result: Theoretically, the Gaussian shared-root model shows that common ancestry does not make reports fully redundant: repeated extractions add information but approach a ceiling determined at the source level, and correlated extraction errors (e.g., induced by a shared base model) lower this ceiling. Empirically, when the number of reports increases from 1 to 32 while holding one evidence root fixed, naive aggregation treating reports as independent causes posterior coverage to drop drastically from 0.940 to 0.263 (severe overconfidence). When the number of true evidence roots increases from 1 to 16 while keeping the number of reports fixed, the coverage gap closes, and the behavior of aggregators becomes statistically indistinguishable by k = 16. The study finds strong correlation in replicate extraction errors (γ_cal = 0.719 out of sample), and an aggregator that explicitly models correlated extraction restores calibration. A separate experiment shows that a clustering-based deduplication mechanism is far more sensitive to representational similarity than to true ancestry: changing representation similarity shifts inferred cluster counts by about 1.425 on average, whereas a fourfold change in true ancestry shifts them by only about 0.040, indicating that similarity-based deduplication is misaligned with evidential structure.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent AI systems cannot safely infer evidential independence from agent count, report multiplicity, or report similarity alone. The epistemic Sybil problem means that multiple apparently independent reports may in fact be redundant, while genuinely independent evidence may look similar. Effective collective inference should explicitly track evidential ancestry and dependence, model correlated errors (e.g., from shared base models), and avoid naive or purely similarity-based aggregation that double-counts shared evidence and yields miscalibrated, overconfident posteriors.

title: How Do Prompt Variations Affect Energy Consumption in On-Device LLMs?
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference; camera-ready version
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed on mobile devices, making energy efficiency a key deployment constraint, yet the energy impact of prompt design remains underexplored. This paper aims to understand how two prompt properties, cognitive load and phrasing pattern, shape the energy behavior of on-device LLM inference. We conduct a broad empirical study covering prompt properties, datasets, models, and devices, with phase-level profiling that separates prefill and decode energy. We find that cognitive load primarily affects the energy cost per token, while phrasing pattern affects energy largely through token usage. Our energy-quality analysis further shows that prompt design reshapes the attainable frontier differently across models, highlighting the need for model-aware prompt design in energy-efficient on-device LLM inference. Code, datasets, and scripts are available at https://amai-gsu.github.io/PromptProperty/.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how prompt design (cognitive load and phrasing pattern) affects energy consumption of on-device LLM inference, showing distinct impacts on per-token energy and token count, and arguing for model-aware, energy-conscious prompt design.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly run directly on mobile and edge devices, energy efficiency becomes a crucial constraint. While model architectures and system optimizations have been studied, the impact of prompt design on energy use is largely unknown. Understanding how different prompt properties influence energy consumption can provide a low-cost lever for improving energy efficiency without changing models or hardware.
AI.method: The authors perform a broad empirical study across multiple prompts, datasets, LLMs, and mobile devices. They focus on two prompt properties: cognitive load and phrasing pattern. Using phase-level profiling, they decompose energy usage into prefill and decode stages of LLM inference. They then analyze how these prompt properties affect energy per token, the total number of tokens generated, and the resulting quality–energy trade-offs for different models.
AI.result: The study finds that higher cognitive load mainly changes the energy cost per token (i.e., how much energy each token requires during inference), whereas different phrasing patterns influence energy mostly by altering how many tokens are processed or generated. The experiments show that these effects are not uniform across models: the same prompt adjustments can shift the energy–quality frontier differently depending on the LLM, revealing heterogeneous model sensitivities to prompt design.
AI.conclusion: Prompt design is a significant and nuanced factor in the energy behavior of on-device LLM inference. Cognitive load and phrasing pattern influence energy through distinct mechanisms, and their impact varies across models. Therefore, energy-efficient deployment on mobile devices should incorporate model-aware prompt design, treating prompts as an optimization dimension alongside model and system choices. The authors provide code, datasets, and scripts to support further research and practical adoption.

title: The Ceiling Is in the Channel: Auditing Learner Gaps and Measurement Frontiers in Clinical Prediction
summary: Clinical prediction can saturate for two different reasons: a fitted learner may fail to extract available information, or the recorded variables may impose a population frontier. We separate these quantities through the \emph{learner gap} and the \emph{measurement-channel ceiling}. Optimal balanced accuracy is characterized by total-variation separation, yielding architecture invariance, a sharp partial-identification result under replacement contamination, a cross-fitted ceiling estimator, and exact conditions for multimodal decision improvement. We add two finite-sample diagnostics, namely a label-permutation optimism floor and an underfit curve, and validate the audit on three real cohorts: UCI readmission ($n=99{,}343$), BRFSS diabetes ($n=253{,}680$), and NHANES HbA1c ($n=10{,}219$). Well-tuned gradient boosting nearly reaches the estimated frontier in UCI and BRFSS, whereas deliberately or practically deficient learners retain large gaps. NHANES yields a null difference between questionnaire and measured marginal frontiers but a significant joint complementarity gain, refining the simplistic claim that an objective modality must dominate. Across all cohorts, modest AUROC gains coexist with substantially larger Bayes decision-flip rates, and several architectures estimate similar frontiers while their achieved balanced accuracy differs sharply. A PRISMA-guided synthesis of 104 clinical tasks then shows that the same channel-level regularities recur across more than 18 disease categories: a broad but non-universal structured-clinical region, diminishing same-channel gains across model families, and higher performance when measurement channels change. The framework converts saturation from an empirical observation into an auditable decision: improve the learner when headroom remains; improve measurement when it does not.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to distinguish whether limits in clinical prediction performance are due to model inadequacy or inherent information limits in the available data, and provides theoretical tools, estimators, and diagnostics to audit this “saturation.”
AI.motivation: In clinical prediction, performance often appears to plateau (“saturate”), but it is unclear whether this is because models are not powerful or well-tuned enough, or because the recorded clinical variables simply do not contain more predictive information. This distinction is crucial for deciding whether to invest effort in better algorithms or in collecting better measurements. Existing practice lacks a principled, quantitative way to separate these two sources of limitation and to characterize how close a given learner is to the best-possible performance allowed by the measurement process.
AI.method: The authors formalize two key quantities: the learner gap (the distance between a model’s performance and the best possible performance given the same variables) and the measurement-channel ceiling (the population-level performance frontier imposed by the recorded variables). Using total-variation separation, they characterize optimal balanced accuracy in an architecture-invariant way. They derive a partial-identification result under label contamination, construct a cross-fitted estimator of the ceiling, and specify exact conditions for when multimodal data can improve decisions. They also propose two finite-sample diagnostics: a label-permutation optimism floor (to quantify overfitting/optimism) and an underfit curve (to detect under-usage of available information). The framework is then validated empirically on three clinical cohorts and via a PRISMA-guided synthesis of 104 clinical prediction tasks.
AI.result: On three real datasets—UCI readmission, BRFSS diabetes, and NHANES HbA1c—the framework shows that well-tuned gradient boosting nearly attains the estimated measurement-channel ceiling in two cohorts, indicating little remaining headroom for algorithmic gains, while intentionally or practically weaker models exhibit sizable learner gaps. In NHANES, questionnaire and biomarker channels have similar marginal frontiers, but combining them yields a significant joint improvement, contradicting the idea that an “objective” modality must always dominate. Across datasets, small AUROC improvements correspond to much larger Bayes decision-flip rates, and different architectures can estimate similar frontiers yet differ sharply in achieved balanced accuracy. The broader meta-analysis of 104 clinical tasks reveals recurring patterns: a common but not universal region where structured clinical data suffice, diminishing returns within a measurement channel across model classes, and larger gains primarily when measurement channels change rather than models alone.
AI.conclusion: The paper turns the vague notion of performance saturation in clinical prediction into a quantitatively auditable concept. By separating model inadequacy (learner gap) from inherent data limitations (measurement-channel ceiling), and providing estimators and diagnostics grounded in total-variation separation, it offers a principled way to decide whether to focus on better learning algorithms or on better measurements. Empirical studies and a large task-level synthesis demonstrate that many clinical prediction problems are limited more by measurement channels than by model architecture, and that meaningful improvements often require new or complementary data rather than just more sophisticated learners.

title: TalkFa: A Unified Benchmark for Farsi Dialogue Generation and Understanding
summary: Farsi, spoken by more than 120 million people, lacks a comprehensive benchmark for dialogue generation and understanding. We introduce TALKFA, a unified benchmark comprising three complementary datasets: (1) WIKI-FADIAL, 4.2K Wikipedia-grounded dialogues for knowledge-grounded generation; (2) DAILYDIALOG-FA, 6.6K dialogues annotated for dialogue acts and emotions; and (3) PLAYDIAL-FA, 2.1K theatrical dialogues with sentiment labels. While LLMs assist data construction, every dialogue undergoes multi-stage review and revision by native Farsi speakers, and only the final human-approved dialogues are released. Experiments with six LLAMA and MISTRAL models show that LoRA substantially improves dialogue generation while requiring only 25-50% of the training data to recover over 90% of the final performance gains. Across classification tasks, FABERT achieves the best dialogue-act performance, LORA-MISTRAL-7B performs best on emotion recognition, and MISTRAL-24B achieves the highest sentiment score. Human evaluation and independent external validation demonstrate the reliability of the benchmark, while comparisons with GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge reveal that automatic metrics substantially overestimate dialogue quality. Zero-shot evaluation with frontier LLMs further shows that TalkFa remains a challenging benchmark. We will release all datasets, annotation guidelines, code, and checkpoints.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TALKFA, the first comprehensive Farsi benchmark for dialogue generation and understanding, built from three curated dialogue datasets and evaluated with multiple LLMs and adaptation methods.
AI.motivation: Farsi, despite having over 120 million speakers, lacks a standardized, large-scale benchmark for dialogue tasks. This gap hinders progress in Farsi conversational AI, limits fair comparison of models, and prevents systematic study of dialogue generation, understanding, and evaluation in this language.
AI.method: The authors construct TALKFA, a unified benchmark consisting of three datasets: (1) WIKI-FADIAL with 4.2K Wikipedia-grounded dialogues for knowledge-grounded generation; (2) DAILYDIALOG-FA with 6.6K dialogues translated/adapted and annotated for dialogue acts and emotions; and (3) PLAYDIAL-FA with 2.1K theatrical dialogues labeled with sentiment. LLMs are used to help with initial data construction, followed by multi-stage human review, correction, and approval by native Farsi speakers. They then train and evaluate several LLAMA and MISTRAL models using LoRA-based fine-tuning for generation and FABERT / other models for classification tasks, comparing different amounts of training data. Evaluation includes automatic metrics, human evaluation, external validation, and comparison against GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge, as well as zero-shot tests with frontier LLMs.
AI.result: LoRA adaptation substantially improves dialogue generation models and can recover over 90% of the achievable performance gains using only 25–50% of the training data. For classification tasks, FABERT yields the best dialogue-act classification performance, LORA-MISTRAL-7B achieves the best emotion recognition results, and MISTRAL-24B reaches the highest sentiment classification scores. Human and external evaluations confirm the benchmark’s reliability, while analysis with GPT-4.1 as an LLM judge shows that standard automatic metrics significantly overestimate dialogue quality. Zero-shot evaluation of strong frontier LLMs indicates that TALKFA remains difficult and not yet saturated.
AI.conclusion: TALKFA provides the first comprehensive, human-vetted Farsi dialogue benchmark, enabling systematic evaluation of both generation and understanding tasks across multiple domains and label types. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) is highly effective for Farsi dialogue generation, even with reduced data. Current automatic metrics are insufficient proxies for human judgments, especially in Farsi dialogue, and frontier LLMs still struggle on TALKFA, leaving substantial headroom for future research. The planned release of data, guidelines, code, and checkpoints is intended to facilitate further progress in Farsi conversational AI.

title: Looped Transformers under the Jacobian Lens: Does the Global Workspace Survive Recurrence?
summary: Recent work identifies a mid-depth band of verbalisable, causally potent representations in a standard feedforward transformer --- a functional analogue of a global workspace.
