Whether the same workspace functionality emerges when depth is implemented through recurrence rather than a stack of distinct layers remains unknown. Looped and depth-recurrent transformers provide a direct test of this question because they reuse the same weights across depth. We extend the Jacobian lens to iterated architectures using a virtual-unrolling adapter. We apply the full workspace suite --- lens fitting, readout, and eleven causal experiment families --- to Ouro-2.6B (48 layers looped 4 times, deeply supervised) and Huginn-0125 (a 4-layer core recurred 16 times, trained for latent reasoning), using Qwen3.6-27B (64 untied layers) as the standard baseline. We find that a workspace forms in the iterated part of each architecture, but that recurrence changes how it can be accessed. Ouro reconstructs workspace content in every loop, and linear transport cannot carry that content across loop boundaries; writes and ablations must therefore span every remaining loop. Huginn carries content forward across all sixteen recurrences, while reads, writes, and ablations act only within a sliding window of roughly two recurrences. Whether newly injected content can be verbalised tracks explicit per-iteration supervision; whether existing content can be steered does not.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether a "global workspace"-like band of causal, interpretable features also appears in recurrent/looped transformers, and how its accessibility differs from standard deep transformers.
AI.motivation: Previous work found a mid-layer band in standard feedforward transformers that behaves like a global workspace: its features are verbalizable and causally influence behavior. It was unknown whether similar structures arise when model depth comes from recurrence (weight sharing across depth) instead of many distinct layers. This matters for understanding mechanistic interpretability and the design of efficient, recurrent transformer architectures.
AI.method: The authors adapt the Jacobian lens (which analyzes how internal representations map to outputs) to recurrent/iterated architectures via a virtual-unrolling adapter that treats recurrences as unfolded layers. They then apply a full "workspace" analysis suite—representation lens fitting, linear readout, and eleven families of causal interventions (reads, writes, ablations, steering)—to two recurrent-style models: Ouro-2.6B (48 layers looped 4 times with deep supervision) and Huginn-0125 (4-layer core recurred 16 times for latent reasoning). They compare both against a standard non-recurrent baseline, Qwen3.6-27B, which has 64 untied layers.
AI.result: In both recurrent models, a workspace-like band of representations emerges within the iterated portion. However, its dynamics and accessibility differ. In Ouro-2.6B, workspace-like content is reconstructed in each loop, and linear transformations cannot transport that content across loop boundaries; thus effective causal interventions (writes/ablations) must cover all remaining loops. In Huginn-0125, workspace content is propagated forward across all 16 recurrences, but causal access (reads, writes, ablations) is limited to a sliding window of about two recurrences. The ability for newly injected content to be verbalized depends on explicit per-iteration supervision, whereas the ability to steer pre-existing content does not.
AI.conclusion: Global-workspace-like structure is not unique to deep, untied-layer transformers: it also appears in recurrent/looped transformers. However, recurrence changes how the workspace operates and how interventions can access it. In one architecture (Ouro) the workspace is repeatedly re-instantiated each loop; in the other (Huginn) it is carried across recurrences but only locally editable. Supervision per recurrence influences how easily new information injected into the workspace becomes verbalizable, but not how steerable existing representations are. This refines our understanding of workspace formation and control in different transformer designs and has implications for mechanistic interpretability and architecture choices.

title: AVERT: Audio-Verified Adjudication for Spoken Dialogue State Tracking
summary: Spoken dialogue state tracking recovers slot-value pairs from speech, where ASR errors concentrate in entity values and persist across turns, making it both a generation and an editing problem. A strong per-turn text editor corrects much of this but, operating on the transcript alone, leaves three recoverable errors: a value predicted inconsistently across turns, an omitted slot, and a value the audio does not support. We present AVERT, which scores each candidate value by combining cross-turn agreement with a trained audio-conditioned verifier and resolves the three error types with three operators, vote, add, and swap, each restricted to the slots where its error is common. On SpokenWOZ, a base speech-LLM reaches 33.04 JGA, a text editor 38.34, and AVERT 40.13, without retraining either. This is in the range of a 1B end-to-end system that consumes the full spoken history (39.32), though AVERT uses two 1B decoders rather than one. The audio verifier contributes a statistically significant gain, and restricting each operator to a selected slot subset matters: removing it lets unrestricted voting overwrite correct categorical values and fall below the editor.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AVERT, a post-editing framework for spoken dialogue state tracking that combines cross-turn text consistency and audio-based verification to fix residual errors left by a strong text editor, achieving state-of-the-art-like performance without retraining base models.
AI.motivation: In spoken dialogue state tracking, automatic speech recognition (ASR) errors often corrupt entity values and persist across multiple dialogue turns. While per-turn text editors can correct many mistakes, they still leave systematic, recoverable errors: inconsistent values across turns, omitted slots, and values unsupported by audio. There is a need for a lightweight method that can leverage both dialogue history and audio to further improve accuracy without expensive end-to-end retraining.
AI.method: The authors propose AVERT, a framework that operates on candidate slot-value pairs produced by an existing speech-LLM plus text editor. AVERT assigns a score to each candidate value using two signals: (1) cross-turn agreement across the dialogue history, and (2) an audio-conditioned verifier that checks whether the value is supported by the speech signal. Based on these scores, AVERT applies three specialized operators to targeted slot subsets: (a) vote, to enforce consistent values across turns; (b) add, to fill in omitted slots; and (c) swap, to replace values not supported by audio. The operators are restricted to slots where each error type is common, to avoid harming correct predictions.
AI.result: On the SpokenWOZ benchmark, a base speech-LLM achieves 33.04 joint goal accuracy (JGA). Adding a per-turn text editor improves JGA to 38.34. Applying AVERT on top further increases JGA to 40.13, without retraining the base speech-LLM or the text editor. This performance is comparable to a 1B-parameter end-to-end system that processes the full spoken history (39.32 JGA), though AVERT uses two 1B decoders (for generation and verification). Ablation studies show that the audio verifier provides a statistically significant improvement and that restricting operators to selected slot subsets is crucial; removing this restriction allows overly aggressive voting that degrades performance below the text editor baseline.
AI.conclusion: AVERT is an effective, modular post-editing layer for spoken dialogue state tracking that leverages cross-turn consistency and audio-conditioned verification to correct residual ASR-induced and modeling errors. It significantly improves over a strong text-only editor and matches or surpasses larger end-to-end baselines, all without retraining the underlying models. Careful design of slot-specific operators and use of audio verification are key to its gains.

title: Post-Training Ternarization of Qwen3-4B Capability, Effective Bit Budget, Storage Compression, and Deployment
comment: Weight-only post-training ternarization of a 4B-parameter instruction-tuned language model. Activation quantization and end-to-end generation throughput are outside the scope of the primary evaluation
summary:
Ultra-low-bit language models can reduce storage and memory bandwidth, but a nominal "1.58-bit" label does not fully describe the stored representation, retained capability, or runtime behavior.
  We study an end-to-end post-training conversion of Qwen, an instruction-tuned 4B-parameter model, using KOTMS rotation, E2M-ATQ ternarization, and GPTQ-style error compensation from TWLA. The experiment is weight-only: activations remain at 16-bit precision, so ILA-AMP is omitted. We evaluate effective bit accounting, task capability retention, perplexity, calibration sensitivity, checkpoint composition, and deployment behavior.
  The final conversion uses 1.641 effective bits per weight for quantized linear weights, with 81.62% of model parameters targeted. Across ten scored capability comparisons, accuracy falls from 64.5% to 54.7%. Degradation is uneven: BoolQ retains 84.6% chance-corrected teacher performance, while ARC-Challenge retains 43.8%. Perplexity rises from 13.639 to 18.748 on WikiText-2, 24.700 to 31.992 on PTB, and 19.831 to 28.966 on C4.
  A subsequent packing run preserves the ternary planes and scales, reducing reported model size from 8.29 GiB to 3.96 GiB with essentially unchanged perplexity. A separate third-party packing attempt was lossy and is excluded from the primary artifact claim. The packed artifact has not been benchmarked end-to-end for task accuracy or generation throughput. A preliminary Triton GEMV microbenchmark is 4.6x slower than FP16 cuBLAS on one tested shape. We therefore do not claim that compression alone yields faster inference.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates an end-to-end pipeline to convert a 4B-parameter Qwen instruction-tuned model to an ultra-low-bit, mostly ternary, weight-only quantized model, carefully accounting for effective bits, capability loss, and deployment behavior.
AI.motivation: Ultra-low-bit (around 1–2 bit) language models are attractive for lowering storage and memory bandwidth, but common bit labels (e.g., “1.58-bit”) don’t fully capture what is actually stored, how much capability is retained, or how the model behaves at runtime. The authors aim to systematically study a concrete 1–2 bit conversion of a real instruction-tuned LLM, filling the gap between nominal bit counts and actual effective compression, accuracy, perplexity, and deployment tradeoffs.
AI.method: They start from an instruction-tuned 4B-parameter Qwen model and apply a post-training, weight-only quantization pipeline: (1) KOTMS rotation to improve quantization readiness, (2) E2M-ATQ ternarization to map weights to a ternary set with associated scales, and (3) GPTQ-style error compensation from TWLA to reduce quantization error. Activations remain at 16-bit precision (no ILA-AMP). They then analyze effective bits per weight, the fraction of parameters quantized, task accuracy on multiple benchmarks, perplexity on several corpora, calibration sensitivity, checkpoint composition, and deployment behavior. Finally, they perform a packing step to compress ternary planes and scales in storage and run Triton GEMV microbenchmarks for performance comparison with FP16 cuBLAS.
AI.result: The final quantized model uses 1.641 effective bits per weight for quantized linear layers, with 81.62% of parameters converted. Aggregate accuracy across ten tasks drops from 64.5% to 54.7%, with uneven degradation: BoolQ retains 84.6% of the teacher’s chance-corrected performance, while ARC-Challenge retains 43.8%. Perplexity increases notably: from 13.639 to 18.748 on WikiText-2, 24.700 to 31.992 on PTB, and 19.831 to 28.966 on C4. After packing, model disk size shrinks from 8.29 GiB to 3.96 GiB with essentially unchanged perplexity. A third-party packing attempt was lossy and excluded. A Triton GEMV microbenchmark shows the low-bit implementation is 4.6× slower than FP16 cuBLAS on one tested configuration.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that a roughly 1.6-bit, weight-only quantization of a 4B Qwen model can more than halve storage with moderate but non-uniform accuracy and perplexity degradation. However, the benefits are currently limited to compression: the packed model has not been fully benchmarked for task accuracy or end-to-end speed, and early microbenchmarks indicate slower inference than FP16 on GPU. The nominal bit label alone is insufficient; detailed accounting of effective bits, retained capability, and actual runtime behavior is essential when evaluating ultra-low-bit LLMs.

title: Interpretable Symptom Vectors for Depression in a Large Language Model
summary: Patients with depression present with diverse symptom profiles, yet clinical practice routinely reduces this variation to a single severity score. Large language models (LLMs) can potentially capture various symptoms and their severity from patient speech. However, how depressive symptoms are represented inside LLMs remains poorly understood, limiting clinical trust. To examine whether internal model activations match clinician judgment, we analyzed the residual stream of Gemma-3-27B-PT using mechanistic interpretability techniques. Recording activations across symptom descriptions drawn from validated clinical instruments, we found that symptom groups geometrically separated the most at layer 21 across multiple distance metrics. Using Semantic Projection, we then projected held-out naturalistic text onto Symptom Vectors constructed from these instruments. The resulting per-symptom coefficients preserved clinician-annotated rank ordering across mood, somatic, and suicidality axes. Furthermore, a single depression vector in Layer 21 separates held-out depressive from non-depressive text (AUC = 0.789), which can be used as an emotional valence gate that restricts symptom projection to depressive speech. These results reveal a decorrelated, clinician-aligned symptom signal readable directly from internal activations, offering a mechanistic foundation for interpretable depression-assessment tools.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how depressive symptoms are internally represented in a large language model and whether these align with clinician assessments.
AI.motivation: In clinical practice, depression severity is often collapsed into a single score despite heterogeneous symptom profiles. There is interest in using LLMs to extract richer, symptom-level information from language, but a lack of understanding of how depressive features are internally encoded in these models undermines clinical trust and interpretability.
AI.method: The authors analyze the residual stream activations of Gemma-3-27B-PT using mechanistic interpretability tools. They feed the model standardized depressive symptom descriptions from validated clinical instruments, quantify geometric separation among symptom groups across layers, and identify the layer with maximal separation. They then use Semantic Projection to construct Symptom Vectors from these instruments and project held-out naturalistic patient-like text onto these vectors, comparing the resulting per-symptom coefficients with clinician annotations. They also derive a single "depression vector" in the most informative layer and test its ability to discriminate depressive from non-depressive text.
AI.result: Symptom groups are most geometrically separable at layer 21 across multiple distance metrics. Projections of held-out naturalistic text onto the Symptom Vectors recover clinician-annotated rank ordering of symptom severity across mood, somatic, and suicidality dimensions. A single depression vector at layer 21 effectively separates depressive from non-depressive text with an AUC of 0.789, and can function as a valence gate to limit further symptom readout to text likely to be depressive in nature.
AI.conclusion: Depressive symptom information is decorrelated and organized in a way that aligns with clinical constructs inside the LLM, especially at a specific middle layer. This enables direct, interpretable readout of symptom-level signals from internal activations and offers a mechanistic basis for building more transparent, clinically aligned depression assessment tools from LLMs.

title: Benchmarking Language Models for Statistical Problem Formulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as assistants for statistical and data science work, yet existing evaluations largely assume the analysis target is already specified. In practice, users arrive with informal goals and heterogeneous data, leaving the model to decide what statistical task is implied and which data are relevant. We first formalize this upstream step as Statistical Problem Formulation and decompose it into two subtasks: (1) Statistical Problem Classification and (2) Variable Identification & Role Assignment. We then introduce StatFormBench, a benchmark built from five cross-domain statistics textbooks and a data science case library, covering diverse problem types, data representations, and scenario styles. It contains 1,013 samples spanning 20 coarse-grained and 85 fine-grained statistical problem categories. Across 14 open- and closed-source LLMs, the best zero-shot models reach only 72.0 fine-grained classification accuracy and 63.2 variable set overlap. No model performs consistently best across the two subtasks, while enhanced prompting strategies yield only limited or inconsistent gains. We release the benchmark data on Hugging Face at https://huggingface.co/datasets/THU-CongLab/StatFormBench and the evaluation code on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-CongLab/StatFormBench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces StatFormBench, a benchmark for evaluating how well large language models can formulate statistical problems from informal user goals and heterogeneous data.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluations in statistics and data science mostly assume that the statistical task is already clearly specified. However, real users often come with vague goals and mixed data, leaving an untested but crucial step where the model must infer the appropriate statistical problem and determine which variables and data are relevant. This gap motivates a systematic study and benchmark of LLMs’ ability to perform this upstream problem formulation stage.
AI.method: The authors formalize the upstream step as Statistical Problem Formulation, decomposed into two subtasks: (1) Statistical Problem Classification, where the model must identify the type of statistical analysis implied; and (2) Variable Identification & Role Assignment, where the model must pick out relevant variables and assign roles (e.g., predictor, outcome). They construct StatFormBench from five cross-domain statistics textbooks and a data science case library, yielding 1,013 samples labeled into 20 coarse-grained and 85 fine-grained problem categories, with varied data formats and scenario styles. They then evaluate 14 open- and closed-source LLMs in zero-shot settings, and also test enhanced prompting strategies.
AI.result: On StatFormBench, the best zero-shot LLMs achieve only 72.0% accuracy on fine-grained statistical problem classification and 63.2% variable set overlap for the variable identification task. No single model dominates across both subtasks, and more elaborate prompting strategies provide only modest or inconsistent performance improvements.
AI.conclusion: LLMs currently struggle with the high-level, upstream step of statistical problem formulation when faced with informal user goals and heterogeneous data. StatFormBench exposes these limitations, showing that even strong models perform far from perfectly and that simple prompting tweaks are insufficient to close the gap. The benchmark and accompanying code are released to facilitate further research on improving LLMs’ capabilities in this critical aspect of data science assistance.

title: Candidate Generation and Definition-Guided Verification for Sentence-Level Depression Symptom Recognition
summary: Sentence-level recognition of depression symptoms is challenging because similar expressions can differ in symptom relevance, and language-model inference is insufficiently grounded in diagnostic definitions. This study proposes a two-stage framework separating symptom-candidate generation from definition-grounded verification. A contrastively fine-tuned sentence encoder generates a symptom candidate per sentence, and a fine-tuned language model verifies whether the candidate is present or absent using the sentence, its context, and a candidate-specific diagnostic definition, checking its judgment against that definition before answering. Evaluated against encoder, inference-based, medical, and general LLM baselines and a matched single-stage supervised classifier, the proposed pipeline attains the best accuracy and F1 scores of all methods, with rationales matching expert-authored annotations. A preliminary clinical audit indicates moderate alignment with diagnostic definitions, with explanation quality strongly dependent on prediction correctness. The results support decomposing symptom recognition into candidate generation and definition-grounded verification, though performance remains limited for rare categories.

AI.tldr: Two-stage NLP framework for sentence-level depression symptom recognition using candidate generation and definition-grounded verification, outperforming baselines but still struggling with rare symptoms.
AI.motivation: Sentence-level detection of depression symptoms is hard because similar sentences can differ in diagnostic relevance and standard language models are not explicitly grounded in formal diagnostic criteria. There is a need for methods that tie model decisions more tightly to clinical definitions while improving accuracy and interpretability over existing encoder- or inference-based approaches.
AI.method: The authors design a two-stage pipeline. First, a sentence encoder, contrastively fine-tuned on symptom labels, outputs a most likely symptom candidate for each sentence. Second, a fine-tuned language model receives the sentence, its surrounding context, the candidate label, and a candidate-specific diagnostic definition. It then decides whether the candidate symptom is present or absent, explicitly checking its reasoning against the definition before producing a final judgment and rationale. They compare this to various baselines, including encoder-only, direct LLM inference, medical and general LLMs, and a single-stage supervised classifier that has equivalent information but no decomposition.
AI.result: The proposed two-stage method yields the highest accuracy and F1 among all tested systems. Its generated rationales align well with expert annotations, and a preliminary clinical audit finds moderate consistency with formal diagnostic definitions. However, explanation quality degrades when predictions are incorrect, and performance is still weak for infrequent symptom categories.
AI.conclusion: Decomposing depression symptom recognition into (1) encoder-based candidate generation and (2) definition-grounded LLM verification is an effective strategy, improving both predictive performance and interpretability over strong baselines. Nevertheless, recognizing rare symptom categories remains a key limitation and area for future work.

title: When Agents Implement Systems: A Case Study in Defects, Detection, and Evaluation Rigor
summary: As LLM coding agents increasingly perform end-to-end engineering work, we lack empirical characterization of how they behave on systems-level requirements: schema design, async orchestration, configuration correctness, and retrieval-filtering trade-offs. We present a case study of one such agent implementing a multi-component data system against a detailed pre-existing specification. Storage technologies, schema, entity-resolution algorithm, and retrieval-filtering strategy were fixed in advance; the agent autonomy was in the implementation, in diagnosing and fixing defects it introduced, and in interaction-design choices left open. Over a single session, we catalog five such defects, categorized by constraint violated and detection method. We further evaluate, on the public HotpotQA benchmark, the one retrieval trade-off specified in that architecture: restricting candidates to a graph-identified entity set before ranking versus unfiltered search. We substitute the benchmark gold evidence labels for entity identification, since we lacked LLM access to run that stage, and report standard recall rather than the benchmark own accuracy metrics. Across retrieval budgets from 1 to 10 and 100 questions against a pooled corpus of 2994 paragraphs, filtered recall reaches its ceiling by a budget of 3, expected once candidates are restricted to the gold paragraphs themselves, while unfiltered search recovers all required evidence only 69 percent of the time even at a budget of 10, a gap that holds at every budget tested, with sign test p less than 0.0001. We close with a discussion of where the agent autonomy succeeded versus required correction, including one instance where a claimed performance fix was never re-measured on the regression that motivated it.

AI.tldr: The paper is a case study analyzing how an LLM-based coding agent behaves when implementing a multi-component data system, plus an empirical comparison of two retrieval strategies within that system.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents are starting to handle full engineering tasks, but we lack empirical understanding of their behavior on complex, systems-level requirements such as schema design, async orchestration, and retrieval configurations. The authors want to characterize typical defects and trade-offs in such settings.
AI.method: They run a single detailed case study where an LLM coding agent implements a multi-component data system from a fixed specification. The agent has autonomy only in concrete implementation details, debugging its own defects, and some interaction design decisions. They catalog five defects, classifying them by violated constraint and how they were detected. Separately, they empirically evaluate a specified retrieval trade-off using the HotpotQA benchmark: filtering candidate documents by a graph-derived entity set before ranking versus unfiltered search. Since they cannot run the entity-identification LLM, they substitute HotpotQA gold evidence labels as the entity filter and measure recall over 100 questions and budgets 1–10 across a 2994-paragraph corpus, using a sign test for significance.
AI.result: In the case study, they observe five concrete defects introduced by the agent and document their nature and detection. In the retrieval experiment, filtering candidates to the gold-identified paragraphs yields recall that saturates by a budget of 3, while unfiltered search only achieves 69% recall even at a budget of 10. The filtered approach outperforms unfiltered search at every budget tested, with the difference statistically significant (sign test p < 0.0001). They also identify at least one instance where the agent claimed a performance improvement but never re-measured on the original regression benchmark.
AI.conclusion: LLM coding agents can implement complex, specified data systems but still exhibit systematic defects, particularly around constraints and verification of performance claims. Structured evaluation reveals both where their autonomy is effective and where human correction or additional tooling is needed. Moreover, retrieval architectures that incorporate strong entity-based filtering can substantially improve evidence recall over naive unfiltered search in multi-hop QA settings.

title: Cite or Decline: A Strict Course-Grounded Chatbot for STEM Lecture Videos
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on EMNLP 2026, Industry Track
summary: Recorded lecture videos, often enhanced with search and summarization features, are a standard study resource. However, students cannot easily ask course specific questions or verify answers against an instructor's lecture. We report a semester-long deployment of VideoPoints platform with a retrieval-augmented chatbot that answers from course lecture materials and returns timestamped citations. The chatbot retrieves only from the active course, uses chapter summaries to guide transcript ranking, and returns clickable timestamped citations. Students used it for quick lookups and exam review. Across 833 messages, 70.5% included citations, none crossed a course boundary, and when no lecture evidence matched, the chatbot usually declined rather than answering. Among the users, citations were the most consistently useful feature, while practice-question generation was the strongest unmet request. We also evaluated the design on the real-world test split of EduVidQA, a public multimodal benchmark for lecture-video question answering. Our design improved correct-lecture retrieval by 6.3 percentage points over dense-only retrieval. Together, the results show that effective deployment depends on course isolation, supported citations, and alignment with students' study practices.

AI.tldr: This paper presents and evaluates a retrieval-augmented chatbot integrated into a lecture video platform, showing that course-isolated retrieval with timestamped citations effectively supports students’ study and review.
AI.motivation: Students frequently use recorded lecture videos but cannot easily ask course-specific questions or verify answers directly against the instructor’s lecture content. Existing video platforms offer search and summarization but lack interactive, grounded Q&A aligned with a particular course. The authors aim to support authentic study behaviors—like quick lookups and exam review—while ensuring reliability and preventing cross-course content contamination.
AI.method: The authors implemented the VideoPoints platform with a retrieval-augmented chatbot that: (1) restricts retrieval to the currently active course to ensure course isolation; (2) uses chapter-level summaries to guide ranking of lecture transcripts; and (3) returns answers with clickable timestamped citations into the videos. They deployed this system in a semester-long real course, logging 833 student messages, and analyzed usage patterns, citation rates, and refusal behaviors when evidence was missing. They also ran a benchmark evaluation on the real-world test split of EduVidQA, comparing their retrieval design against a dense-only retrieval baseline and measuring correct-lecture retrieval rates.
AI.result: In the classroom deployment, 70.5% of chatbot messages included timestamped citations, and no retrieved citation crossed course boundaries, indicating effective course isolation. When no supporting lecture evidence was found, the chatbot usually declined to answer, suggesting conservative behavior rather than hallucination. Students mainly used the chatbot for quick information lookups and exam review. User feedback highlighted timestamped citations as the consistently most useful feature, while automatic practice-question generation emerged as the main missing capability. In the EduVidQA benchmark evaluation, the proposed retrieval design improved correct-lecture retrieval by 6.3 percentage points over a dense-only retrieval baseline.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that successful deployment of lecture-video chatbots in real courses hinges on three factors: strict course isolation in retrieval, provision of clear and usable timestamped citations for transparency and verifiability, and alignment of capabilities with students’ study habits (e.g., quick lookups, exam review, practice questions). Their design choices demonstrably reduce cross-course contamination, support grounded answers, and improve lecture retrieval accuracy compared to dense-only approaches, suggesting a practical blueprint for integrating retrieval-augmented chatbots into educational video platforms.

title: ClaimReceipt: Verifying Evidence Sufficiency and Coverage in Agent Evaluations
comment: Submitted to Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development (NeurIPS 2026 workshop). 8 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables
summary: Agent evaluations face two distinct evidentiary questions: whether a reported claim is recomputable from retained evidence (sufficiency), and whether the retained records cover the committed experiment set (coverage). Generic logs and hash-linked transcripts answer neither reliably. We introduce ClaimReceipt, a claim-relative receipt specification and selective verifier that binds typed transaction evidence to a signed experiment manifest and returns PASS, INVALID, or INCONCLUSIVE per claim. We freeze the specification before implementation (SHA-256 18d109...b81). On 1,392 historical buyer--seller records, a CR-2 verifier reproduces all five manually labeled audit verdicts, exactly replays 600 deterministic and 792 post-generation records, makes every one of 13 declared field groups non-redundant under tested ablations, and returns the expected result on 11/11 semantic faults with 0/8 false positives. We then run a separate prospective CR-3 epoch: 30 assignments are committed before inference, terminal receipts are signed and chained, and private evidence is encrypted for an auditor. Complete evidence yields coverage and accounting PASS; withholding one terminal receipt returns INCONCLUSIVE_COVERAGE, while withholding all private openings preserves coverage and protocol verification but makes economic claims inconclusive, exactly matching a preregistered prediction. Receipt instrumentation adds 0.021% of model-inference time and 9.9 KB per transaction. A specification-legibility probe indicates that our own frozen specification is not yet unambiguous to an independent reader. Claim verification therefore requires both claim-sufficient evidence and a committed universe against which omissions become visible.

AI.tldr: They propose ClaimReceipt, a verification framework that ties claims to precise experimental evidence, distinguishing between recomputability (sufficiency) and completeness of records (coverage), and empirically validate it on historical and prospective agent experiments.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches using generic logs or hash-linked transcripts cannot reliably show that (1) a specific reported claim can be recomputed from retained evidence, or (2) that the retained evidence actually covers all experiments that were supposedly run. This makes audits and trustworthy evaluation of agent behavior difficult, especially when multiple economic or experimental commitments are involved.
AI.method: They define a formal, claim-relative receipt specification "ClaimReceipt" that binds typed transaction evidence to a signed experiment manifest. A selective verifier then checks each claim and returns PASS, INVALID, or INCONCLUSIVE. They freeze the specification hash pre-implementation, implement different verifier versions (CR-2 and CR-3), and evaluate them on 1,392 historical buyer–seller records plus a new prospective epoch of 30 precommitted assignments. They test replayability, redundancy of logged fields via ablations, detection of semantic faults, behavior under partially withheld evidence, and overhead of receipt instrumentation. They also probe whether the frozen specification is legible and unambiguous to an independent reader.
AI.result: On the historical dataset, CR-2 matches all five manual audit labels, exactly replays 600 deterministic and 792 post-generation records, shows that each of 13 declared field groups is non-redundant, and detects 11/11 seeded semantic faults with no false positives. In the prospective CR-3 epoch, complete evidence leads to PASS for coverage and accounting; withholding one terminal receipt yields an inconclusive coverage verdict; withholding all private openings preserves coverage/protocol verification but makes economic claims inconclusive. These outcomes align with preregistered expectations. Overhead is low: about 0.021% of inference time and 9.9 KB additional data per transaction. The legibility probe reveals that the frozen specification is still not fully unambiguous to outside readers.
AI.conclusion: ClaimReceipt shows that reliable verification of agent claims needs both claim-sufficient evidence and a committed, signed experiment universe so that omissions are detectable. Their framework operationalizes this via typed, claim-relative receipts and selective verification, achieving accurate verdicts with minimal overhead. However, the specification still requires refinement to be fully clear to independent implementers, highlighting that formal legibility is itself a critical part of trustworthy verification systems.

title: Thinking effort aligns between humans and reasoning models in abductive reasoning
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures. To appear in Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: A major question in cognitive modeling concerns the behavioral alignment between large language models and humans across linguistic and non-linguistic tasks. Unlike standard LLMs, large reasoning models (LRMs) are optimized with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, encouraging correct solutions to reasoning tasks rather than preference-aligned responses. Recent work (de Varda et al., 2025) investigates the cost of thinking in humans and LRMs by comparing human reaction times with model reasoning traces across a range of reasoning tasks. We isolate this alignment by turning to abductive reasoning: unlike deductive tasks, its difficulty cannot be inferred from formal structure and offers no shortcuts a model could exploit to mimic effort without genuine search, providing firmer ground for empirical claims of shared effort. We find further evidence of alignment between LRM and human reasoning effort, as well as evidence that models and humans tend to make similar errors. Finally, we show that decoding methods that let models explore multiple reasoning paths increase alignment in reasoning cost between humans and LRMs across the three models tested.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how similarly large reasoning models (LRMs) and humans expend mental effort on abductive reasoning tasks, and how decoding strategies affect this alignment.
AI.motivation: To understand whether LRMs, which are optimized for correct reasoning via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, exhibit human-like patterns of cognitive effort and error on tasks where difficulty cannot be guessed from surface structure, addressing a key question in cognitive modeling about genuine vs. mimicked reasoning effort.
AI.method: Compare human reaction times with LRMs’ internal reasoning traces on abductive reasoning tasks whose difficulty is not predictable from formal structure. Analyze both effort (time/trace length) and error patterns, and systematically vary decoding methods to allow models to explore multiple reasoning paths, then measure how this affects alignment with human reasoning cost across three different models.
AI.result: The authors find that LRMs’ reasoning effort is aligned with humans’ on abductive tasks: items that take humans longer also induce longer or more intensive reasoning traces in LRMs. Moreover, LRMs and humans tend to make similar types of errors. Allowing models to explore multiple reasoning paths via modified decoding further increases the correlation between human reaction times and model reasoning cost across all three tested LRMs.
AI.conclusion: Abductive reasoning provides a robust testbed for assessing shared cognitive effort between humans and LRMs, since its difficulty cannot be gamed by exploiting formal shortcuts. The observed alignment of effort and errors suggests that LRMs’ optimization for verifiable reasoning yields human-like patterns of search rather than superficial mimicry. Additionally, decoding strategies that promote multi-path exploration enhance this human–model alignment in reasoning cost, with implications for both cognitive science and the design of future reasoning models.

title: HeadWiseKV: Budgeted Per-Head Cache Residency for Hybrid Long-Context Language Models
summary: Long-context inference retains a growing key--value (KV) cache during decoding, which consumes substantial GPU memory and can reduce generation throughput. This bottleneck remains in hybrid language models because their residual global-attention layers can dominate context-dependent cache demand. We study how to allocate this state under an aggregate KV-residency budget. We introduce HeadWiseKV, a training-free framework that compresses the residual global KV caches of hybrid language models while preserving their native local, recurrent, and linear paths. It assigns each physical KV head a static, multilevel history window, making cache demand predictable before serving. We formulate this allocation as a restricted operational rate--distortion problem and propose SeqCalib as the core policy-generation algorithm in HeadWiseKV. SeqCalib processes layers in execution order and conditions each decision on the lower-layer policy used at deployment, thereby accounting for interactions across depth. A grouped-cache runtime materializes the selected policy as actual per-head KV residency rather than a mask over a full cache. We evaluate downstream quality across four hybrid long-context models and study physical residency and serving behavior on Qwen3.6-27B. HeadWiseKV retains near-Full-KV RULER and LoCoMo quality across the evaluated models. In the fixed-model systems study, it reduces sampled peak device memory by 8.59\% at a 112K context length and extends the largest verified successful context from 114K to 161K.

AI.tldr: HeadWiseKV is a training-free framework that compresses KV caches in hybrid long-context language models via per-head static multilevel history windows, reducing memory while preserving quality.
AI.motivation: Long-context inference requires storing large and growing key–value (KV) caches for attention, which consumes substantial GPU memory and hurts throughput. Hybrid models with residual global-attention layers still suffer from high context-dependent KV memory, even if they use more efficient local or recurrent mechanisms elsewhere. There is a need for a principled way to allocate limited KV cache “residency” across attention heads under a fixed memory budget, without retraining models, while maintaining task quality.
AI.method: The authors propose HeadWiseKV, a training-free KV compression framework for hybrid long-context LMs. HeadWiseKV assigns each physical attention head a static multilevel history window that determines how far back in the sequence its KV cache can extend, making total cache usage predictable ahead of serving. They cast cache allocation under a global KV-residency budget as a restricted operational rate–distortion problem. To solve it, they develop SeqCalib, an algorithm that generates per-layer, per-head policies by processing layers in execution order and conditioning each layer’s allocation on the already-chosen policies of lower layers, capturing cross-layer interactions. At runtime, a grouped-cache mechanism enforces the resulting policy as actual per-head KV residency rather than just masking entries in a full cache, ensuring real memory savings.
AI.result: On four hybrid long-context models, HeadWiseKV preserves downstream quality close to that of using full uncompressed KV caches, as measured by RULER and LoCoMo benchmarks. In a systems study on Qwen3.6-27B, under a fixed model configuration, HeadWiseKV reduces sampled peak device memory usage by about 8.59% at a 112K-token context length. It also extends the maximum verified successful context length from 114K tokens to 161K tokens, demonstrating improved scalability of inference without model changes.
AI.conclusion: HeadWiseKV offers a practical, training-free approach to KV cache compression for hybrid long-context language models. By assigning per-head static history windows via the SeqCalib policy-generation algorithm and enforcing them with a grouped-cache runtime, it makes KV memory usage predictable and significantly reduces peak memory while largely preserving task performance. This enables serving long-context models at longer sequence lengths and under tighter memory budgets without retraining or major architectural changes.

title: GAPS: Dimension-Level Gates for Conditional Activation Steering
summary: Activation steering suppresses undesired behaviors in language models by adding a steering vector to the hidden state during generation. Recent conditional methods such as CAST and DSAS improve the behavior-capability trade-off by deciding when to intervene, but once active, they apply the full dense vector to all hidden dimensions, regardless of whether a neuron carries concept information or already lies in the desired regime. We introduce dimension-level conditioning as a complementary axis of selectivity that also decides which neurons to intervene on. Our method, GAPS (Gated Activation steering via Posterior and Separability), combines two training-free gates: a static separability gate that restricts steering to neurons with statistically reliable concept information (via AUROC), and a dynamic posterior gate that steers a neuron only when its current activation is better explained by the undesired concept under a Gaussian model. The gates add O(D) overhead per token, and they plug into existing conditional methods. On toxicity mitigation (RealToxicityPrompts) and concept removal (OneSeC) with Gemma-3 (4B) and Qwen-3 (1.7B), GAPS consistently matches or improves the Pareto front of its token-level counterparts; under a fixed capability budget, DSAS+GAPS reduces Gemma-3's toxicity rate from 6.52% to 0.48%, versus 3.52% for DSAS alone. Ablations attribute most of the gain to the posterior gate.

AI.tldr: Introduces GAPS, a dimension-level, gated activation steering method that selectively intervenes on specific neurons to better suppress undesired behaviors in language models while preserving capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods either always intervene or, in conditional variants, decide only when to intervene at the token level. Once activated, they apply a dense steering vector to all hidden dimensions, ignoring whether individual neurons actually encode the target concept or are already in a good state. This leads to unnecessary interference with model capabilities and a suboptimal behavior–capability trade-off. The authors aim to increase the selectivity of steering at the neuron level to achieve stronger mitigation of undesired behaviors without degrading useful abilities.
AI.method: They propose GAPS (Gated Activation steering via Posterior and Separability), which adds dimension-level conditioning through two training-free gating mechanisms that operate on each hidden dimension (neuron). (1) A static separability gate selects neurons that carry reliable information about the concept to be controlled, assessed via AUROC-based separability between desired and undesired concept activations. (2) A dynamic posterior gate, assuming Gaussian activation distributions for concepts, decides at generation time whether a neuron’s current activation is more likely under the undesired concept and only then applies steering. These gates introduce O(D) overhead per token and can be combined with existing token-level conditional steering methods like CAST and DSAS.
AI.result: On toxicity mitigation (RealToxicityPrompts) and concept removal (OneSeC), tested with Gemma-3 (4B) and Qwen-3 (1.7B), GAPS improves or matches the Pareto front of baseline conditional steering methods that operate only at the token level. When combined with DSAS under a fixed capability budget, DSAS+GAPS reduces Gemma-3’s toxicity rate from 6.52% to 0.48%, significantly outperforming DSAS alone, which achieves 3.52%. Ablation studies indicate that the dynamic posterior gate contributes the majority of the performance improvements.
AI.conclusion: Dimension-level, gated activation steering via GAPS provides a more selective and effective way to control undesired behaviors in language models than token-level methods alone. By intervening only on neurons that reliably encode the concept and only when their activations suggest the undesired concept, GAPS improves the behavior–capability trade-off with modest computational overhead and integrates seamlessly with existing conditional steering approaches. The posterior gating mechanism is identified as the key driver of the gains.

title: Monitoring Web Agents Without Internal Signals: Observable Trajectories and Key-Step Supervision
summary: Reliable web-agent monitoring is difficult when model-internal uncertainty signals such as token logits are unavailable. In this work, we study prefix-level risk prediction for web agents using observable trajectory signals: given an evolving prefix, estimate whether the current execution remains on track or is tending toward failure. We derive two observable trajectory representations: Macro features summarize cross-step agent--environment behavior and feedback, while Micro features measure the consistency of intention, action, and anticipated state change through repeated black-box queries. Instead of inheriting the final result label, we label the first critical error that remains uncorrected in the observed continuation and is associated with final failure as a key-step boundary, preserving valid early prefixes of failed trajectories as on track. Across WebArena-Lite and Online Mind2Web web agent benchmarks with five open- and closed-source backbones, observable trajectory signals are competitive with internal-signal baselines. The resulting predictors also support early intervention under fixed false-cut budgets and transfer across held-out website categories. These findings show that observable trajectory signals support valuable risk prediction abilities.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a way to predict, using only observable behavior (not model internals), whether a web agent is still on track or heading toward failure, by analyzing trajectory prefixes.
AI.motivation: Monitoring web agents is hard when we cannot access internal uncertainty measures like token-level logits. Practical deployment often involves black-box agents (e.g., closed-source APIs), yet we still need to know early if an agent is going off track so that we can intervene or stop it. Existing approaches largely rely on final outcome labels or internal signals and do not adequately exploit what can be observed from the interaction trajectory itself. The paper aims to fill this gap by providing a method to do prefix-level risk prediction based purely on observable signals.
AI.method: The authors define the task of prefix-level risk prediction: given a growing interaction prefix of a web agent with the environment, predict whether the execution is on track. They construct two kinds of trajectory-based feature representations from observable behavior. Macro features capture high-level cross-step patterns in agent–environment interaction and feedback. Micro features are built via repeated black-box queries to assess the consistency between the agent’s stated intention, its chosen actions, and the anticipated state changes on the web page. They introduce a new labeling scheme: instead of labeling all steps in a failed trajectory as bad, they identify the first critical error that is not corrected later and that leads to final failure as a key-step boundary, so that steps before this boundary in failed trajectories are treated as on-track prefixes. They then train predictive models over these features and evaluate them on WebArena-Lite and Online Mind2Web benchmarks with multiple underlying agent backbones (both open- and closed-source).
AI.result: Across two web-agent benchmarks and five different backbones, models using the proposed observable trajectory features achieve risk prediction performance that is competitive with baselines that rely on internal model signals. The predictors enable effective early intervention under constraints on how often they can prematurely cut off trajectories (fixed false-cut budgets). The learned predictors also generalize across previously unseen website categories, indicating some robustness and transferability of the learned risk signals.
AI.conclusion: Observable, black-box trajectory signals—without any access to internal model states—are sufficient to build effective prefix-level risk predictors for web agents. Carefully designed macro and micro features, along with a key-step labeling scheme, allow monitoring systems to detect emerging failures early, intervene under resource or false-cut constraints, and transfer across different sites and agent backbones. This demonstrates that practical, model-agnostic monitoring of web agents is feasible and useful.

title: Grounded, Compute-Efficient LLM Policy Agents for Energy-Poverty Equity in Physically-Constrained Peer-to-Peer Energy Markets
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Accepted to the 5th Workshop on NLP for Positive Impact (NLP4PI) at EMNLP 2026
summary: Energy poverty is nearly absent from NLP-for-social-good, and the little existing work is either static retrieval/QA or relies on carbon-intensive cloud LLMs, a self-defeating "computational irony" for a humanitarian setting. We present EqGrid, a closed-loop simulation in which a low-frequency, open-weight LLM policy agent sets price and carbon bounds and targeted subsidies over a community of empirically-grounded household personas, while high-frequency multi-agent RL traders clear a continuous double auction constrained by a physical distribution grid (IEEE-33-bus with Dynamic Operating Envelopes). Our contribution is threefold and directly addresses how to measure the social impact of AI: (i) grounded personas (region-matched socio-demographics) whose load curves are checked for shape and level realism against real smart-meter data; (ii) formal energy-poverty equity metrics (Energy Burden, Gini of EB, LIHC) showing the intervention reduces burden inequality without raising net grid cost; and (iii) a compute-efficiency frontier that measures how much equity performance survives compressing the policy agent from a 235B teacher down to a sub-1B model deployable on a laptop, in estimated energy/carbon per decision. A decoupled-safety design (the LLM sets bounds; a validate-and-project grid gate executes) yields zero grid-constraint violations versus 55 under direct LLM control. On energy-poverty equity, the LLM policy lowers the Gini of energy burden to 0.305 (from 0.351) and mean burden by 28% while cutting cost (outperforming a tuned rule baseline), and a 3B-active model retains 95% of the benefit at roughly 9x lower inference energy than the teacher, with even a 0.8B on-device model retaining 92% at roughly 24x lower energy. We will release code and configs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EqGrid, a simulation framework where an efficient, smaller LLM acts as a policy agent to reduce energy poverty via dynamic pricing and subsidies, evaluated with equity metrics, grid safety, and compute/energy efficiency trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Energy poverty is underexplored in NLP-for-social-good, and current approaches either do static retrieval/QA or depend on large, carbon-intensive cloud LLMs, which is counterproductive in a humanitarian, climate-related context. The authors want to create a practical, low-carbon AI intervention that directly improves energy equity while operating within physical power grid constraints.
AI.method: They build EqGrid, a closed-loop simulation of a real distribution grid (IEEE-33-bus with Dynamic Operating Envelopes) populated by realistic household personas matched to regional socio-demographics and validated against smart-meter load-shape data. A low-frequency LLM policy agent sets price/carbon bounds and targeted subsidies; then high-frequency multi-agent RL traders run a continuous double auction to clear the market under grid constraints. They introduce formal energy-poverty metrics, compare LLM control to rule-based baselines and to direct LLM grid control, and study a distillation/compression frontier from a 235B-parameter teacher down to sub-1B models to quantify equity vs compute/energy trade-offs. Safety is enforced via a validate-and-project grid gate that ensures actions respect grid limits.
AI.result: The persona models produce realistic demand profiles; the equity metrics (Energy Burden, Gini of EB, LIHC) show that the LLM policy reduces energy-burden inequality and average burden without increasing overall grid costs, and it outperforms a tuned rule-based baseline. The decoupled-safety design eliminates grid-constraint violations (0 vs 55 under direct LLM control). The Gini of energy burden drops from 0.351 to 0.305 and mean burden decreases by 28% while reducing cost. A 3B active model preserves 95% of the equity benefit at about 9x lower inference energy than the 235B teacher; a 0.8B on-device model preserves 92% of the benefit at about 24x lower energy.
AI.conclusion: AI for social good can concretely address energy poverty if framed as a closed-loop control problem with realistic personas, explicit equity metrics, and grid-aware safety. Effective, equitable energy policies do not require massive cloud LLMs: compressed, sub-1B models running on modest hardware can retain most of the social-impact benefits while drastically cutting compute energy and carbon. The EqGrid framework offers a reproducible testbed for measuring social impact, equity, and safety of AI interventions in energy systems, and the authors plan to release their code and configurations.

title: DocHop: Benchmarking Out-of-domain Multi-hop Reasoning in Information-Dense Documents
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on structured visual understanding tasks such as chart and document question answering. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate these domains in isolation, leaving underexplored a key capability: whether models can use textual context to determine how chart evidence should be selected, interpreted, and aggregated. We introduce DocHop, a benchmark for integrated chart--context reasoning in document-style images. In DocHop, the document narrative specifies multi-step compositional constraints, while charts provide the corresponding data values. Questions are grounded on a semantic reference label defined in the narrative, requiring models to resolve target entities from context before aggregating evidence across multiple charts. To enable systematic evaluation, we construct DocHop via a stochastic logic-first generation pipeline with controllable reasoning depth and visual density, covering 2,074 examples across six task categories. Experiments on a wide range of proprietary and open-source MLLMs show a substantial gap to human performance: annotators achieve over 90% accuracy, while the best model reaches only 62.83%. Reasoning-enhanced models consistently show improved results, but performance degrades as reasoning complexity increases. Overall, DocHop provides a controlled testbed for challenging multi-hop document reasoning.

AI.tldr: DocHop is a benchmark for testing whether multimodal LLMs can jointly reason over document text and charts via multi-step, multi-hop compositional reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal benchmarks usually test chart understanding and document understanding separately, so they do not adequately measure a model’s ability to use textual narrative context to decide what chart information to retrieve, how to interpret it, and how to aggregate it. The authors want a controlled setting to study integrated chart–document reasoning, especially multi-hop reasoning that mirrors real-world analytic reading of reports.
AI.method: The authors build DocHop, a synthetic yet realistic benchmark of document-style images where text and multiple charts must be jointly reasoned over. They design a stochastic, logic-first generation pipeline: first generate latent logical structures and multi-step constraints, then realize them as narrative text plus corresponding charts. Each question is grounded in semantic reference labels defined in the narrative, forcing models to resolve entities in context before aggregating chart data. They control reasoning depth and visual density and organize 2,074 examples into six task categories, then evaluate a range of proprietary and open-source MLLMs, including reasoning-augmented variants.
AI.result: Human annotators achieve over 90% accuracy on DocHop, while the best evaluated MLLM reaches only 62.83%. Models that incorporate explicit reasoning mechanisms outperform their non-reasoning counterparts, but across all systems, accuracy drops as the required reasoning complexity and number of hops increase. This reveals a substantial and systematic performance gap in integrated chart–context reasoning.
AI.conclusion: DocHop serves as a challenging, controlled benchmark for multi-hop reasoning over document-style images that combine narrative text and charts. Current state-of-the-art MLLMs are far from human-level performance, especially as reasoning depth grows, indicating that integrated, compositional multimodal reasoning remains an open challenge and providing a testbed for future model and method development.

title: Sparse Readout Prism: Explaining Logit-Lens Scores in Features Instead of Tokens
comment: 55 pages, 33 figures, 42 tables. Under review. Code: https://github.com/hematteo/sparse-readout-prism Dictionaries: https://huggingface.co/hematteo/sparse-readout-prism
summary: A language model's prediction of its next token develops across layers, and lens methods track this process by decoding intermediate hidden states into tokens. But a lens reading reflects both the hidden state and the readout (the unembedding matrix) used to decode it. Many lenses are fit on a corpus, and we show that two lenses differing only in their fitting corpus can report different tokens for the same hidden states. We call this dependence corpus conditionality. To examine readout structure independently of the fitting corpus, we introduce Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), which decomposes the readout using only its weights and expresses any token logit or logit difference as a sum of contributions from sparse readout features. This reveals readout features as a new unit of analysis for lens readings, exposing structure that token identities can obscure and enabling comparisons across tokens, contexts, layers, and lenses. Replacing the original readout with SRP's sparse approximation reconstructs 8.9-17.3 percentage points more of the tested logit differences than the strongest of six baselines built on geometric relations among readout rows. Ablating features shifts logit differences in proportion to their SRP contributions. Although token readings vary with the fitting corpus, the dominant readout feature remains stable. Because SRP uses no corpus in its construction, it provides a control independent of the fitting corpus for lens analyses.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how language model lens methods depend on the corpus used to fit their readout, and introduces Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), a corpus-free, sparse decomposition of the readout matrix that reveals stable, interpretable readout features and better reconstructs logit differences than existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Lens methods interpret intermediate hidden states in language models by decoding them into tokens using a readout matrix. However, these interpretations conflate properties of the hidden states with properties of the readout fitted on a specific corpus. Different fitting corpora can yield different lens readings for the same hidden state (corpus conditionality), undermining stability and comparability of analyses. The authors want a way to analyze the readout structure itself, independent of any particular corpus, and to find more stable, interpretable units than individual token identities.
AI.method: They empirically demonstrate corpus conditionality by comparing lenses that differ only in the corpus on which their readout is fit, showing that they yield different decoded tokens for identical hidden states. To address this, they propose Sparse Readout Prism (SRP), a method that factorizes or decomposes the readout (unembedding) matrix into a sparse set of "readout features" using only the readout weights and no corpus. SRP expresses any token logit or logit difference as a sum of contributions from these sparse features, which serves as a new unit of analysis. They evaluate SRP by measuring how well its sparse approximation reconstructs token logit differences, comparing it to six baselines based on geometric relationships among readout rows, and by ablating individual features to test causal impact on logits.
AI.result: SRP yields a sparse approximation of the readout that reconstructs 8.9–17.3 percentage points more of tested logit differences than the best of six geometric baselines. The feature-level decomposition allows token logits and logit differences to be expressed as sums of feature contributions, and ablating features shifts logit differences roughly in proportion to their SRP-assigned contributions, validating the decomposition. Across lenses trained on different corpora, token-level readings change, but the dominant readout feature identified by SRP remains stable, indicating that these features capture corpus-agnostic structure of the readout.
AI.conclusion: Corpus conditionality shows that lens-based interpretability can be unstable because lens readings depend on which corpus was used to fit the readout. Sparse Readout Prism offers a corpus-independent way to analyze the readout: it reveals sparse, stable readout features that serve as a more fundamental unit of analysis than tokens, and it better reconstructs logit differences than several baselines. Because SRP is defined purely from the readout weights and not from data, it can act as a control in lens studies, helping disentangle properties of the model’s internal representations from artifacts of corpus choice and enabling more robust comparisons across tokens, layers, contexts, and lenses.

title: MineTRACE: An Evidence-Grounded Interactive Reasoning System for Mineral Prospectivity
summary: Mineral exploration requires integrating heterogeneous geochemical, geophysical, and geological evidence, yet existing prospectivity systems often provide only opaque scores or heatmaps. We present MineTRACE, a web-based system for evidence-grounded exploration of eight commodities: Cu, Au, Ni, W, Sn, Co, Ta, and Mn. Users can explore prospectivity maps, query locations or regions, inspect supporting evidence, and interact through natural language. A transparent expert tree, informed by geological knowledge and known deposits, combines multi-source evidence into interpretable prospectivity scores. For a new location, the conversational assistant retrieves the score and supporting evidence from the analysis pipeline and presents them in natural language. The scorer achieves spatial AUC values of up to 0.917 across different test scenarios, while end-to-end evaluation assesses query accuracy and response grounding. MineTRACE makes public geoscience data easier to access, interpret, and verify, supporting more efficient and transparent mineral exploration.

AI.tldr: MineTRACE is a web system that integrates diverse geoscience data to produce interpretable mineral prospectivity scores and explanations, accessible via maps and natural-language interaction.
AI.motivation: Mineral exploration relies on many heterogeneous data sources (geochemical, geophysical, geological), but current prospectivity tools usually output opaque scores or heatmaps with limited interpretability or ability to inspect underlying evidence. There is a need for systems that are both accurate and transparent so that geologists can understand, verify, and interact with the evidence used to rank potential mineral targets.
AI.method: The authors build MineTRACE, a web-based exploration system covering eight commodities (Cu, Au, Ni, W, Sn, Co, Ta, Mn). They design a transparent expert decision tree that encodes geological knowledge and information from known deposits to combine multi-source evidence into prospectivity scores. The system exposes prospectivity maps and allows users to query specific locations or regions, inspect the evidence feeding into the score, and interact via a conversational natural-language interface. For each query, the assistant retrieves the computed prospectivity score and its evidence from the analysis pipeline and verbalizes them in natural language. They evaluate both the spatial prediction quality (AUC) and the correctness/grounding of the end-to-end conversational responses.
AI.result: MineTRACE’s prospectivity scorer achieves spatial AUC values up to 0.917 across test scenarios, indicating strong predictive performance in distinguishing known deposits from background areas. The system successfully supports interactive querying of maps and locations, returns prospectivity scores together with the underlying evidence, and provides grounded natural-language responses. End-to-end evaluation shows that the conversational interface can accurately retrieve and explain scores while staying grounded in the underlying data and model outputs.
AI.conclusion: MineTRACE demonstrates that mineral prospectivity analysis can be made both accurate and interpretable by combining a transparent expert tree with an evidence-aware conversational interface. The system lowers barriers to accessing and understanding public geoscience data, enabling geologists and other stakeholders to explore, verify, and interpret mineral prospectivity for multiple commodities. This supports more efficient, transparent, and trustworthy mineral exploration workflows and sets a direction for future systems that integrate interpretable models with natural-language interaction over scientific data.

title: NS-Copilot: An LLM-Driven Agent System for Autonomous Neuroscience Analysis
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 20 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables
summary: AI is rapidly advancing neuroscience, yet many laboratories fail to fully unleash its potential due to significant interdisciplinary barriers. While pre-trained neural models for physiological data are progressing quickly, their heterogeneous architectures and modality-specific constraints hinder systematic integration, selection, and evaluation. Despite recent advances in large language model (LLM)-based agent systems for intelligent scientific applications, existing approaches often still lack the domain expertise required to effectively select and coordinate diverse neuroscience pre-trained models and handle unique data types in this domain. We present NS-Copilot, an LLM-driven multi-agent system for neuroscience analysis that autonomously supports end-to-end workflows for diverse professional tasks. It unifies domain-specific pre-trained models and supports key neuroscience modalities, including EEG and extracellular spike data, through a natural-language interface. Given raw data and a task description, NS-Copilot orchestrates agents with specialized roles for planning, adaptive control, code generation, and result synthesis, enabling analysis without dataset-specific heuristics. We evaluate NS-Copilot on neuroscience benchmarks spanning Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and working memory spike decoding. Across 8 trials per task, the system consistently outperforms strong baselines on the primary metric, demonstrating the ability of NS-Copilot for effective and scalable neuroscience analysis.

AI.tldr: NS-Copilot is an LLM-driven multi-agent system that integrates diverse neuroscience pre-trained models to autonomously perform end-to-end analysis on EEG and spike data, outperforming baselines on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Although AI and pre-trained neural models are advancing rapidly in neuroscience, labs struggle to use them effectively due to interdisciplinary barriers, heterogeneous architectures, and modality-specific constraints, and existing LLM-agent systems lack sufficient domain expertise to coordinate these tools for neuroscience.
AI.method: The authors design NS-Copilot, an LLM-based multi-agent system with specialized roles (planning, adaptive control, code generation, result synthesis) that interfaces through natural language, unifies multiple domain-specific pre-trained models, and supports key neuroscience modalities such as EEG and extracellular spikes to run end-to-end analyses from raw data and task descriptions without dataset-specific heuristics.
AI.result: On neuroscience benchmarks involving Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and working memory spike decoding, and evaluated over 8 trials per task, NS-Copilot consistently outperforms strong baselines on the primary evaluation metric.
AI.conclusion: NS-Copilot effectively enables scalable, end-to-end neuroscience analysis by autonomously orchestrating heterogeneous pre-trained models and handling multiple modalities via an LLM-driven multi-agent framework, lowering the barrier for labs to apply advanced AI to neuroscience data.

title: ToolGate: An Executable Acceptance Pipeline for Tool-Dependent Scientific Benchmark Construction
summary: Scientific benchmarks are commonly built by domain experts who write tasks and cross-check one another's work, or who adapt existing material from textbooks, published papers, and online resources. These routes can produce strong evaluations, but they require substantial per-item labor. Language models can reduce this repeated work by proposing candidates quickly. The remaining problem is acceptance. We target scientific questions whose answers require computations with specialist software rather than unaided reasoning alone. A candidate is invalid if its script fails or returns a different answer, or trivial if a model answers it without the software. We present ToolGate, which treats every generated item as a proposal and keeps it only if three gates pass. First, an executable solution script must reproduce the proposed answer when run with the scientific software. Second, randomized no-tool screening rejects candidates that models can already solve from the prompt alone. Third, a tool-using agent must solve each survivor within a fixed time limit. We instantiate ToolGate in FEniCSx with 500 generation attempts. The local-verification gate retains 478 candidates. For final reporting, we rescreen this pool after generation: two randomized no-tool screens exclude 222 from the reported pool, and direct GPT-5.5 API calls at medium reasoning (the API default) exclude another 121. Of the remaining 135, a GPT-5.5 Codex CLI agent with access to FEniCSx solves 130; exact deduplication leaves 128 unique protocol survivors. ToolGate turns repeated answer checking and difficulty screening into an auditable process while leaving domain design and final review to experts.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ToolGate, an automated, software-grounded pipeline for generating and filtering scientific benchmark questions that require specialist computational tools, significantly reducing expert labor while preserving difficulty and reliability.
AI.motivation: Manually constructing scientific benchmarks is labor-intensive because domain experts must author tasks, verify answers, and ensure appropriate difficulty. Existing benchmarks often rely on textbook-style questions or previously published material, which does not scale and may not stress models’ ability to use specialized software. The authors want a scalable way to generate many high-quality, non-trivial questions whose solutions genuinely require scientific tools rather than pure reasoning, turning ad hoc expert checking into a systematic, auditable procedure.
AI.method: They propose ToolGate, a three-gate filtering pipeline applied to model-generated candidate items. 1) Local verification gate: each candidate includes an executable solution script and proposed answer; the script is run with domain-specific scientific software (here, FEniCSx) and only candidates whose scripts execute successfully and reproduce the proposed answer are kept. 2) No-tool difficulty gate: randomized screenings with language models that are not allowed to call tools; any candidate that can be correctly solved from the text alone is discarded as trivial. 3) Tool-using gate: a tool-augmented agent (e.g., GPT-5.5 Codex via CLI with access to FEniCSx) must successfully solve each remaining question within a fixed time budget, ensuring that the task is solvable by a competent tool-using model and is properly posed. They also perform additional rescreening and exact deduplication at the end.
AI.result: In a concrete instantiation with FEniCSx and 500 initial generation attempts, 478 candidates pass the local verification gate. After generation, two rounds of randomized no-tool screening remove 222 candidates that are solvable without tools, and direct GPT-5.5 API calls at default (medium) reasoning remove another 121 as too easy. Of the 135 remaining, a GPT-5.5 Codex CLI agent with FEniCSx access solves 130. After exact deduplication, 128 unique, high-quality protocol survivors remain, each representing a verified, non-trivial, tool-requiring benchmark item.
AI.conclusion: ToolGate provides a principled, auditable framework for transforming model-proposed scientific questions into a curated benchmark that is both correctness-checked via software and filtered for non-triviality and solvability by tool-using agents. This approach substantially reduces repeated expert labor in answer checking and difficulty calibration, while still leaving critical tasks—like domain selection, prompt design, and final content review—to human experts. It offers a scalable recipe for building software-grounded scientific benchmarks in other domains beyond FEniCSx.

title: How Output Format Confounds Data Quality and Capability in Instruction Tuning
summary: Instruction-tuning data are judged by quality metrics, and tuned models are judged by benchmarks, but both judgments pass through an output interface: the surface format in which an answer is written. Using gradient signatures across 12 tasks, four semantically equivalent interfaces, three model families, and controlled corruptions, we show that this interface confounds both measurements. Spectral statistics such as effective rank are provably invariant to interface rotation and empirically blind to semantic corruption, while the direction of the update carries the quality signal. The interface-varying residual is not noise: it identifies each unit's own target task perfectly across all three families. Capability itself is stored relative to the training interface: a skill that raises accuracy by more than 40 points under the training format can be nearly invisible under every other, and correcting a single generation budget flips the measured effect of fine-tuning on GSM8K from a gain into a large loss. Pre-registered interventions delimit where this geometry stops short of control. Data quality and model capability are interface-conditioned quantities, and current practice often reports the interface instead of the content.
