AI.tldr: This paper argues that the way model outputs are formatted (the interface) strongly affects how we measure both data quality and model capability, and that many common statistics miss this effect.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify how much the surface format of model outputs (instruction interfaces, answer templates, etc.) interferes with the evaluation of instruction-tuning data and the capabilities of language models. The authors suspect that current metrics may conflate interface artifacts with genuine model competence.
AI.method: They study gradient signatures across 12 tasks, using four semantically equivalent but differently formatted interfaces, three distinct model families, and controlled corruptions of the data. They analyze spectral statistics like effective rank and perform pre-registered interventions, examining how gradient directions and residuals change when the interface is rotated or corrupted.
AI.result: They find that the output interface systematically confounds both data-quality and model-capability measurements. Spectral statistics such as effective rank remain unchanged under rotations of the interface and do not respond to semantic corruptions, meaning they miss quality differences. The informative signal about quality lies in the direction of the gradient updates. The interface-varying residuals are structured enough to perfectly identify each unit’s target task across model families. They also show that skills acquired under one interface may not transfer: a skill yielding >40-point accuracy gains under the training format can be nearly undetectable under other formats. Adjusting a single generation budget parameter can reverse the apparent effect of fine-tuning on GSM8K from a gain to a large loss.
AI.conclusion: Data quality and model capability are not intrinsic but depend on the chosen interface: changing formatting or generation protocols can dramatically change measured performance. Many current evaluation practices inadvertently measure interface-specific behavior rather than underlying competence or data quality. The paper delimits, via pre-registered interventions, where this interface geometry ceases to provide control, and it calls for rethinking how we design benchmarks and metrics so they disentangle format from content.

title: CHIME: Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agentic Planning
summary: Planning is a central capability that enables agents to decompose complex long-horizon tasks into manageable steps. Test-time search and training-based methods improve planning but incur high inference costs or require expensive training data. Self-evolving memory instead accumulates reusable experience from agent interaction outcomes into an external memory bank, so planning capability keeps improving at inference time without parameter updates. However, existing self-evolving memory methods share an inherent credit assignment problem: they rely on final task outcomes as feedback, but such outcomes conflate plan quality with execution errors and environmental factors, so the accumulated planning experience is often biased and noisy. To address this problem, we propose Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution (CHIME), a self-evolving memory framework that maintains a separate planning bank and execution bank and follows an attribute-before-memorize principle: CHIME first attributes each task outcome to the plan, the execution, both, or neither, and then updates only the corresponding memory bank. Extensive experiments on four long-horizon agent benchmarks show that CHIME consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-based and self-evolving memory baselines. Further analyses reveal several interesting findings. For example, CHIME accumulates effective memory with far fewer items. In addition, the learned memory values faithfully reflect downstream utility: high-quality planning memories are more valuable than execution memories. Finally, the accumulated memory effectively transfers across backbone models. Code will be released at https://github.com/ATH-MaaS/Marco-DeepResearch.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CHIME, a credit-aware self-evolving memory framework that separates planning and execution memories to improve long-horizon planning for agents while reducing bias from conflated outcome feedback.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving memory approaches improve agent planning by accumulating experience from task outcomes, but they suffer from a credit assignment problem: final outcomes mix the effects of planning quality, execution errors, and environmental randomness. This leads to biased, noisy memory that degrades planning improvement over time. The paper is motivated by the need for a self-improving planning mechanism that can better disentangle these factors at inference time, without expensive retraining or high-cost test-time search.
AI.method: The authors propose Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution (CHIME), which maintains two distinct external memory banks: a planning bank and an execution bank. For each completed task, CHIME performs an attribution step (“attribute-before-memorize”) that classifies the outcome as being due mainly to the plan, the execution, both, or neither. Based on this attribution, only the relevant memory bank(s) is updated. This hierarchical and credit-aware update mechanism aims to reduce noise in the stored experiences and make the self-evolving memory more faithful to the underlying contribution of planning versus execution.
AI.result: On four long-horizon agent benchmarks, CHIME consistently outperforms both state-of-the-art training-based methods and prior self-evolving memory baselines. Empirical results show that CHIME can reach strong performance while using significantly fewer memory items than competitors. The learned memory values correlate well with downstream task utility, revealing that high-quality planning memories contribute more to performance gains than execution memories. Moreover, the memory learned by CHIME can be transferred effectively across different backbone models, indicating robustness and generality of the learned experience.
AI.conclusion: Separating planning and execution memories and updating them via a credit-aware attribution mechanism allows self-evolving memory systems to learn more accurate and compact experience representations. CHIME demonstrates that such structured, hierarchical memory evolution can substantially improve long-horizon planning performance at inference time, without parameter updates or large training sets, and that the resulting memories are both interpretable (via their value estimates) and transferable across different models.

title: A Tri-Agent Framework for Evaluating and Aligning Question Clarification Capabilities of Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive systems where understanding user intent precisely is paramount. A key capability for such systems is effective question clarification, especially when user queries are ambiguous or underspecified. This paper introduces a novel tri-agent framework for the robust evaluation of an LLM's ability to engage in clarifying dialogue. Our framework comprises three distinct LLM-based agents: (1) a Question Clarifying Agent (QCA), the system under evaluation, tasked with identifying ambiguities and posing clarifying questions; (2) a Respondent Agent (RA), designed to simulate human user responses, potentially including irrelevant or challenging replies; and (3) an Evaluator Agent (EA), an LLM-as-a-judge, which assesses the quality of the dialogue based on a comprehensive set of metrics. We detail a methodology for synthetic data generation in the supply chain domain as an example. We propose metrics evaluating ambiguity handling, question quality, dialogue efficiency, language appropriateness, and final intent alignment. We also briefly discuss the validation of the EA against human judgments. This work provides a structured approach to benchmark, validate, and improve the clarification capabilities of conversational LLM applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a tri-agent LLM framework to evaluate how well a language model clarifies ambiguous user questions through simulated dialogues and LLM-based judging.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in interactive systems, accurately understanding user intent is critical, yet user queries are often ambiguous or underspecified. Existing evaluations focus on final answer quality, not on the model’s ability to recognize ambiguity, ask good clarifying questions, and converge to the correct intent through dialogue. There is a need for a systematic way to benchmark and improve this clarification capability.
AI.method: The authors design a tri-agent framework with three LLM-based components: (1) a Question Clarifying Agent (QCA) being evaluated, which must detect ambiguities and ask clarifying questions; (2) a Respondent Agent (RA) that simulates human users and can provide relevant, irrelevant, or challenging replies; and (3) an Evaluator Agent (EA) acting as an LLM judge that scores the resultant dialogues. They generate synthetic scenarios in the supply chain domain and define evaluation metrics spanning ambiguity detection and handling, quality of clarifying questions, dialogue efficiency, language appropriateness, and alignment of inferred final intent with the ground truth. They also conduct an initial validation of the EA by comparing its judgments with human evaluations.
AI.result: The framework successfully produces synthetic clarification dialogues and allows the QCA’s performance to be assessed along multiple dimensions related to clarification behavior. The EA can automatically score dialogues according to the proposed metrics, and preliminary evidence indicates its judgments correlate reasonably with human assessments, supporting its use as an automated evaluator.
AI.conclusion: The tri-agent framework offers a structured, LLM-driven methodology to benchmark and analyze an LLM’s clarification abilities in interactive settings. By combining synthetic data generation, simulated users, and an LLM-as-a-judge, it enables scalable evaluation and targeted improvement of clarifying-question behavior, particularly in domain-specific applications such as supply chain. The approach can be extended to other domains and refined through further validation against human judgements.

title: Beyond Outcome Gaps: Process-Aware Fairness Diagnosis for LLM-based Multi-Agent Decision Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) are increasingly considered for high-stakes decision-making, yet outcome-based fairness audits can miss where risks arise within the decision trajectory. We present SCOPED-Hiring, a process-aware fairness diagnosis pipeline for LLM-based hiring MAS. SCOPED-Hiring constructs controlled resume variants, runs role-based hiring committees, logs over 311K structured decision trajectories, and converts trajectory fields into quantitative fairness signals organized by six diagnostic lenses: final outcome, counterfactual, process, pathway, dynamic, and design effects. SCOPED-Hiring reveals that balanced final hire rates can mask hidden trajectory unfairness in multi-agent decision trajectories: career gaps trigger suspicion, proxy cues shape qualification judgments, and identity cues lead to unequal investigation. Targeted repair guided by these diagnoses reduces total layered burden by 72.3% while shifting the hire rate by only 1.86 pp, showing that process diagnosis can guide effective repair. Project Page: https://scoped-hiring-project-page.vercel.app/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SCOPED-Hiring, a process-aware fairness diagnosis pipeline for LLM-based multi-agent hiring systems, revealing hidden unfairness in decision trajectories that balanced final hire rates alone cannot detect, and demonstrating targeted repairs that greatly reduce unfair burden with minimal impact on overall hire rates.
AI.motivation: Existing fairness audits for LLM-based multi-agent systems mainly focus on final outcomes, which can overlook where and how unfairness arises within complex, multi-step decision processes, especially in high-stakes domains like hiring. The authors seek a way to systematically examine the entire decision trajectory to uncover subtle and layered forms of unfair treatment that are invisible in aggregate outcome metrics.
AI.method: They build SCOPED-Hiring, a pipeline that: (1) generates controlled resume variants; (2) configures role-based LLM hiring committees as a multi-agent system; (3) logs over 311K structured decision trajectories; and (4) transforms each trajectory field into quantitative fairness indicators. These indicators are organized into six diagnostic lenses: final outcome effects, counterfactual effects, process effects (step-by-step), pathway effects (different routes to decisions), dynamic effects (how early signals influence later steps), and design effects (impacts of system configuration and prompts).
AI.result: Using SCOPED-Hiring on LLM-based hiring committees, they find that superficially balanced hire rates can hide substantial trajectory-level unfairness: career gaps tend to trigger extra suspicion, proxies in resumes affect perceived qualification, and identity-related cues yield unequal levels of scrutiny and investigation. They further show that targeted mitigations informed by these diagnoses can reduce total layered burden by 72.3% while altering the overall hire rate by only 1.86 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that outcome-only fairness audits are insufficient for LLM-based multi-agent hiring systems, as they can miss significant unfairness in the decision process itself. Process-aware, trajectory-level diagnosis—operationalized through SCOPED-Hiring and its six fairness lenses—can reveal hidden biases and guide precise, effective interventions that meaningfully reduce unfair burdens without substantially disrupting aggregate outcomes.

title: HyGRAIL: Cost-Aware and Evidence-Grounded Scientific Hypothesis Discovery over Knowledge Graphs
summary: Scientific knowledge graphs organize entities and relations extracted from scientific literature, but they remain inherently incomplete. Missing typed links in such graphs can therefore represent plausible scientific hypotheses, such as unexplored associations between materials and applications. However, scientific hypothesis discovery is challenging because true discoveries are extremely sparse among typed candidate pairs: graph neural networks (GNNs) are efficient but unreliable for ambiguous cases, while large language models (LLMs) are knowledgeable but too costly to apply exhaustively and are not naturally grounded in graph structures. We propose HyGRAIL, a cost-aware and evidence-grounded framework that combines heterogeneous GNN triage with LLM-based hypothesis review. HyGRAIL first uses a GNN to score candidate hypotheses and identify a validation-calibrated ambiguous region, routing only graph-uncertain cases to LLM review. For each routed hypothesis, HyGRAIL retrieves node-level associations and multi-hop relational paths from the knowledge graph (KG), then converts this structured evidence into natural language through template-based or LLM-based naturalization. An LLM review agent finally judges each hard hypothesis using the naturalized evidence and validation-selected decision criteria. On MatKG, HyGRAIL achieves the best F1 score of 0.429, improving over the strongest prior baseline by 0.242 F1 points and over the GNN-only baseline by 0.322. Meanwhile, GNN triage reduces the LLM call rate by 54.36% on average. Ablation studies further show that retrieved graph evidence is crucial for reliable hypothesis verification and that compact, two-sided evidence is more effective than simply increasing retrieval quantity.

AI.tldr: HyGRAIL is a hybrid, cost-aware framework that combines GNN-based triage with LLM-based review, grounded in KG evidence, to more accurately and efficiently discover missing links (hypotheses) in scientific knowledge graphs.
AI.motivation: Scientific knowledge graphs are valuable for discovering new scientific hypotheses, such as unexplored material–application associations, but they are highly incomplete. True new discoveries are extremely sparse among all possible typed node pairs, so most candidate links are false. Existing GNN-based link prediction is scalable but unreliable on ambiguous cases, while LLMs are powerful but too expensive to apply everywhere and not naturally aligned with graph structure. There is a need for a method that is both accurate and cost-efficient, and that grounds LLM reasoning in explicit graph evidence.
AI.method: HyGRAIL uses a two-stage, cost-aware pipeline. (1) A heterogeneous GNN scores all candidate hypotheses (typed KG links) and identifies a calibrated ambiguous region based on validation performance. Only hypotheses whose scores fall into this uncertain band are routed to the next stage. (2) For routed hypotheses, the system retrieves relevant evidence from the knowledge graph, including node-level associations and multi-hop relational paths. This structured evidence is then transformed ("naturalized") into text using either templates or an LLM. Finally, an LLM review agent evaluates each ambiguous hypothesis using the naturalized evidence and decision criteria chosen via validation, outputting a final accept/reject decision. The approach explicitly balances prediction performance against LLM query cost.
AI.result: On the MatKG dataset, HyGRAIL attains an F1 score of 0.429, which is a +0.242 improvement over the strongest previous baseline and a +0.322 gain over a GNN-only baseline. The initial GNN triage step reduces the fraction of hypotheses requiring LLM evaluation by an average of 54.36%. Ablation experiments indicate that incorporating KG-derived evidence significantly improves verification reliability and that using compact, balanced evidence from both sides of a candidate link is more effective than simply retrieving more evidence.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid, cost-aware architecture that uses GNNs for large-scale triage and LLMs for focused review, grounded in retrieved KG evidence, leads to substantially better and more efficient scientific hypothesis discovery in knowledge graphs. The work demonstrates that careful calibration of the ambiguous region, explicit retrieval and naturalization of graph evidence, and compact two-sided context are all key to harnessing LLMs effectively for link prediction in sparse scientific domains.

title: MASkills: Continual Skills Optimization for Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems have shown strong performance on complex tasks, yet continual improvement from interaction experience remains challenging. Existing self-reflection methods build experience memories, but memories are mostly hard to invoke, refine, or scale, while agent skills offer a more actionable unit: structured procedural knowledge that specifies when to act, how to act, and which resources or tools to use. We introduce MASkills, a continual learning framework that optimizes multi-agent LLM systems through agent skills. MASkills presents a new agent-optimization pipeline that integrates skill-conditioned credit assignment, hierarchical credit aggregation, and momentum-smoothed optimization, enabling agent skill libraries to evolve through refinement, induction, consolidation, and pruning. Experiments on HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA demonstrate the effectiveness of MASkills across multiple agentic tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/DaRL-GenAI/MASkills

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MASkills, a continual learning framework that improves LLM-based multi-agent systems by treating reusable agent skills—not raw memories—as the main unit of learning and optimization.
AI.motivation: While LLM-based multi-agent systems perform well on complex tasks, they struggle to continually improve from interaction experience. Existing self-reflection approaches rely on memory-like experience logs that are hard to retrieve, refine, or scale. The authors are motivated to find a more structured, actionable representation of experience that better supports updating and optimizing multi-agent systems over time.
AI.method: The authors introduce MASkills, a continual learning framework where the core learning unit is an "agent skill"—structured procedural knowledge specifying when to act, how to act, and which tools/resources to use. MASkills defines an agent-optimization pipeline with: (1) skill-conditioned credit assignment to attribute task performance to specific skills, (2) hierarchical credit aggregation to combine signal across skills and agents, and (3) momentum-smoothed optimization to stably update the skill library. Skills are evolved via refinement, induction of new skills, consolidation of overlapping skills, and pruning of unhelpful ones.
AI.result: On three benchmarks—HotpotQA, LoCoMo, and GAIA—MASkills improves the performance of LLM-based multi-agent systems on various complex, agentic tasks, demonstrating effective continual learning and optimization via skills rather than unstructured memories.
AI.conclusion: Treating structured agent skills as the central unit of learning enables more effective continual optimization of LLM-based multi-agent systems than prior memory-based self-reflection approaches. MASkills provides a practical pipeline for evolving a skill library (refine, induce, consolidate, prune) and empirically improves performance across diverse benchmarks.

title: IDEEA: training-free Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching
summary: Steering aligns large language models (LLMs) by injecting a bias into selected activations at inference time, offering a far cheaper alternative to weight-update methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. However, most existing training-free steering methods are input-independent: a single direction is fitted once and shared across all inputs. This is fundamentally limiting as different inputs occupy different regions of the activation space and admit different optimal steering directions toward the same target concept, much as the gradient with respect to a fixed loss varies from input to input. We close this gap with IDEEA (Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching), a training-free framework for input-dependent steering. IDEEA clusters the positive and negative activation supports per attention head, and solves an optimal-matching problem to construct a set of cluster-conditional directions, all about the target concept. At inference time, it picks from this pool of directions and uses the one that best matches the input's own activation for steering. IDEEA aligns the model toward the target concept while preserving the input's original representation, evidence that activations encoding a concept occupy several distinct sub-regions of the representation space rather than a single one. IDEEA improves the truth $\times$ info rate in TruthfulQA by an average of 9.9% (up to 23.5%) over the best input-independent baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes IDEEA, a training-free, input-dependent steering method that adjusts LLM activations using cluster-conditioned directions, improving alignment on benchmarks like TruthfulQA over input-independent steering.
AI.motivation: Existing steering methods for aligning LLMs typically apply a single, global direction in activation space for a given target concept. This ignores that different inputs lie in different parts of the representation space and thus may require different steering directions, similar to how gradients are input-specific. The authors aim to develop a more flexible, input-sensitive steering mechanism without expensive retraining or fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors introduce IDEEA (Input-Dependent stEEring via Activation cluster matching). For a given target concept and attention head, they collect activations with positive and negative labels for that concept and cluster them separately. They then solve an optimal matching problem between positive and negative clusters to obtain multiple paired, cluster-conditional steering directions that all encode the same concept shift. At inference time, for a new input, IDEEA computes the current activation, finds the best-matching cluster pair, and applies the corresponding steering direction to bias the model outputs toward the desired concept while leaving other aspects of the representation as intact as possible.
AI.result: IDEEA is evaluated on alignment tasks, especially TruthfulQA, measuring the product of truthfulness and informativeness. Compared to the strongest input-independent steering baselines, IDEEA yields an average improvement of 9.9% and up to 23.5% in the truth × info rate, showing that input-dependent steering can deliver significantly better alignment performance. Qualitative analyses suggest that IDEEA maintains the input’s original semantic content while selectively nudging concept-related activations.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that concept-related activations in LLMs are distributed across multiple distinct sub-regions of the representation space, making single global steering directions inherently limited. By modeling this structure with clustering and activation matching, IDEEA enables effective, training-free, input-dependent steering that improves alignment metrics like TruthfulQA without harming the preservation of input meaning. This suggests a promising, scalable alternative to weight-updating methods for fine-grained, concept-level control of LLM behavior.

title: READY or Not: Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment
summary: An AI agent can perform well on benchmarks and still be unsuitable for deployment. Existing AI-agent benchmarks measure whether an agent can complete realistic professional work, whereas enterprise deployment asks a different question: whether an agent can meet a required reliability level, under acceptable human oversight, and at tolerable cost. We introduce Reliable Enterprise Agent Deployment (READY), a framework for qualifying AI agents for deployment on enterprise workflows. READY preserves each workflow's own definition of successful execution while applying a common qualification procedure. Given an agent, a workflow, and a class of candidate oversight policies, READY measures the reliability and operating cost of the human-AI system, selects the minimum-cost policy that satisfies a specified reliability target, and statistically qualifies it on held-out cases. The resulting deployment profile characterizes the supported operating point: reliability, human-oversight burden, and cost. READY is implemented as an open testbed that decouples workflow specification, execution, evaluation, and qualification, and runs on existing agent-evaluation infrastructure. In an end-to-end clinical-audit case study spanning 16 agent systems and 750 cases, READY reveals differences hidden by autonomous performance: two systems separated by only 0.3 points in autonomous accuracy (72.8% vs. 72.5%) require 39.2% versus 29.6% human review, respectively, to qualify at the same 76% reliability target under the evaluated oversight policy. READY thus shifts enterprise agent evaluation from how well can the agent perform the work? to under what conditions, and at what cost, can it be reliably deployed? By making those conditions explicit and statistically testable, READY provides a basis for comparing agent systems, setting oversight requirements, and making evidence-based deployment decisions.

AI.tldr: Introduces READY, a framework to assess when and how AI agents can be reliably and cost-effectively deployed in enterprise workflows, rather than just how well they perform autonomously.
AI.motivation: Benchmarking of AI agents has focused on whether they can complete realistic professional tasks, but this is insufficient for real-world enterprise deployment where reliability thresholds, human-oversight requirements, and cost constraints are critical. Organizations need a principled way to decide if and how an AI agent can be safely integrated into actual workflows.
AI.method: Proposes READY, a framework and open testbed that, for a given agent, workflow, and class of oversight policies, empirically measures the joint human-AI system’s reliability and operating cost. It searches over candidate oversight policies to find the minimum-cost policy that meets a specified reliability target, and then statistically qualifies this configuration on held-out cases. The framework preserves workflow-specific success criteria while applying a standardized evaluation and qualification procedure using existing agent-evaluation infrastructure.
AI.result: In a clinical-audit case study involving 16 agent systems and 750 cases, READY uncovers meaningful differences between systems that look similar under standard autonomous accuracy metrics. For example, two agents with almost identical autonomous accuracy (72.8% vs. 72.5%) differ substantially in the required human oversight to reach the same reliability target (39.2% vs. 29.6% human review, respectively, to achieve 76% reliability under the tested oversight policy).
AI.conclusion: READY reframes evaluation from "how well can the agent do the work autonomously?" to "under what oversight conditions and costs can the agent be reliably deployed?" By explicitly quantifying reliability, human-oversight burden, and cost, and statistically qualifying deployment profiles, READY supports principled comparison of agent systems, the setting of oversight requirements, and evidence-based decisions about enterprise deployment.

title: Selective Knowledge Edit Reversal via Gated Singular Vector Shrinkage
summary: Knowledge editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in large language models. However, malicious edits may introduce safety risks, making it necessary to reverse undesirable editing effects. Existing reversal methods for parameter-modifying edits mainly focus on global removal, which may also erase beneficial edits that should be preserved. In this paper, we study selective reversal of edited knowledge, where the goal is to reverse targeted edited facts while preserving the remaining edited facts. Based on the hypothesis that each edit is sparsely encoded within the dominant subspace of the edited matrix, we propose a spectral-based reversal framework that locates edit-sensitive components within the dominant singular subspace of edited weights. Experiments across multiple settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reversing selected edits while preserving unrelated edited facts. These results suggest that different edits are sparsely encoded within dominant singular components and can be separable when the number of edits is moderate, making selective spectral reversal a promising direction for locating edit-specific components and repairing edited language models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a spectral method to selectively reverse specific knowledge edits in language models without undoing all edits.
AI.motivation: Knowledge editing lets us efficiently update facts in large language models, but malicious or erroneous edits can introduce safety and reliability issues. Existing reversal approaches tend to globally remove the effects of parameter changes, which unintentionally erases useful edits alongside harmful ones. There is a need for a method that can precisely undo only targeted, undesirable edits while preserving other beneficial modifications.
AI.method: The authors hypothesize that each individual edit is sparsely encoded within the dominant subspace of the edited weight matrices. Building on this, they develop a spectral-based reversal framework: they analyze the singular value decomposition (SVD) of the edited weights, identify edit-sensitive components within the dominant singular subspace, and manipulate these components to reverse only the targeted edits. The approach leverages spectral properties to separate and selectively cancel specific edit directions while leaving unrelated edits largely untouched.
AI.result: Across various experimental settings, the proposed method successfully reverses specific edited facts while maintaining the effects of other edits. Quantitative evaluations show that targeted edits are effectively undone, and unrelated edited knowledge remains functional, outperforming global-reversal baselines that remove all edits together.
AI.conclusion: The experiments support the view that different knowledge edits tend to be sparsely encoded within dominant singular components of the weight matrices and can be separated when the number of edits is not too large. This makes selective spectral reversal a promising avenue for isolating edit-specific components and repairing or sanitizing edited language models without sacrificing beneficial edits.

title: Semantic Signal-Assisted Inspection and Recovery Allocation in Reverse Logistics
comment: Accepted at the IEEE 4th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Blockchain, and Internet of Things (AIBThings 2026). 7 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/jiani19980225/ssads-reverse-logistics
summary: Reverse-logistics operators often decide how to inspect and route returned assets before their condition is fully observed, while full inspection consumes scarce labor. Semantic Signal-Assisted Decision Support converts return notes into a condition factor and a signal-quality score that guide inspection depth and recovery allocation under shared labor capacity. We evaluate the framework in three synthetic benchmark scenarios spanning information technology decommissioning, aircraft maintenance, and consumer-electronics returns. Across 30 paired simulation seeds, the keyword implementation improves net recovery value relative to a structured-feature comparator with noisy full inspection while reducing inspection cost in all three scenarios. A risk-blind comparator that skips inspection altogether still records higher value under the benchmark's purely economic objective. At matched inspection cost, score-guided targeting adds 53.9 thousand United States dollars per batch in the aircraft scenario but has little economic effect in the other two configurations; phrase and large language model extractors provide further gains in the aircraft scenario. These results show how narrative evidence can support inspection allocation before recovery decisions are made.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using semantic signals from textual return notes to guide how deeply to inspect returned assets and how to allocate them for recovery under limited labor, showing that text-based decision support can increase net recovery value and reduce inspection costs in synthetic reverse-logistics scenarios, especially in an aircraft maintenance setting.
AI.motivation: In reverse logistics, operators must decide inspection depth and routing of returned assets before fully knowing their condition; full inspections are labor-intensive and costly, yet skipping inspection risks misallocating assets. Existing approaches either rely on structured features that may be limited or assume full but noisy inspections. There is a need to better exploit narrative, unstructured information (like return notes) to make more efficient inspection and recovery decisions under shared labor constraints, and to quantify when such semantic information is economically valuable.
AI.method: The paper introduces a Semantic Signal-Assisted Decision Support framework that transforms narrative return notes into two quantitative signals: a condition factor and a signal-quality score. These outputs guide how much inspection effort to allocate and how to route assets for recovery, under a shared labor-capacity constraint. The framework is instantiated using different text-extraction implementations (keywords, phrases, and large language models) and benchmarked via simulation in three synthetic scenarios: IT decommissioning, aircraft maintenance, and consumer-electronics returns. Performance is compared against (i) a structured-feature-based policy with noisy full inspection and (ii) a risk-blind policy that skips inspection entirely. The evaluations use paired simulation seeds to measure differences in net recovery value and inspection cost.
AI.result: In all three benchmark scenarios, the keyword-based semantic implementation improves net recovery value compared with a structured-feature comparator that relies on noisy full inspection, while simultaneously lowering inspection costs. However, a risk-blind policy that conducts no inspection can still achieve higher net value under a purely economic objective, highlighting that inspection has to justify its cost. When inspection costs are matched, score-guided targeting adds around 53.9k USD per batch in the aircraft-maintenance scenario but yields minimal economic benefit in the IT decommissioning and consumer-electronics scenarios. Using more sophisticated text extractors, such as phrase-based methods and large language models, produces additional performance gains in the aircraft scenario, where the narrative information seems particularly informative.
AI.conclusion: Semantic Signal-Assisted Decision Support demonstrates that narrative evidence from return notes can be systematically converted into actionable signals for inspection allocation and recovery routing in reverse logistics. The framework can outperform structured-feature approaches with full but noisy inspections and cut inspection costs, though its economic advantage depends on scenario characteristics and objective functions. In settings like aircraft maintenance, where textual descriptions are rich and informative, both basic and advanced semantic extractors significantly enhance value, whereas in other contexts the benefit may be limited. Overall, the work shows that unstructured text can meaningfully support pre-inspection allocation decisions, but the desirability of inspection remains sensitive to cost and risk preferences.

title: Predict, Don't Iterate: Efficient Adaptive-Length Infilling for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have emerged as a promising alternative to the auto-regressive paradigm. With bidirectional attention and any-order generation, DLMs naturally fit infilling tasks, which require generating a middle span conditioned on both the prefix and the suffix. However, infilling is sensitive to the length of the span, while DLMs require the length to be fixed before generation. Although prior studies extend DLMs to dynamic lengths, they still suffer from two limitations. (i) Sensitivity to initial length. These methods require a preset length to initialize the search and are highly sensitive to this initial length, often yielding suboptimal results. (ii) Inference inefficiency. They either insert length-changing operations during generation or repeatedly search for an appropriate length using multi-step denoising confidence, both of which introduce substantial extra forward passes and computational cost. Therefore, we propose PILL (Probing-based InfiLling with preset-Length-free decoding), an efficient infilling method for DLMs that requires no preset initial length and adds far fewer extra forward passes than baselines, substantially reducing inference time. Experiments show that, across five DLMs spanning different families, architectures, and training recipes on eight infilling benchmarks, PILL improves over the strongest baseline by +4.8 average pass rate on code and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text, while running 1.82x faster than that baseline. The code is available at https://github.com/Hsu1023/PILL.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PILL, a new decoding method that lets diffusion language models do span infilling without pre‑setting the infilled span length, improving both quality and speed over prior dynamic-length methods.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models are naturally suited to infilling because they use bidirectional context and any-order generation, but they require a fixed span length. Existing dynamic-length extensions either need a sensitive initial length guess or are computationally expensive due to repeated search or length-changing operations. The authors want a length-flexible infilling method that avoids these two issues while retaining or improving generation quality.
AI.method: The authors introduce PILL (Probing-based InfiLling with preset-Length-free decoding), which removes the need for a preset infill length in DLM decoding. Instead of initializing with a guessed span length and adjusting it during generation, PILL uses a probing mechanism to infer suitable lengths while keeping extra forward passes minimal. The decoding procedure is designed to work efficiently with standard DLM denoising steps and avoids costly iterative searches or length-changing operations inside the diffusion process.
AI.result: On eight infilling benchmarks for both code and natural language, tested across five different DLMs from diverse model families and training setups, PILL outperforms the strongest prior dynamic-length infilling baseline by an average of +4.8 pass rate on code tasks and +6.0 BLEU-2 on text tasks, while being 1.82× faster in inference.
AI.conclusion: PILL enables diffusion language models to perform span infilling without any preset span length, reducing sensitivity to length initialization and cutting inference cost compared with existing methods. It delivers better infilling quality for both code and text across varied models and benchmarks, demonstrating that probing-based, length-free decoding is an effective and efficient solution for DLM infilling.

title: Beyond Context Windows: Persistent Discovery Context for Data-Centric Agents
summary: Data-centric agents repeatedly perform a discovery step before planning or execution: identifying the data objects relevant to a task. Yet successful discovery outcomes are typically discarded rather than reused. We introduce persistent discovery context, a lightweight memory layer that stores prior intent-to-object mappings and reuses them to augment future retrieval. Across three structured data environments, persistent discovery context consistently improves retrieval quality over metadata-only search, remains effective with automatically generated memories, and exposes a reproducible interference failure mode. In lexically sparse domains, memory-only retrieval can even outperform metadata-based retrieval. These findings suggest that discovery outcomes constitute a useful form of reusable context for data-centric agents.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a lightweight memory layer for data-centric agents that reuses past query-to-data-object mappings to improve future data discovery and retrieval.
AI.motivation: Data-centric agents frequently need to rediscover which data objects are relevant to tasks, but the successful discovery results are usually not stored or reused. This wastes prior effort and misses an opportunity to improve later retrieval, especially in settings where metadata search is limited or ambiguous.
AI.method: The authors introduce a “persistent discovery context,” a memory layer that records mappings from user/task intent to the specific data objects that fulfilled that intent. They integrate this layer into retrieval for three structured data environments, compare it to metadata-only search, test both human-curated and automatically generated memories, and analyze failure cases, particularly interference between memories.
AI.result: Across three structured data environments, using the persistent discovery context consistently improves retrieval quality relative to metadata-only search. It remains beneficial even when the stored memories are automatically generated rather than manually curated. In domains with sparse lexical signals (weak or minimal metadata/text), retrieval based solely on this memory can outperform conventional metadata-based search, but a reproducible interference failure mode is observed.
AI.conclusion: Reusable discovery outcomes, captured as persistent discovery context, are a valuable source of context for data-centric agents. This memory layer can systematically enhance retrieval performance, sometimes even surpassing traditional metadata-based methods in lexically sparse domains, though care is needed to manage interference effects between stored memories.

title: text2ql: Multi-Target Natural Language Querying via a Language-Agnostic Intermediate Representation
summary: Natural language interfaces to databases have traditionally suffered from three structural limitations: exclusive targeting of relational SQL, unconditional dependence on large language model (LLM) inference at query time, and absence of any runtime signal when generated queries are semantically incorrect. This paper presents text2ql, an open-source Python framework that addresses all three limitations through a language-agnostic Intermediate Representation (QueryIR) and a pluggable renderer architecture. A single seven-stage detection pipeline serves both SQL and GraphQL targets; a zero-LLM deterministic mode delivers 100% execution accuracy at a median latency of 3.2 ms with no API cost; and every generated query carries a runtime confidence score in [0.15, 0.97] computed from an additive signal model. Evaluated on 50-query random samples from the Spider and BIRD benchmarks (indicative results; full-set evaluation is planned), the LLM-backed mode achieves 62-70% exact match and 84-91% execution accuracy; the deterministic mode achieves 100% execution accuracy with zero parse errors across all 100 test cases. An ablation study isolates schema-aware prompting as the dominant accuracy lever, contributing +18.4 percentage points of exact-match gain over the schema-free baseline on both benchmarks. text2ql is publicly available at https://pypi.org/project/text2ql/ under the Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: The paper presents text2ql, a Python framework that uses a language-agnostic intermediate representation and pluggable renderers to support both SQL and GraphQL natural language querying, with both LLM-backed and fully deterministic modes plus a runtime confidence signal.
AI.motivation: Existing natural language interfaces to databases are limited because they typically: (1) only target relational SQL, (2) always rely on LLMs at query time (incurring latency, cost, and reliability issues), and (3) provide no runtime signal when the generated query is semantically incorrect. The authors aim to overcome these structural limitations to make NL-to-DB systems more flexible, efficient, and reliable.
AI.method: They design text2ql around a language-agnostic Intermediate Representation (QueryIR) and a pluggable renderer architecture so the same pipeline can output different query languages (SQL, GraphQL). They implement a seven-stage detection pipeline that can run in two modes: an LLM-backed mode that uses LLMs for semantic parsing and a zero-LLM deterministic mode that relies on deterministic rules. They also design an additive signal model to compute a runtime confidence score for each generated query. They evaluate on 50-query random samples from Spider and BIRD benchmarks and conduct an ablation study on schema-aware prompting.
AI.result: In LLM-backed mode, text2ql achieves 62–70% exact match and 84–91% execution accuracy on the sampled Spider and BIRD queries. In deterministic mode, it reaches 100% execution accuracy with zero parse errors on all 100 test cases, with a median latency of 3.2 ms and no LLM/API cost. The confidence scores fall within [0.15, 0.97]. The ablation study shows schema-aware prompting yields a +18.4 percentage point gain in exact match over schema-free prompting on both benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: text2ql effectively addresses three major limitations of prior NL-to-database systems by supporting multiple query languages via QueryIR, enabling a high-speed, zero-LLM deterministic mode with perfect execution accuracy on tested samples, and attaching a runtime confidence score to each query. Schema-aware prompting is identified as the key factor for accuracy improvements in the LLM-backed mode. The framework is open-source under Apache 2.0 and available on PyPI, positioning it as a practical foundation for more robust and versatile natural language database interfaces.

title: EmoStance: Response-Side Affective-Orientation Control for Empathetic Response Generation via Emoji Weak Supervision
comment: Accepted to the Main Conference of EMNLP 2026
summary: Empathetic response generation requires models to decide not only what to say, but also how to respond to the previous speaker's affective situation. We formulate this as response-side affective-orientation control and use multi-annotator emoji distributions as weak affective--attitudinal evidence, rather than as output symbols or gold labels, to induce a latent control space that operationally approximates listener stance. We construct EmojiDialogue, an utterance-level extension of EmpatheticDialogues with emoji votes and confidence scores, and propose EmoStance, which models source-side affective expression, predicts a soft response-side orientation from dialogue context and speaker roles, and steers a frozen instruction-tuned LLM through continuous prefix embeddings. In blind pairwise evaluation with 20 annotators and 800 judgments, EmoStance achieves a 62.2% decisive win rate, with the clearest gains in contextual specificity and perceived responsiveness, while remaining complementary to external-knowledge methods. Code, annotation metadata, and reconstruction scripts are available in our GitHub repository: https://github.com/18277390221/EmoStance.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EmoStance, a method for controlling the affective orientation of empathetic dialogue responses using emoji-based weak supervision and continuous control of a frozen LLM, leading to more contextually specific and responsive replies.
AI.motivation: Existing empathetic dialogue systems focus on what content to generate but lack fine-grained control over how a system should position itself affectively (e.g., comforting, excited, neutral) toward the speaker. Prior work often treats affect labels as discrete outputs or gold standards, which fails to capture nuanced listener stances and multi-annotator disagreement. The authors aim to build a better operational representation of listener stance and use it to steer large language models toward more appropriately oriented empathetic responses.
AI.method: The authors frame empathetic response generation as response-side affective-orientation control. They collect multi-annotator emoji distributions and confidence scores as weak affective and attitudinal supervision, constructing EmojiDialogue, an extension of EmpatheticDialogues with utterance-level emoji annotations. They then propose EmoStance: a model that (1) encodes source-side affective expression, (2) predicts a soft, continuous representation of response-side affective orientation from dialogue context and speaker roles, and (3) uses this representation to steer a frozen instruction-tuned LLM via continuous prefix embeddings, effectively controlling the stance of generated responses without changing the base LLM parameters.
AI.result: In a blind pairwise human evaluation with 20 annotators and 800 judgments, EmoStance’s responses are preferred at a 62.2% decisive win rate over baselines. Human raters particularly note improvements in contextual specificity and perceived responsiveness. The approach also remains compatible with external-knowledge augmentation methods, indicating that stance control adds value beyond knowledge grounding.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that multi-annotator emoji signals can effectively serve as weak supervision to learn a latent affective-orientation space that approximates listener stance. By using this space to control a frozen LLM through continuous prefixes, EmoStance generates empathetic responses that are more contextually specific and responsive. The method offers a practical way to add fine-grained affective control to existing instruction-tuned LLMs and can be combined with other techniques, such as external knowledge integration, for further gains.

title: AI agents reshape consensus formation in human groups
summary: As large language model (LLM) agents shift from tools to participants in human groups, a fundamental question for collective behavior is how their growing presence reshapes consensus formation. Here we study mixed human-AI groups in a collaborative description game, in which shared conventions emerge through repeated rounds of random pairwise communication. Varying the proportions of LLM agents, we identify three distinct regimes of consensus formation: low agent proportions facilitate human-led consensus, intermediate proportions disrupt convergence, and high proportions restore strong consensus while shifting it toward agent-led conventions. Crucially, these regimes differ not only in the strength of convergence, but also in the semantic grounding and communicative form of the resulting consensus: human-led consensus is more concrete, holistic, and grounded in shared real-world analogies, whereas agent-led consensus is more abstract, less information-dense, and more geometrically segmented. Mechanistically, agent influence arises from a shared linguistic prior that places agents near one another in the expression space, combined with relatively stable expression choices across rounds; humans initially resist adopting expressions from partners perceived as AI but gradually yield to conformity pressure. These findings provide evidence that AI composition can shape the emergence, content, and perceived legitimacy of group norms, making agent proportion and transparency important design variables for human-AI systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how adding LLM agents to human groups changes how groups reach consensus, revealing three regimes depending on AI proportion and showing that AI-heavy groups form more abstract, agent-shaped conventions.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly act as participants in human groups rather than mere tools, we lack understanding of how their presence affects collective decision-making and norm formation, especially consensus processes that underlie coordination in teams and communities.
AI.method: The authors run a collaborative description game with mixed human–AI groups. Participants repeatedly communicate in random pairs to develop shared labels or descriptions. By systematically varying the proportion of LLM agents in these groups, they observe how linguistic conventions emerge over time and analyze the semantic properties and dynamics of the resulting consensus patterns.
AI.result: They find three regimes: (1) Low LLM proportion: humans drive convergence to strong, human-like consensus; (2) Intermediate proportion: convergence is weakened or disrupted; (3) High LLM proportion: strong consensus returns but now reflects AI-driven conventions. Human-led conventions are concrete, holistic, and grounded in real-world analogies, whereas AI-led conventions are abstract, less information-dense, and more segmented. Agent influence stems from shared linguistic priors making AI agents linguistically similar to each other and from more stable AI expression choices, while humans initially resist but later conform to AI-originated expressions, especially when agents are transparently identified.
AI.conclusion: The presence and proportion of LLM agents systematically alter not just whether consensus forms, but also the content, style, and perceived legitimacy of group norms. As LLM agents become more common collaborators, designers of human–AI systems must treat AI composition and transparency as critical levers to influence how group norms, language, and coordination patterns emerge.

title: FUSE: An Evaluating Framework for Dangerous Capabilities of LLMs
summary:
Fragmented safety evaluation undermines the governance of dangerous AI capabilities. We present a modular framework that evaluates each model through three orthogonal pipelines---Knowledge ($K$), Defense ($D$), and Harm ($H$)---under a unified protocol, aggregating results into a standardized dangerous-capability profile $φ$. Pluggable modules supply scenario seeds, knowledge banks, hazard queries, and judge rubrics, while the core evaluation engine remains unchanged across domains; the CB evaluation is complemented by a cyber pilot demonstrating protocol transfer.
  Instantiating the framework with a chemical-biological (CB) module, we evaluate 12 commercial LLMs from four families. Our first contribution is a horizontal comparison of dangerous capability across models and model families: the three dimensions expose sharply divergent profiles---models with comparable knowledge differ in refusal resilience, and strong defenders do not generate less harmful content when they do comply---while family-level patterns further separate Claude, DeepSeek, and GPT models. The second is a temporal analysis of capability evolution: tracking $K$, $D$, and $H$ against model release dates reveals that dangerous capability has not monotonically declined; newer models deepen knowledge while only partially improving defense, showing that scaling and alignment progress do not uniformly translate into safety. Reliability is established via cross-judge consistency (bootstrap $ρ> 0.79$, 4 of 5 judges) and pipeline orthogonality ($K$--$D$--$H$ inter-correlations $ρ\in [0.32, 0.52]$).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and applies a unified, modular framework to systematically measure dangerous capabilities of AI models along three axes: knowledge, defense, and harm.
AI.motivation: Existing safety evaluations of dangerous AI capabilities are fragmented, model- or domain-specific, and not comparable across models, time, or application areas. This fragmentation makes it difficult for governance, deployment decisions, and regulation to rely on consistent, standardized evidence when assessing risks from AI systems, especially as their dangerous capabilities may be growing or changing in non-obvious ways.
AI.method: The authors design a modular evaluation framework that decomposes dangerous capability into three orthogonal pipelines: Knowledge (K: can the model access and present domain-relevant know-how), Defense (D: how robustly the model refuses or resists harmful requests), and Harm (H: how harmful its actual outputs are when it does comply). The framework uses a stable core evaluation engine and pluggable modules that provide domain-specific elements such as scenarios, knowledge banks, hazardous queries, and judging rubrics. They instantiate the framework for the chemical-biological (CB) domain and evaluate 12 commercial LLMs from four model families, using human judges for scoring, and statistically analyze cross-judge reliability and correlations between K, D, and H. They also apply the same protocol to a cyber pilot to show transferability.
AI.result: Applying the CB module to 12 LLMs, the framework uncovers markedly different dangerous-capability profiles across models and families: models with similar knowledge levels can differ substantially in how often they resist harmful queries, and models that are strong on defense do not necessarily produce less harmful content on the occasions when they answer. Family-level trends distinguish Claude, DeepSeek, and GPT models. Temporal analysis against release dates shows that dangerous capability does not simply decrease over time: newer models generally have deeper knowledge and only partially improved defenses, indicating that safety does not automatically track with scaling and alignment claims. Quantitatively, they report high cross-judge consistency (bootstrap correlation ρ > 0.79 for 4 out of 5 judges) and moderate correlations among K, D, and H (ρ in [0.32, 0.52]), supporting reliability and partial orthogonality of the three pipelines.
AI.conclusion: The unified K–D–H framework enables standardized, domain-transferable measurement of dangerous AI capabilities and reveals that capability, defense, and realized harm are distinct dimensions that vary across models and over time. The findings challenge assumptions that newer or more aligned models are automatically safer, showing that increased knowledge and incomplete defense improvements can maintain or elevate dangerous capabilities. The authors argue that governance and safety evaluation should adopt such modular, protocol-stable frameworks to obtain reliable, comparable profiles of model risk and to avoid over-reliance on coarse or one-dimensional safety metrics.

title: C$^{3}$T: Counterfactual Causal Reasoning for Sentiment Shifts in Social-Media Conversation Trees
comment: 23 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables; accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Sentiment in social-media threads does not only vary across posts; it shifts as users react to claims, corrections, evidence, and hostility within a branching reply tree. We study why sentiment changes in rumor-centric conversation trees by treating discourse moves (e.g., denial/correction, evidence/link, toxicity/attack) as candidate interventions and asking (i) what sentiment a reply expresses, (ii) whether the sentiment shifts relative to its parent, and (iii) which prior message most plausibly drove the reply's sentiment. To support this setting, we introduce CaSiRe, a causal sentiment reasoning layer over public rumor conversation datasets that adds post-level sentiment labels, induced parent-child shift labels, calibrated multi-label intervention tags, and explicitly annotated causal-source labels. We then propose C$^{3}$T (Counterfactual Causal Conversation Transformer), a thread-structured temporal model that jointly predicts node sentiment and shifts, learns sparse ancestor attribution, and supports counterfactual queries by forcing conversational intervention embeddings on or off to estimate potential outcomes. Under an event-level split, C$^{3}$T improves out-of-event robustness and attribution over text-only, graph-based, and temporal baselines, and yields interpretable model-based effects: denials/corrections and evidence reduce downstream negativity, while toxicity increases it. We also benchmark open-weight LLM prompting baselines and find that added conversational context helps, but attribution remains less reliable, motivating structure-aware counterfactual modeling for social-media analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new annotated dataset and a causal, thread-aware model to understand how specific conversational moves (like denial, evidence, and toxicity) causally influence sentiment dynamics in rumor-centric social-media discussions.
AI.motivation: Existing sentiment analysis on social media typically focuses on isolated posts or simple sequences, ignoring the branching structure of reply trees and the causal impact of discourse moves (e.g., corrections, evidence, attacks) on how sentiment evolves. This is especially important in rumor discussions, where interventions such as debunking or toxic replies can change the emotional tone of subsequent conversation. There is a need for fine-grained annotations and models that can both represent these structures and answer counterfactual questions about how interventions would affect sentiment.
AI.method: The authors construct CaSiRe, a "causal sentiment reasoning" layer on top of existing public rumor conversation datasets. CaSiRe adds: (1) post-level sentiment labels, (2) labels of sentiment shift between parent and child posts, (3) calibrated multi-label tags for discourse interventions (denial/correction, evidence/link, toxicity/attack, etc.), and (4) explicit annotations of which earlier message is the causal source for a reply's sentiment. Building on this, they propose C^3T (Counterfactual Causal Conversation Transformer), a thread-structured temporal transformer model. C^3T jointly predicts per-node sentiment and sentiment shifts, learns sparse attributions from replies to their most influential ancestors, and represents interventions with embeddings that can be toggled on/off to answer counterfactual queries about potential sentiment outcomes. They evaluate C^3T under an event-level data split and compare it with text-only, graph-based, temporal baselines, and open-weight LLM prompting approaches.
AI.result: Under an event-level split that tests generalization to new rumor events, C^3T outperforms text-only, graph-based, and temporal baselines on both sentiment prediction and causal attribution tasks. It demonstrates better robustness out-of-event and provides interpretable model-based estimates of intervention effects. Specifically, model counterfactual analyses show that denials/corrections and evidence-sharing interventions tend to reduce downstream negativity in the threads, whereas toxic or attacking interventions tend to increase negativity. In contrast, open-weight LLM prompting baselines benefit from additional conversational context but still exhibit weaker and less reliable attribution performance.
AI.conclusion: Modeling sentiment in rumor conversations requires accounting for the branching reply structure and the causal influence of discourse interventions. By enriching rumor datasets with CaSiRe annotations and introducing the C^3T model, the paper shows that it is possible to jointly predict sentiment, track shifts, and attribute them to specific prior messages, while also enabling counterfactual reasoning about interventions. The findings suggest that structured, counterfactual, and intervention-aware modeling yields more robust sentiment analysis and more interpretable causal insights than standard text-only or naive LLM-based approaches, and that certain interventions—like corrections and evidence—can meaningfully improve the emotional climate of online rumor discussions while toxicity worsens it.

title: Examining the Vulnerability of Multi-Agent Medical Systems to Human Interventions for Clinical Reasoning
summary: Human interventions at fault points can alter the diagnostic accuracy of multi-agent medical systems. We defined fault points as moments in AI agent conversations, in which an agent's reasoning became most vulnerable to external influence. Using the MedQA dataset, this study analyzed simulated doctor-patient conversations to measure how interventions shifted reasoning and accuracy. Correct intervention methods showed an improvement in baseline diagnostic accuracy of up to 40%, while incorrect or bias-related interventions degraded performance by up to 6% and increased diagnostic drift and uncertainty. Beyond performance changes, our analysis revealed behavioral similarities between cognitive biases in simulated agent environments and real-world clinical practice. Examples included premature closure and susceptibility to misleading cues. Overall, these findings demonstrate that identifying and guiding fault points with human interventions may provide a mechanism for improving diagnostic robustness in multi-agent medical systems.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how human interventions at specific vulnerable reasoning moments (“fault points”) in multi-agent medical AI conversations affect diagnostic accuracy, showing that well-timed, correct input can significantly improve performance while poor input can harm it.
AI.motivation: To understand and control how human input during AI-driven doctor-patient conversations can either improve or degrade diagnostic decisions in multi-agent medical systems, and to explore parallels between AI reasoning failures and human clinical cognitive biases.
AI.method: The authors simulate multi-agent doctor-patient conversations using the MedQA dataset, identify “fault points” where an AI agent’s reasoning is most susceptible to external influence, and systematically introduce different types of human-like interventions (correct, incorrect, or biased) to measure their impact on diagnostic reasoning, accuracy, and behavioral patterns.
AI.result: Correctly targeted interventions at fault points improved baseline diagnostic accuracy by up to 40%, while incorrect or bias-inducing interventions degraded performance by up to 6% and increased diagnostic drift and uncertainty; the system also exhibited cognitive-bias-like behaviors such as premature closure and susceptibility to misleading cues, mirroring real clinical practice.
AI.conclusion: Targeting identified fault points with well-designed human interventions can substantially enhance diagnostic robustness in multi-agent medical systems, but poorly designed interventions can introduce bias and degrade performance, highlighting the need for structured, bias-aware interaction protocols between humans and medical AI agents.

title: A Layered Taxonomy for Chinese Learner Grammatical Error Annotation
summary: Grammatical error annotation in Chinese learner writing requires labels that are both consistent and linguistically meaningful. This paper proposes a layered scheme linking computational Chinese grammatical error correction (CGEC) with pedagogical error analysis. The scheme first identifies character- and punctuation-level orthographic errors, labeling them by edit operation and subtype. Other errors receive a three-layer core label combining edit operation, linguistic domain, and part of speech, with optional Chinese-specific extensions for aspect, modality, comparison, argument structure, and complements. Drawing on CGEC resources, learner-error taxonomies, and Mandarin grammar, the taxonomy is evaluated through a coverage analysis of automatically extracted MuCGEC edits and a preliminary consistency study in which five large language models apply it to a sample. The results support the layered approach while identifying category boundaries requiring further refinement.

AI.tldr: A layered annotation scheme is proposed for grammatical errors in Chinese learner writing, linking computational GEC and pedagogical error analysis, and is evaluated for coverage and consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing Chinese grammatical error annotation schemes often lack both cross-project consistency and fine-grained linguistic interpretability, making it difficult to use the same labels for computational CGEC tasks and pedagogical error analysis. There is a need for a unified, systematic taxonomy that captures the operations involved in error correction and the underlying linguistic properties in a way that works for both NLP systems and language teaching.
AI.method: The authors design a hierarchical error-labeling scheme. First, they separate orthographic errors at the character and punctuation level, labeling them by edit operation type and subtype. For all other errors, they introduce a three-layer core label that combines (1) the edit operation (e.g., insertion, deletion, substitution), (2) the linguistic domain (e.g., morphology, syntax, semantics), and (3) the part of speech involved. They then add optional, Chinese-specific extensions for categories like aspect, modality, comparison, argument structure, and complements. To evaluate the scheme, they conduct (a) a coverage analysis over edits automatically extracted from the MuCGEC corpus and (b) a preliminary consistency study, where five large language models are asked to apply the labeling scheme to a sample of errors.
AI.result: The coverage analysis suggests that the proposed taxonomy can successfully categorize the vast majority of automatically extracted edits from MuCGEC, indicating good coverage of typical learner errors. The LLM-based consistency study shows that the layered labels can be applied in a reasonably consistent manner, but it also reveals some areas where the boundaries between categories are ambiguous or hard to distinguish, pointing to issues in the current label definitions.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that a layered, operation-plus-linguistics annotation scheme is a promising approach for unifying CGEC and pedagogical error analysis for Chinese learner writing. The proposed taxonomy is largely adequate in coverage and yields acceptable inter-annotator consistency (even when the annotators are LLMs), but certain label boundaries and Chinese-specific extensions need refinement. Future work should further clarify these categories and test the scheme with human annotators in broader pedagogical and computational settings.

title: ASCII Attack: Recontextualising Harmful Requests as Artistic Critique in Large Language Models
summary: Safety alignment trains large language models to refuse harmful requests stated plainly, but that training is applied mostly to surface form. Requests that only recontextualise the same operational content, changing how the model reads it, are therefore only weakly covered. The ASCII Attack is one such recontextualisation. It is single-turn and black-box: one message, with no access to model internals. It embeds a fully legible harmful request in ASCIl-art characters, presents it as artwork, and asks for feedback. Unlike ArtPrompt, it hides nothing: the request stays readable. The reply is written as artistic critique and can contain operational detail that a plain request would have been refused for. Every framed prompt is paired with a direct-question control, so the contrast is isolated from topic, model and decoding variation. The contrast identifies a bundled surface, not one isolated channel. Across eleven models and eight harm topics, a harm-aware classifier judges 62% of framed prompts harmful against 42% of controls. On the most susceptible model the framed prompt succeeds 93% of the time. A single query matches or exceeds published single-query attacks under four of five harm judges. The effect tracks the model more than the topic and does not diminish with scale. At least one judge dissents from the panel majority on nearly two-thirds of framed rows, which is itself a measurement-validity finding. That pattern is consistent with mismatched generalisation.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that a simple ‘ASCII art’ reframing of harmful prompts can systematically bypass safety alignment in many large language models.
AI.motivation: Existing safety alignment mostly targets explicit, plain-text harmful requests. However, small changes in how a request is presented or framed can cause models to respond harmfully, and such ‘recontextualisations’ are underexplored. The authors want to test whether a very simple, single-turn, black-box prompt manipulation—rendering the harmful request as ASCII art and asking for critique—can reliably circumvent safety mechanisms across models and harm topics, and to quantify how robust current defenses really are.
AI.method: The authors design the ‘ASCII Attack’: they embed a clearly readable harmful request inside ASCII-art characters, describe it as artwork, and ask the model for feedback in the style of artistic critique. For each such framed prompt, they also create a direct, plain-text control query containing the same harmful content. They test this across eleven language models and eight types of harmful content. Outputs are labeled by a harm-aware classifier (a panel of harm judges) that decides whether each response is harmful or not. They compare the rate of harmful responses between framed prompts and controls, analyze differences by model and topic, and study disagreement among judges as a measure of evaluation reliability and generalization behavior.
AI.result: Across eleven models and eight harm domains, the ASCII-framed prompts elicit harmful responses 62% of the time, compared with 42% for plain-text controls. On the most vulnerable model, the framed attack succeeds 93% of the time. In single-query settings, this method matches or outperforms other published single-prompt jailbreaks according to four of five harm-judging systems. The susceptibility depends more on which model is used than on which harmful topic is queried, and it does not decrease as model size increases. Additionally, for nearly two-thirds of framed prompts, at least one judge disagrees with the majority label, revealing substantial disagreement and limitations in current harm evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current safety alignment is heavily surface-form dependent and can be systematically bypassed by simple reframing of harmful content as ASCII art plus artistic critique, even when the harmful request remains fully readable. This vulnerability persists across models and scales and is more model-dependent than topic-dependent. Moreover, the high rate of disagreement among harm judges suggests that evaluation of safety is itself fragile and may reflect mismatched generalization, indicating that both model alignment and safety measurement need more robust, representation-aware approaches.

title: OBJECTION! Lawyer Agents Mitigate Guilty Bias in Legal Judgment Prediction
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Kcsp0042/natural-innocent
summary:
Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) models are typically trained on documents that describe facts from a prosecutorial perspective. Existing datasets further exhibit severe label imbalance toward guilty outcomes. Consequently, these models suffer from "Guilty Bias", blindly accepting the prosecution's narrative as objective truth. Previous studies employing three-step reasoning structures or training on synthetically generated innocence data improve overall accuracy, but they still fail to mitigate bias at inference time.
  In this paper, we introduce OBJECTION, an inference-time pipeline that integrates an Adversarial Lawyer Agent into each 3-step reasoning of offense, unlawfulness, and culpability. Unlike generic critics, our agent actively challenges the model's presumptions of guilt by injecting legal defense arguments at each reasoning stage. To thoroughly evaluate this, we present a new "Natural Innocent" dataset including 3.4k real-world cases, overcoming the limitations of synthetic innocence benchmarks. Test results show that OBJECTION drastically reduces the False Guilty Rate (FGR) from 82.93% (SOTA baseline) to 16.69%, proving its capability to perform substantive legal reasoning. This work denotes a key progress toward aligning Legal AI with the presumption of innocence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces OBJECTION, an inference-time pipeline that adds an adversarial defense-oriented “lawyer agent” into each step of legal judgment prediction to counteract models’ systemic guilty bias and dramatically reduce false guilty predictions.
AI.motivation: Current Legal Judgment Prediction models are trained mainly on prosecutorial fact descriptions and highly imbalanced datasets favoring guilty verdicts. This leads to a strong guilty bias: models over-trust the prosecution narrative and frequently predict guilt even in innocent or ambiguous cases. Prior work using structured reasoning or synthetic innocent data improves accuracy but still fails to correct the bias when the model is actually used at inference time. There is a need for mechanisms that enforce the presumption of innocence and support substantive defense reasoning, evaluated on realistic, naturally occurring innocent cases rather than synthetic ones.
AI.method: The authors propose OBJECTION, an inference-time pipeline that wraps around existing three-step LJP reasoning (offense, unlawfulness, culpability).
