Retrieval-augmented generation is not reliably beneficial and can even be harmful unless carefully controlled and combined with NER in a fine-tuned model. The best-performing configuration is fine-tuned BioBART with NER, suggesting future work should prioritize robust clinical entity extraction over generic retrieval mechanisms for patient-facing radiology communication.

title: SCX Router: Streaming Zero-Shot Model Selection with a Decoder-KV Classifier and a Real-World Task Ontology
summary: The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs) and the growing diversity of their applications presents a unique optimization opportunity: selecting the right model for the task, while optimizing for speed, cost, and quality at a per-task level. However, inference endpoints can vary widely in quality, price, latency, context support, tool use, domain expertise, and reasoning behavior. This heterogeneity makes manual heuristics difficult to maintain and unlikely to achieve consistently favorable speed--cost--quality trade-offs on their own. We introduce \router{}, a lightweight GLiClass-based router that assigns a suitability score to each inference-time model label without autoregressive generation. The released 0.6B-parameter checkpoint combines a Qwen3 decoder with a shallow bidirectional scorer. Its decoder-KV execution path preserves a text-only key--value cache across a session, encodes only new dialogue turns, and evaluates transient candidate-label tokens without adding them to the persistent cache. The same checkpoint also predicts task type, difficulty, reasoning mode, and expected output length, and supports custom zero-shot labels. For task generation, we construct a task ontology with 23 families, 115 task types, 345 routable subtypes, 1,173 synthetic examples, and an orthogonal axis of 30 domains. Using this structure, we generate 150,000 verifier-scored tasks and 15,000 open-ended tasks. We then train the Qwen3 decoder on these tasks, while explicitly separating learned request prediction from per-task policies for attributes such as eligibility, cost, cache reuse, safety, and sovereignty. Across six LiveBench subsets, the router outperforms the mean candidate; on the selected 1,000-task subset, it achieves an aggregate top-1 score of 0.707 versus 0.696 for the strongest fixed model, with benchmark-dependent gains.

AI.tldr: They propose a lightweight LLM-based router that, without full generation, predicts which model is best for each incoming task to optimize speed, cost, and quality, and show it can outperform always using a single strong model.
AI.motivation: Many different LLM endpoints exist with varying cost, latency, context size, reasoning skills, and quality. Manually deciding which model to use per request is complex and brittle, and naive static choices fail to exploit the trade-off between cost, speed, and quality. The paper aims to automatically and efficiently route each task to the most suitable model while also characterizing the task itself.
AI.method: They build a 0.6B-parameter router based on GLiClass and a Qwen3 decoder combined with a shallow bidirectional scorer. The model assigns suitability scores to model labels without autoregressive generation. It reuses a text-only key–value cache across a session, only encodes new dialogue turns, and evaluates candidate model-label tokens transiently. The same checkpoint is multitask: it predicts task type, difficulty, reasoning mode, expected output length, and can handle custom zero-shot labels. They design a detailed task ontology (23 families, 115 task types, 345 subtypes, 30 domains) and generate 150k verifier-scored and 15k open-ended tasks. They train the Qwen3 decoder on this structured dataset, separating learned request prediction from policy rules governing eligibility, cost, cache reuse, safety, and sovereignty.
AI.result: On six subsets of LiveBench, the router’s model-selection strategy beats the mean performance of the candidate models. On a focused 1,000-task benchmark subset, routing achieves a top-1 aggregated score of 0.707, slightly higher than the best single fixed model (0.696), with improvements varying across benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A small, efficient LLM-based router can effectively predict task properties and choose among heterogeneous LLM endpoints without full generation, yielding better overall performance than simply using a single strong model. The structured task ontology and separation between prediction and policy make the system flexible for real-world deployment constraints like cost, safety, and sovereignty.

title: Before the Script, Set the Stage: How Worldview Simulation Amplifies Psychologically Grounded Persuasion in Multi-Turn Jailbreaking
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-turn jailbreak attacks demonstrate that harmful intent can be distributed across dialogue, yet existing methods obscure what conversational mechanisms drive vulnerability. We introduce BLUEPRINT, a safety-evaluation framework separating a factorized social-influence strategy space from WORLDVIEWSIM, a cross-turn situational context module. Monte Carlo Tree Search optimizes turn-level combinations of 18 theory-grounded influence factors across a four-turn trajectory. Across six frontier models, BLUEPRINT achieves near-ceiling ASR on major open-weight and proprietary models, while requiring the fewest average queries (2.46). The resulting trajectories further reveal model-specific vulnerability among resistant targets: each responds to distinct influence factors and strategy transitions, yet all share a common recovery pathway-shifting toward concrete, executable task framing consistently escapes hard-refusal states. Ablations confirm operational cues matter most: making requests actionable has the largest impact, gain framing is unusually potent, and some legitimacy appeals can backfire. These findings suggest robust multi-turn safety requires monitoring not only harmful content, but also how dialogue state makes unsafe requests appear concrete and locally executable.

AI.tldr: BLUEPRINT is a framework to systematically generate and analyze multi-turn jailbreak attacks on LLMs using a factorized social-influence strategy space and situational context modeling, achieving high attack success and revealing model-specific yet patterned vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-turn jailbreak studies show that malicious intent can be spread across a dialogue, but they don’t clearly explain which conversational strategies and mechanisms actually drive models to break safety rules. The authors want a principled, theory-grounded way to probe and understand these vulnerabilities rather than treating jailbreak prompts as ad-hoc tricks.
AI.method: They propose BLUEPRINT, which separates (1) a space of 18 social-influence strategies (e.g., framing, legitimacy, operationalization) from (2) WORLDVIEWSIM, a module modeling cross-turn situational context. Using Monte Carlo Tree Search, they search over combinations of these strategies across a 4-turn conversation to find effective attack trajectories. They then evaluate BLUEPRINT-generated conversations against six advanced LLMs (both open-weight and proprietary) and perform ablation studies on specific influence factors.
AI.result: BLUEPRINT attains near-maximum attack success rates on several leading models while using relatively few queries on average (2.46 turns). The discovered conversations show that different models are vulnerable to different social-influence strategies and different points of transition during the dialogue, but they also display a shared pattern: re-framing the interaction into specific, concrete, executable tasks tends to break through refusal states. Ablation experiments further show that operational cues (concreteness and actionability) are the most influential, gain framing is particularly effective, and some attempts to appeal to legitimacy can actually decrease attack success.
AI.conclusion: Multi-turn LLM safety cannot be guaranteed by only filtering explicit harmful content; it must also consider how dialogue dynamics and social-influence strategies can gradually transform a vague or high-level request into a concrete, executable task that appears locally safe to the model. BLUEPRINT offers a structured way to study these dynamics, and its findings highlight specific risk factors (actionable framing, gain framing, certain legitimacy cues) that designers need to monitor and defend against to build more robust safety mechanisms.

title: Improving Evaluation Realism with Inference-Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
comment: 70 pages, 43 figures, 4 tables (13 figures in the main text). Under review at NeurIPS 2026. Code: https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/petri_dish and https://github.com/AxelAhlqvist1995/petri-bon ; reproduction assets: https://github.com/AxelAhlqvist1995/petri-realism-reproduction
summary: A core obstacle to alignment evaluation is evaluation awareness: capable models can tell when they are being tested rather than deployed, weakening the conclusions a safety evaluation can support. We present two techniques that make simulated alignment evaluations harder to distinguish from real deployments. Our first technique, critique refinement, spends additional inference-time compute on each simulator action: the simulator generates multiple candidate actions, refines them using feedback from an instance of the target model on how to make them more realistic, and continues the evaluation with the most deployment-like candidate. Our second technique, DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), wraps the target in an agent harness, reducing the gap between simulated and real deployment environments in coding settings. We test the techniques on multiple target models and find that they compose: applying both yields larger realism gains than either alone. Our results show that automated approaches can improve the realism of alignment evaluations, and that these improvements use additional compute more effectively than making the audits longer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes methods to make simulated alignment evaluations harder for AI models to distinguish from real-world deployments, improving the realism and reliability of safety assessments.
AI.motivation: AI models may behave differently when they detect they are under evaluation (being 'tested') versus real deployment, undermining the validity of alignment and safety evaluations. The authors want to close this gap so that evaluation better reflects real-world behavior.
AI.method: They introduce two techniques: (1) critique refinement, where a simulator generates multiple candidate actions and uses feedback from the target model to iteratively refine these towards more realistic, deployment-like behaviors, and then chooses the best candidate; (2) DISH (Deployment-Imitating SWE-Agent Harness), an agent harness that embeds the target model in an environment that closely mimics real software engineering deployment conditions. They also study the combination of both methods.
AI.result: Across several target models, both critique refinement and DISH increase the realism of simulated deployments, and using both together results in larger realism gains than either alone. They show that spending additional compute via these structured methods improves realism more effectively than simply lengthening audits or evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Automated techniques that better approximate deployment conditions—particularly critique refinement and deployment-imitating harnesses—can substantially improve the realism and thus reliability of alignment evaluations, and targeted use of extra compute is more effective than naively increasing evaluation length.

title: When Decodability Is Not Enough: Logical Validity Representations, Behavioral Dissociation, and Causal Tests in Language Models
summary: Large language models can look capable of logical reasoning, but correct or incorrect answers alone tell us little about what the model represents internally. We study logical verification in five open-weight transformer models using matched valid--invalid premise--claim pairs that vary across inference families, semantic domains, templates, and difficulty levels. Despite near-chance behavioral performance, logical validity is often almost perfectly decodable from hidden states and remains strongly decodable under held-out templates, domains, and inference families. Validity also remains highly decodable on behaviorally incorrect examples in the conditions where correctness-conditioned evaluation is well defined. At the same time, exhaustive leave-one-out tests reveal clear limits to this generalization, and interventions along probe-derived validity directions have only weak, nonspecific effects compared with random controls. Our results suggest that representing validity, expressing it in behavior, and using it causally are distinct. Validity related information can be strongly decodable from a model's hidden states without being reliably expressed in its output.

AI.tldr: They test whether transformers internally represent logical validity even when their answers are mostly wrong, finding that validity is highly decodable from hidden states but not reliably used to produce correct outputs.
AI.motivation: Behavioral evaluations of large language models on logical reasoning tasks cannot reveal what is actually represented inside the network. The authors want to know whether models internally encode logical validity and how this internal representation relates to observed behavior and causal use of information.
AI.method: They construct matched pairs of valid and invalid premise–claim examples spanning different inference families, semantic domains, templates, and difficulty. Using five open-weight transformer models, they train linear probes on hidden states to decode whether an input is logically valid. They test generalization across held-out templates, domains, and inference families, evaluate decodability even on examples where the model’s answer is wrong, run exhaustive leave-one-out generalization tests, and perform activation interventions along probe-identified validity directions, comparing them with random control directions.
AI.result: Even when models’ explicit answers are near chance, logical validity can often be decoded from hidden states with near-perfect accuracy. This decodability remains strong across new templates, domains, and inference families and persists on behaviorally incorrect instances (where conditioning on correctness is well-defined). However, leave-one-out tests expose limits to generalization, and steering activations along the probe-derived validity directions produces only weak, nonspecific behavioral changes, not stronger than random controls.
AI.conclusion: Transformer models can internally represent information about logical validity that is strongly linearly decodable yet not reliably expressed in their outputs or causally involved in reasoning. The work argues that representation, behavioral expression, and causal use of logical knowledge are distinct phenomena, challenging simple interpretations of probing results and the assumption that decodable structure is necessarily functionally used by the model.

title: SALA: Semantic-Aware Logical Alignment for Complex Reasoning in In-Context Learning
comment: Accepted for publication in Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Effective in-context learning (ICL) for complex reasoning relies on selecting the right demonstrations. Traditional retrieval methods based on surface similarity fail to capture the underlying problem-solving logic. Recent logic-based methods address this by matching predefined reasoning steps, but the rigid rules and exact-match criteria is improper to handle flexible or diverse reasoning processes. To address the problem, we propose SALA, a Semantic-Aware Logical Alignment framework. Instead of relying on a fixed inventory, SALA automatically learns task-specific reasoning operations. It then embeds these operations into a continuous semantic space and uses dynamic time warping (DTW) to align the reasoning sequences. This approach allows for soft, flexible matching of reasoning logic while remaining highly interpretable. Experiments across four reasoning benchmarks and three LLMs demonstrate that SALA outperforms existing demonstration selection methods. Further analysis confirms the roles of the operation induction and the logical semantic alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SALA, a framework that improves in-context learning for complex reasoning by selecting demonstrations via semantic-aware logical alignment rather than surface similarity or rigid logic templates.
AI.motivation: Existing in-context learning demonstration retrieval methods either rely on surface similarity, which fails to capture deep reasoning logic, or on predefined logic templates, which are too rigid and require exact matches, making them unsuitable for flexible and diverse reasoning processes.
AI.method: SALA first automatically induces task-specific reasoning operations from examples, without relying on a fixed, predefined operation inventory. It then embeds these operations into a continuous semantic space and represents each example’s reasoning as a sequence of such operation embeddings. Using dynamic time warping (DTW), SALA aligns and compares reasoning sequences to measure similarity in underlying problem-solving logic, enabling flexible, soft matching while preserving interpretability of the induced operations and alignments.
AI.result: Across four reasoning benchmarks and three different large language models, SALA consistently outperforms existing demonstration selection approaches (both surface-similarity-based and template-based logical methods) in in-context learning performance. Ablation and analytical experiments show that both the operation induction component and the semantic alignment via DTW are crucial to the observed gains.
AI.conclusion: Automatically learning and semantically embedding task-specific reasoning operations, combined with sequence alignment via DTW, yields a more flexible and interpretable way to compare reasoning processes. This enables better retrieval of demonstrations for in-context learning, improving complex reasoning performance over prior similarity- or rule-based methods.

title: Learning to Fuse LLMs with Ontology Rankers for Rare-Disease Diagnosis
summary: Ontology rankers remain useful for rare-disease diagnosis because each candidate can be traced to matched patient phenotypes. Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses from the same patient description, but their predictions lack an equally clear evidence trail. Rather than asking which system should replace the other, we ask whether an LLM can improve the ranker without giving up its evidence. Our behavior-based fusion model examines the two ranked lists, their agreement, and the ontology support behind each candidate, and learns how much to rely on each system for the individual case. Before comparison, we remove a documented test-set leakage pathway caused by benchmark cases and ontology annotations being derived from the same publications. Across eight open LLMs, fusion improves Phenomizer Recall@1 by 7.86 percentage points on Phenopacket Store and 20.18 points on RAMEDIS. When paired with DeepSeek-V4-Flash through an API, a fusion model trained only on the other LLMs improves Recall@1 from 0.1657 to 0.2176, a 5.19-point gain, without retraining. For 90.8% of correct fused diagnoses, the disease retains candidate-level ontology evidence that can be inspected. These results show that LLMs can strengthen an established diagnostic tool without discarding the structured evidence that makes it useful.

AI.tldr: The paper integrates large language model (LLM) differential diagnoses with ontology-based rankers to improve rare-disease diagnosis while preserving interpretable ontology evidence.
AI.motivation: Ontology-based rankers like Phenomizer provide traceable, phenotype-based rare-disease diagnoses but are limited in performance. LLMs can generate strong differential diagnoses from text but lack transparent evidence. The authors aim to combine the strengths of both: LLM accuracy and ontology interpretability, instead of replacing one with the other. They also address evaluation bias from test-set leakage between benchmarks and ontologies.
AI.method: They propose a behavior-based fusion model that takes as input two ranked disease lists—one from an ontology ranker and one from an LLM—along with features describing their agreement and ontology support for each candidate. The model learns, per case, how much to trust each system. Prior to fusion, they remove a known test-set leakage path where benchmark cases and ontology annotations originate from the same publications. The model is trained across eight open LLMs and evaluated on two rare-disease datasets (Phenopacket Store and RAMEDIS), and also tested in a zero-shot fusion setting with DeepSeek-V4-Flash accessed via API, without retraining on that specific model.
AI.result: Behavior-based fusion substantially improves top-1 diagnostic accuracy (Recall@1) of the ontology ranker (Phenomizer) across datasets and LLMs. On Phenopacket Store, Recall@1 improves by 7.86 percentage points; on RAMEDIS, by 20.18 points. When fusing with DeepSeek-V4-Flash using a fusion model trained only on other LLMs, Recall@1 improves from 0.1657 to 0.2176 (a 5.19-point gain) without retraining. In 90.8% of correctly diagnosed fused cases, the selected disease still has inspectable candidate-level ontology evidence.
AI.conclusion: LLMs and ontology rankers are complementary for rare-disease diagnosis. A behavior-based fusion approach can leverage LLM suggestions to boost diagnostic performance while maintaining the structured, interpretable ontology evidence that makes traditional rankers clinically useful. Proper leakage control is important for fair evaluation. This suggests a practical path to integrating LLMs into clinical decision support without sacrificing transparency.

title: Diagnosing with Insights: Structured Analysis of Agent Failures via Behavioral Abstractions
summary: With the proliferation of LLM agents, the ability to understand and diagnose failures in agents is essential to achieving superior effectiveness and trustworthiness. As agent failures often manifest via long and complex trajectories, manually finding the needles in the haystack is untenable. However, traditional diagnosis techniques for software bugs can hardly address LLM agent failures, while completely relying on LLMs as the judge yields unreliable diagnosis results. To overcome these challenges, this paper presents AGENTSCOPE, a new neuro-symbolic approach for agent failure mode diagnosis. The key principle of AGENTSCOPE is to abstract agent behavior, based on its trajectories, into structured representations. Furthermore, AGENTSCOPE introduces the concept of neural invariants to specify agent behavior properties. AGENTSCOPE leverages LLM-guided reasoning atop the structured representation against neural invariants to pinpoint both the failure step and its type in the trajectory. We show the effectiveness of AGENTSCOPE on publicly available agent failure datasets (Who&When) and a more comprehensive dataset created by us (AgentErrata), where AGENTSCOPE significantly outperforms the current state of the art in fault localization and attribution accuracy. Our work shows that integrating structured abstractions with LLM-guided reasoning enables effective, reliable, and interpretable diagnosis for agent failures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AGENTSCOPE, a neuro-symbolic framework that diagnoses failures in LLM-based agents by turning long trajectories into structured representations and checking them against learned behavior properties (neural invariants) to localize where and why the agent failed.
AI.motivation: LLM agents often fail in complex ways that show up over long action-observation trajectories, making manual inspection infeasible. Conventional software debugging tools do not translate well to LLM agents, and letting LLMs judge their own failures is unreliable. There is a need for a more systematic, accurate, and interpretable way to understand, localize, and categorize failure modes of LLM agents.
AI.method: AGENTSCOPE first abstracts an agent’s trajectory into a structured, symbolic representation that captures key elements of its behavior. It then defines neural invariants—behavioral properties expressed in a way that can be evaluated with neural models. Using LLM-guided reasoning over the structured trajectory with respect to these invariants, AGENTSCOPE identifies both the specific step where the failure occurs and the type of failure, effectively combining symbolic structure with neural reasoning (a neuro-symbolic approach).
AI.result: On existing public datasets of agent failures (Who&When) and a new, more comprehensive benchmark constructed by the authors (AgentErrata), AGENTSCOPE substantially improves fault localization and failure-type attribution compared to prior state-of-the-art approaches for diagnosing LLM agent failures.
AI.conclusion: By combining structured abstractions of agent trajectories with LLM-guided reasoning via neural invariants, AGENTSCOPE enables more effective, reliable, and interpretable diagnosis of failure modes in LLM agents, demonstrating that neuro-symbolic techniques are a promising direction for understanding and improving complex agent behavior.

title: PragAlign: Feedback-Guided Pragmatic Alignment for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation
summary: Synthetic dialogue generation can support research in privacy-restricted service settings, but generated conversations must preserve communicative intent, affective meaning, and natural dialogue flow. We introduce PragAlign, a feedback-guided framework for controlled synthetic dialogue generation conditioned on service context, target intent, and target emotion, with auxiliary trait-style controls. PragAlign uses a generate--evaluate--revise loop in which an LLM-based evaluator scores intent alignment, emotion alignment, coherence, fluency, and aggregate quality, then provides criterion-specific feedback for up to three refinement rounds. On 800 matched dialogue specifications, PragAlign achieves 99.50\% evaluator-defined acceptance, compared with 72.25\% for one-shot generation and 95.88\% for repeated generation without structured feedback. This indicates that repeated attempts account for much of the gain over one-shot generation, while structured feedback primarily improves last-mile multi-constraint satisfaction rather than broad average quality. Refinement gains are concentrated in emotion alignment, which is also the dominant failure mode in ablations. A separate human evaluation of 1,200 generated dialogues shows that intent expression and dialogue flow are highly recognizable to annotators, while emotion appropriateness is less stable and more subjective. These results support PragAlign as a quality-control framework for improving evaluator-defined communicative constraint satisfaction, while showing that affective realization and independent human-perceived quality remain open challenges.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PragAlign, a feedback-guided framework for synthetic dialogue generation that iteratively refines LLM-generated service dialogues to better satisfy intent, emotion, and quality constraints.
AI.motivation: Research and development in service dialogue systems often require conversational data, but privacy restrictions limit the use of real customer–service interactions. Synthetic dialogue can help, but only if it preserves key communicative properties such as intent, affect, and natural flow. Existing LLM-based generation either uses one-shot prompting or naive repetition, which may not reliably satisfy multiple constraints like intent, emotion, and coherence simultaneously. The authors aim to build a controllable, quality-controlled generation process tailored to service contexts.
AI.method: PragAlign is a controlled dialogue generation framework that conditions an LLM generator on service context, target intent, target emotion, and optional trait-style controls. It operates in a generate–evaluate–revise loop: (1) an LLM generates an initial dialogue given the specification; (2) an LLM-based evaluator scores the dialogue on intent alignment, emotion alignment, coherence, fluency, and aggregate quality; (3) based on criterion-specific feedback, the generator revises the dialogue, with up to three refinement rounds. The system is evaluated on 800 matched dialogue specifications and compared against one-shot generation and repeated generation without structured feedback. Ablation studies analyze where gains originate, and a separate human evaluation of 1,200 dialogues assesses recognizability of intent, flow, and emotion appropriateness.
AI.result: On 800 dialogue specifications, PragAlign achieves 99.50% acceptance according to the LLM-based evaluator, outperforming one-shot generation (72.25%) and repeated generation without structured feedback (95.88%). Analysis shows that multiple attempts already yield most improvements over one-shot, while structured, criterion-specific feedback mainly improves final multi-constraint satisfaction rather than average quality. The largest refinement gains are in emotion alignment, and when components are ablated, emotion alignment emerges as the primary failure mode. Human evaluation of 1,200 dialogues finds that intent and dialogue flow are reliably recognized by annotators, but perceived emotional appropriateness is less consistent and more subjective.
AI.conclusion: PragAlign is an effective quality-control framework for synthetic dialogue generation in service contexts, significantly improving evaluator-defined satisfaction of communicative constraints—especially for emotion alignment—over baseline generation strategies. The generate–evaluate–revise loop with structured feedback is particularly useful for achieving high success under multiple simultaneous constraints, even though much of the improvement over one-shot comes simply from repeated generation. However, affective realization remains difficult, and there is a gap between evaluator-based metrics and human-perceived emotional quality, indicating that emotion modeling and subjective quality assessment are important open challenges.

title: Contrastive Explanations in Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks
summary: Argumentation frameworks are useful tools for representing and reasoning with information in a variety of settings, e.g. in supplementing AI models as they perform classification tasks, with a notable benefit of providing additional explainability. In this paper, we introduce contrastive explanations for Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks (QBAFs), one such formalism. Unlike most existing explanations for QBAFs, which explain the reasoning outcome of a single argument of interest (i.e. a topic argument), contrastive explanations explain the difference between two topic arguments. We introduce a general form of contrastive attribution functions (CAFs) and establish a set of general properties they should satisfy. We introduce CAFs based on removal, gradients and Shapley-values, and study their properties. Finally, to illustrate contrastive explanations, we demonstrate their usefulness in healthcare and bias identification settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces contrastive explanations for Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks (QBAFs), defining general contrastive attribution functions (CAFs), instantiating them via removal, gradients, and Shapley values, analysing their properties, and demonstrating applications in healthcare and bias detection.
AI.motivation: Existing explanations in QBAFs typically focus on explaining the acceptance or score of a single argument (topic argument) in isolation. However, in many practical AI settings, users want to understand why one option or classification was chosen over another. The paper aims to fill this gap by formalising contrastive explanations that explain differences between two arguments’ outcomes in QBAFs, thereby improving explainability and practical usefulness, particularly in sensitive domains like healthcare and bias analysis.
AI.method: The authors formalise the notion of contrastive explanations in the context of Quantitative Bipolar Argumentation Frameworks by introducing contrastive attribution functions (CAFs), which assign responsibility scores to arguments for the *difference* in outcomes between two topic arguments. They propose a general schema for CAFs and specify a set of desirable axiomatic properties. Then, they instantiate this schema via three families of CAFs: removal-based (measuring effect via argument deletion), gradient-based (using sensitivity of quantitative scores to perturbations), and Shapley-value-based (cooperative game–theoretic attribution). They conduct an axiomatic analysis to see which properties each CAF variant satisfies. Finally, they demonstrate the approach on case studies in healthcare decision support and bias identification.
AI.result: The paper provides: (1) a general formal definition of contrastive attribution functions for QBAFs; (2) an axiomatic framework specifying key properties that such functions should satisfy; (3) three concrete CAF instantiations—removal-based, gradient-based, and Shapley-based—together with an analysis of which axioms they satisfy or violate; and (4) illustrative examples showing how these contrastive explanations can reveal why one argument (e.g., a diagnosis or decision) is preferred over another and how they can highlight sources of bias in AI-supported decision making.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive explanations for QBAFs are both formally well-founded and practically useful. By focusing on differences between two topic arguments, the proposed CAF framework complements traditional single-argument explanations and better matches real user queries in many decision-making scenarios. The instantiated CAFs (removal, gradients, Shapley) each offer distinct trade-offs with respect to axiomatic properties and computational aspects. The case studies suggest that contrastive QBAF explanations can enhance transparency and assist in identifying biases in AI systems, particularly in domains such as healthcare.

title: How LLMs Build Fictional Worlds: Setting and Narrative Space in AI-Generated Creative Storytelling
summary: In this paper, we analyze how Large Language Models (LLMs) employ worldbuilding strategies, focusing on setting as one measurable dimension of storyworld construction. We compare 1,000 AI-generated stories per model in English and German with human-authored fiction from Project Gutenberg. Building on prior work, we operationalize setting through five types of narrative space: "action", "perceived," "visual," "descriptive" and "no space", identified using fine-tuned BERT classifiers for German and English. We generate narratives using GPT 4.1, LlaMA 3.3, Mistral 3.2, and Gemma 3 and compare their spatial distributions to a human-authored baseline. We find that human-authored texts predominantly employ "action space," grounding narratives in embodied character-environment interaction, whereas LLMs systematically overproduce "perceived space," emphasizing atmosphere and affect. This divergence remains stable across narrative time. Overall, our findings show that LLMs exhibit worldbuilding patterns that differ consistently from human-authored fiction in ways that are both model-specific and language-sensitive.

AI.tldr: The paper compares how LLMs and humans build fictional settings, showing that LLMs favor atmospheric, perception-focused spaces while humans favor action-grounded spaces.
AI.motivation: To understand whether and how LLM-generated stories differ from human fiction in their worldbuilding practices, particularly in how they construct narrative settings across languages and models.
AI.method: Collect 1,000 AI-generated stories per model (GPT 4.1, LlaMA 3.3, Mistral 3.2, Gemma 3) in English and German, plus human fiction from Project Gutenberg. Use fine-tuned BERT classifiers (separate for German and English) to label text spans according to five types of narrative space: action, perceived, visual, descriptive, and no space. Compare the distributions of these spatial categories over narrative time across models and against the human baseline.
AI.result: Human-authored texts are dominated by action space, where settings are grounded through characters’ embodied interaction with their environments. In contrast, LLM-generated stories systematically overproduce perceived space, which centers on atmosphere and affect rather than concrete interaction. These differences are robust across narrative time and show consistent model- and language-specific patterns.
AI.conclusion: LLMs construct storyworlds in ways that systematically diverge from human-authored fiction, favoring perception- and mood-oriented setting descriptions over action-based grounding. These divergences are stable across the narrative and vary by model and language, indicating that current LLMs have characteristic, non-human worldbuilding signatures.

title: UTP-Bench: Uncertainty-aware Travel Planning Benchmark
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated strong capabilities in automated travel itinerary generation. However, real- world travel planning is inherently uncertain: transportation delays, crowd fluctuations, and unexpected stochastic delays frequently inval- idate otherwise feasible schedules. Existing benchmarks like TravelPlanner and TripCraft assume deterministic environments, evaluating only static constraint satisfaction and ignoring whether generated plans remain robust when such uncertainties arise. To address this limitation, we introduce UTP-Bench1 , a large-scale benchmark for uncertainty-aware travel planning. The dataset integrates real-world travel data spanning 504 cities of India, including attractions, restau- rants, accommodations, and multi-modal trans- portation networks. To model realistic disrup- tions, UTP-Bench incorporates empirical delay distributions and crowd-density patterns col- lected from major cities, enabling evaluation of travel plans under stochastic conditions. We further propose three evaluation metrics, namely Buffer Adequacy Score (BAS), Crowd- Aware Timing Score (CATS), and Transport Delay Absorption Score (TDAS), which quan- tify the ability of generated itineraries to main- tain robustness against transit delays and crowd variability. Experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-5, Qwen3, Mistral and Phi-4 re- veal substantial gaps between model-generated and human-authored plans, particularly in tem- poral buffering, delay-aware transportation scheduling, and crowd-sensitive planning.

AI.tldr: Introduces UTP-Bench, a benchmark for testing how well LLM-generated travel itineraries handle real-world uncertainty like delays and crowds.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM travel-planning benchmarks assume a deterministic world and only test static constraint satisfaction, ignoring that real travel involves uncertainty from delays, crowding, and stochastic disruptions that can invalidate plans.
AI.method: Construct a large-scale benchmark, UTP-Bench, using real travel data from 504 Indian cities (attractions, restaurants, accommodations, multi-modal transport) combined with empirical distributions of delays and crowd-density patterns; design three new metrics—Buffer Adequacy Score, Crowd-Aware Timing Score, and Transport Delay Absorption Score—to evaluate the robustness of itineraries under stochastic conditions; evaluate several state-of-the-art LLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: State-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-5, Qwen3, Mistral, Phi-4) perform significantly worse than human-authored itineraries, especially in temporal buffering, scheduling transportation with delay awareness, and adapting plans to crowd variability, as reflected by the new robustness metrics.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs, though competent at generating static travel plans, lack robustness to real-world uncertainty; UTP-Bench and its metrics provide a more realistic, uncertainty-aware benchmark that exposes these shortcomings and can guide future improvements in robust travel-planning models.

title: Debias-SparseGPT: Bias-Aware Pruning for Large Language Models
summary: Model compression techniques such as pruning and quantization facilitate the efficient deployment and acceleration of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, recent studies show that weight sparsification methods, such as SparseGPT, can amplify existing biases in models, with outputs varying significantly depending on persona cues in the prompt. In this paper, we introduce Debias-SparseGPT, a post-training pruning method incorporating representational debiasing using a second-order term defined over demographically contrasting inputs. We perform empirical validation of our method over a wide range of generative LLMs. Across models and sparsity regimes (25%, 50%, and structured 2:4 sparsity), Debias-SparseGPT consistently reduces pruning-induced bias compared to SparseGPT while preserving model perplexity and zero-shot accuracy. Under the most restrictive 2:4 structured sparsity pattern, which most aggressively degrades model quality, augmenting the calibration set with long-context, content-rich examples further improves both downstream performance and fairness. Overall, Debias-SparseGPT advances the bias-performance trade-off while preserving the computational efficiency of sparse models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Debias-SparseGPT, a pruning method for large language models that reduces pruning-induced demographic bias while maintaining model quality and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Standard sparsification/pruning methods like SparseGPT improve efficiency of LLMs but have been found to amplify existing demographic biases, especially when prompts include persona cues. There is a need for compression methods that preserve both performance and fairness, rather than worsening bias as a side effect of efficiency gains.
AI.method: Debias-SparseGPT is a post-training pruning approach that integrates representational debiasing into the pruning objective. It uses a second-order term computed over pairs of demographically contrasting inputs during calibration, encouraging the pruned model to align or regularize internal representations across demographic groups while pruning weights. The method is evaluated at different sparsity levels (25%, 50%) and under a structured 2:4 sparsity pattern across several generative LLMs. For the strict 2:4 regime, the authors further augment the calibration set with long-context, content-rich examples to strengthen both downstream accuracy and fairness.
AI.result: Across multiple LLMs and pruning regimes, Debias-SparseGPT consistently reduces the additional demographic bias introduced by pruning when compared to the baseline SparseGPT approach. At the same time, it preserves key utility metrics such as perplexity and zero-shot task accuracy. In the challenging 2:4 structured sparsity setting, where model quality typically degrades the most, adding richer calibration data leads to further improvements in both performance and fairness metrics.
AI.conclusion: Debias-SparseGPT provides a better bias–performance trade-off than standard sparsification, mitigating pruning-induced demographic bias without sacrificing efficiency benefits of sparse models. The approach is especially useful in high-sparsity regimes and shows that careful, debiasing-aware pruning can maintain both fairness and accuracy in compressed LLMs.

title: CivBench: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Tool-Mediated Agents in Civilization VI
summary:
We present CivBench, an open-source benchmark for evaluating language model agents in long-horizon, tool-mediated environments through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A single episode spans 300+ turns and produces thousands of tool calls over a large action space, requiring sustained planning, state monitoring, and execution under partial observability. The environment exposes 76 MCP tools and a narration layer that converts visual game state into structured text.
  We use CivBench to characterise agent behaviour across four model families in 23 admissible runs. The sample is a pilot, not a model ranking: aggregate outcomes do not reliably discriminate models at this scale. Instead, we introduce two interface-level metrics that the environment makes measurable: Proactive Monitoring Rate (PMR), capturing whether agents actively query latent strategic state, and RAG@10, capturing whether commitments stated in structured planning reflections are executed within ten subsequent turns.
  Across runs we observe two consistent patterns under a shared playbook protocol. Agents under-monitor strategically relevant state that is available but requires explicit querying: despite playbook guidance to query victory progress every 20 turns, agents do so only every 30 to 75 turns, and in 7 of 20 detectable defeats they failed to query within the 20 turn warning window before game end. Agents also frequently fail to execute near-term commitments stated in their own planning reflections (RAG@10 between 48.2% and 65.8% across models). Both patterns arise despite tool access and explicit guidance, and we interpret them as deviations under instruction rather than absences of capability.
  We release the environment, scenarios, logs, metrics, and analysis pipeline at https://github.com/lmwilki/civ6-mcp

AI.tldr: CivBench is a benchmark for testing how well language model agents can plan and act over very long, multi-tool game scenarios using the Model Context Protocol.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks often test language models on short, static, or low-tool-use tasks, which do not reflect the challenges of real agent deployments that must plan over long horizons, manage partial information, and coordinate many tool calls. The authors want a realistic, open, and measurable environment to study these behaviors, especially around how agents monitor state and follow through on their own plans.
AI.method: They build an MCP-based environment around a complex strategy game, where each episode has 300+ turns and thousands of tool calls over 76 tools, plus a narration layer that turns visual state into structured text. They run 23 episodes with agents from four model families under a common playbook protocol. Instead of focusing on win rates, they define two new metrics: Proactive Monitoring Rate (PMR) for how often agents query latent strategic state, and RAG@10 for how often agents actually execute actions they committed to in planning reflections within 10 turns. They analyze logs, tool usage, and these metrics across runs.
AI.result: The small-scale pilot does not yield robust model rankings, but it exposes consistent behavioral patterns across all tested models. Agents query important latent state, like victory progress, far less often than instructed, typically every 30–75 turns instead of the recommended 20, and sometimes miss critical warning windows before defeat. RAG@10 scores are relatively low (48.2–65.8%), showing agents often fail to carry out near-term commitments they themselves stated. These failures occur despite clear tool access and explicit guidance.
AI.conclusion: CivBench demonstrates that language model agents can be systematically evaluated in long-horizon, tool-mediated settings, and that interface-level metrics like PMR and RAG@10 reveal important deviations from intended behavior. The observed under-monitoring of strategic state and poor adherence to self-stated plans appear to be instruction-following failures rather than fundamental capability limits. The authors release all code, scenarios, logs, and analysis tools to support further research on improving agent monitoring, planning, and execution in complex environments.

title: When Persona Attributes Improve Population Alignment in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to predict the responses of human participants in survey panels. Towards that goal, persona prompting has recently emerged as a technique to inform and align large pretrained language models. Persona prompting refers to the practice of using short textual descriptions of 'personas' in prompts to steer the LLM's generations. Personas describe individuals through different attributes such as their socio-demographics, attitudes, or behaviors, with the aim of aligning LLMs to produce responses that correlate with the corresponding human responses. Yet, recent work has produced mixed and partly conflicting results of persona prompting without clear patterns of success and failure. Among the few consistent findings is that the selection of persona attributes matters, and that using more attributes does not necessarily lead to better performance. It remains unclear how different attribute selection methods perform and how to choose among them. In this paper, we propose that observed human response variation of a survey question is a potential explanation for the mixed performance observed so far. In addition, we compare the performance of persona prompting associated with different methods for selecting persona attributes. We evaluate these methods on four different (general) social surveys across two countries, six LLMs, and twenty prediction tasks per survey. Our work helps to identify when persona prompting can be expected to be useful in survey prediction tasks, and provides new insights on the effectiveness of different attribute selection methods for LLM-based survey prediction using persona prompting.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well persona prompting helps large language models predict human survey responses, focusing on how the choice of persona attributes and the amount of human response variation affect performance.
AI.motivation: Persona prompting is increasingly used to make LLMs mimic survey panel respondents, but existing studies show mixed and sometimes contradictory results with no clear understanding of when it works. A key open problem is how to select persona attributes (demographics, attitudes, behaviors) that align LLM outputs with human responses, given that more attributes do not always yield better predictions. The authors are motivated to explain the mixed results and to systematically compare attribute selection strategies.
AI.method: The authors hypothesize that the observed variation in human responses to each survey question helps explain when persona prompting succeeds or fails. They operationalize different strategies for selecting persona attributes and then empirically evaluate persona prompting across four general social surveys from two countries, six different LLMs, and twenty prediction tasks per survey. Performance is compared across attribute-selection methods and tasks with differing levels of human response variation.
AI.result: The study finds that the effectiveness of persona prompting depends strongly on the level of human response variation in the target survey questions and on how persona attributes are selected. Some attribute-selection methods outperform others, and simply increasing the number of attributes does not guarantee better predictive alignment with human responses. The experiments across multiple surveys, countries, and LLMs reveal systematic patterns in when and how persona prompting improves survey prediction.
AI.conclusion: Persona prompting is not universally beneficial for LLM-based survey prediction; its usefulness depends on both task characteristics (especially human response variation) and the chosen persona attribute-selection strategy. The paper offers guidance on when persona prompting is likely to help and which attribute-selection approaches tend to be more effective, clarifying previously mixed findings and informing future work on LLM-based survey prediction and persona design.

title: Collective creativity in hybrid societies
summary: Generative AI is changing how cultural artifacts are created and circulated, and with it our understanding of creativity itself. Researchers disagree about whether these tools enrich or impoverish culture, and we argue that much of that disagreement comes from conflating two distinct components of creativity: novelty, a property of single artifacts, and diversity, a property of populations. We argue further that creativity in the context of generative AI is best understood as a property of hybrid collectives, or populations of interacting people and algorithms, rather than of individuals. AI-assisted ideation reliably raises the novelty of individual output while narrowing diversity in the aggregate, but this is not an inevitable consequence of putting machines in the loop. Because humans and models search in complementary ways, mixed groups can outperform and out-diversify groups of either kind alone, and machine-discovered solutions can enter human culture and persist there. What decides the outcome is composition: which agents are present, in what proportion, and how they are connected. The question is no longer whether AI helps or harms creativity, but which mixtures let individual gains accumulate without eroding collective diversity.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that generative AI reshapes creativity by increasing the novelty of individual works while often reducing diversity across a population of works, and proposes analyzing creativity at the level of human–AI collectives instead of individuals.
AI.motivation: Ongoing debates about whether generative AI enhances or harms creativity often treat creativity as a single, individual-level property. The authors see conceptual confusion: people mix up novelty (how new a single artifact is) with diversity (how varied a whole set of artifacts is). They also note that current discourse under-theorizes the collective, socio-technical nature of creativity when AI is involved. The paper aims to clarify these concepts and provide a better framework for evaluating AI’s cultural impact.
AI.method: Conceptual and theoretical analysis rather than an empirical experiment: the authors distinguish novelty from diversity, introduce the idea of hybrid collectives (interacting humans and algorithms) as the right unit of analysis, and reason about search processes in humans versus models. They synthesize prior empirical findings suggesting AI-assisted ideation raises individual novelty but narrows population-level diversity, and use this to argue about mechanisms and design implications.
AI.result: They propose that AI assistance tends to increase the novelty of individual outputs while reducing diversity across a population because models channel creators into similar regions of the creative space. However, they argue this outcome is contingent: because humans and models explore differently, appropriately structured human–AI collectives can both outperform and out-diversify purely human or purely machine groups, and AI-generated ideas can be assimilated into and sustained within human cultures.
AI.conclusion: Creativity in the age of generative AI should be understood as a property of hybrid human–AI collectives. The key design and policy question is not whether AI is good or bad for creativity, but how to configure compositions and connections—who participates, in what proportions, and how they interact—so that gains in individual-level novelty do not come at the expense of collective diversity of cultural artifacts.

title: Predictors of Loneliness in Older Adults Using Multimodal Analysis of Speech and Language
summary: Loneliness is a critical public health issue among older adults, linked to higher risks of depression, cognitive decline, and mortality. Scalable, objective methods for its detection remain limited, particularly in natural conversational contexts. We analyzed speech and language markers of loneliness in 310 older adults using semi-structured telephone interviews to help understand how they process feeling lonely and how their language differs at different levels of feeling loneliness. Our multimodal framework combined linguistic features (psycholinguistic dictionaries, n-grams, and topic models) with acoustic features (pitch, tone, loudness) to examine associations with self-reported loneliness scores. Both predefined and data-driven methods captured patterns in verbal content and vocal delivery. Higher loneliness was associated with negations(r = 0.11), negative tone(r = 0.12), and conflict-related language. Lower loneliness was linked to social references(r = -0.18), motivational drives(r = -0.11), and emotional richness in speech(r = -0.12). We also found that the multimodal model (r = 0.298) outperforms the text-only and audio-only models. Findings suggest that loneliness manifests through both linguistic and acoustic cues, supporting the potential of speech-based analysis in psychological assessments and as an early indicator of emotional loneliness when used alongside existing assessments, rather than as standalone diagnostic tools.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and tests a multimodal (text + audio) model to detect and characterize loneliness in older adults’ natural speech from telephone interviews.
AI.motivation: Loneliness in older adults is a serious public health problem, associated with depression, cognitive decline, and mortality. Current assessments mostly rely on self-report questionnaires or clinical judgment, which are not easily scalable or continuously deployable, and objective markers in natural conversations are poorly understood. The authors aim to identify linguistic and acoustic markers that correlate with loneliness so that speech in everyday-like settings could be leveraged for early detection and monitoring.
AI.method: The study collected semi-structured telephone interview recordings from 310 older adults, along with their self-reported loneliness scores. From transcripts, the authors extracted linguistic features including psycholinguistic dictionary categories (e.g., LIWC-style categories), n-grams, and topic-model-derived themes. From audio, they extracted acoustic features such as pitch, tone, and loudness. Using both predefined (dictionary-based) and data-driven (n-grams, topics, statistical models) approaches, they examined correlations between these features and loneliness scores and built unimodal (text-only, audio-only) and multimodal predictive models to evaluate how well loneliness could be inferred from speech.
AI.result: Higher loneliness scores were modestly but significantly associated with more negations (r = 0.11), more negative tone (r = 0.12), and more conflict-related language. Lower loneliness was associated with more social references (r = -0.18), stronger motivational drive language (r = -0.11), and more emotionally rich speech (r = -0.12). A combined text+audio (multimodal) model achieved a correlation of r = 0.298 with self-reported loneliness scores, outperforming models that used only linguistic or only acoustic features.
AI.conclusion: Loneliness among older adults is reflected not only in what they say but also how they say it. Specific linguistic patterns (e.g., negations, social references) and acoustic cues (e.g., tone) are systematically related to loneliness levels. Integrating linguistic and acoustic features in a multimodal framework improves the ability to estimate loneliness from speech compared to unimodal approaches. The authors conclude that speech-based analysis can serve as an informative adjunct tool for psychological assessments and early identification of emotional loneliness, but should complement, not replace, established diagnostic instruments.

title: Loom: Weaving Diagnostic Strands into Free-Text Consensus via Embedding-Space Reweighting
summary: Aggregating noisy, conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable consensus is a fundamental challenge when deploying NLP systems in real-world industrial settings. While monolithic Large Language Model (LLM) agents offer unbounded expressivity for tasks like Root Cause Analysis (RCA), they suffer from context limits, compounding hallucinations, and prohibitive inference latency. Traditional weak supervision offers statistical rigor but is mathematically restricted to discrete classes. We present Loom, a generative consensus framework deployed for real-world RCA that bridges these paradigms. Loom aggregates open-form hypotheses emitted by modular heuristics (diagnostic templates dynamically populated with episode-specific entities, times, and metrics) by projecting them into a continuous embedding space, and resolves conflicting signals with an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm. The resulting consensus weights ground a single lightweight LLM synthesis step. Evaluated on the OpenRCA benchmark, Loom occupies the accuracy--efficiency Pareto frontier: it matches a state-of-the-art autonomous agent on Bank and Market-2 and trails on Market-1 and Telecom, while using a single LLM call per incident on all four datasets ($\sim$26$\times$ faster; $\sim$33$\times$ with an 8B-parameter synthesizer). We discuss our deployment experience, highlighting lessons learned regarding the trade-offs between agentic depth and inference latency, negative results in redundancy detection, and how deterministic consensus fosters trust among Subject Matter Experts~(SMEs).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Loom, a framework that combines modular heuristic generators with a continuous-embedding consensus algorithm and a single lightweight LLM call to perform fast, accurate root cause analysis from noisy textual hypotheses.
AI.motivation: In industrial NLP settings like Root Cause Analysis, practitioners must aggregate many noisy, conflicting textual hypotheses into a reliable explanation. Existing options are unsatisfactory: large monolithic LLM agents are expressive but slow, context-limited, and prone to compounding hallucinations, whereas traditional weak supervision is statistically sound but restricted to discrete labels and cannot handle open-form hypotheses. There is a need for a method that brings the rigor and efficiency of weak supervision to open-ended generative RCA while avoiding the computational and reliability issues of full agents.
AI.method: The authors propose Loom, a generative consensus framework. First, domain-specific modular heuristics (diagnostic templates) produce open-form textual hypotheses for each incident, instantiated with concrete entities, timestamps, and metrics. Loom then maps these hypotheses into a continuous embedding space and applies an iterative centroid-based reweighting algorithm to resolve conflicts and estimate consensus weights over the hypotheses. These consensus weights are finally used to condition a single lightweight LLM that synthesizes a final RCA narrative, effectively separating hypothesis generation, consensus formation, and narrative generation into distinct stages.
AI.result: On the OpenRCA benchmark across four datasets (Bank, Market-1, Market-2, and Telecom), Loom lies on the accuracy–efficiency Pareto frontier. It matches the performance of a state-of-the-art autonomous LLM agent on Bank and Market-2, and is slightly worse on Market-1 and Telecom, but achieves dramatically lower computational cost, requiring only one LLM call per incident—about 26× faster, increasing to roughly 33× faster when using an 8B-parameter LLM as the synthesizer.
AI.conclusion: Loom demonstrates that a deterministic, embedding-based consensus layer over modular heuristics, coupled with a single lightweight LLM synthesis step, can provide an attractive balance between accuracy and efficiency for industrial RCA. The framework mitigates the latency and reliability issues of full agentic LLM systems while extending weak-supervision-style rigor to open-form text. The authors’ deployment experience suggests useful practical trade-offs between agentic depth and latency, documents negative findings on redundancy detection, and indicates that deterministic consensus mechanisms can enhance trust among subject matter experts.

title: TaRA: Training-Aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a de facto standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet its performance is highly sensitive to initialization due to the information bottleneck imposed by low-rank decomposition. Existing approaches attempt to construct high-quality LoRA initializations by exploiting principal components of pretrained weights, activations, or gradients. However, these methods do not directly account for the training dynamics of the full-rank model. In this paper, we propose Training-aware Low-Rank Adaptation Initialization (TaRA), a method that initializes LoRA such that the gradients induced by the low-rank factors closely approximate the gradient of the corresponding full-rank weight matrix. Derived from a mathematical formulation, TaRA improves gradient fidelity at the start of training while introducing negligible computational overhead. Across diverse and challenging fine-tuning tasks, TaRA consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, establishing a simple, robust, and scalable solution for effective LoRA initialization.

AI.tldr: They propose TaRA, a new way to initialize LoRA so its early gradients better match those of a full-rank model, improving fine-tuning performance with negligible extra cost.
AI.motivation: LoRA is widely used for parameter-efficient fine-tuning but is very sensitive to how its low-rank matrices are initialized. Current initializations use principal components of weights, activations, or gradients, but they ignore the actual gradient behavior of the full-rank model during training, leading to suboptimal optimization dynamics and performance.
AI.method: They mathematically derive an initialization scheme (TaRA) that chooses the low-rank factors so that the gradient w.r.t. LoRA parameters closely approximates the gradient of the corresponding full-rank weight matrix at the start of fine-tuning. This is done by optimizing gradient fidelity under the low-rank constraint, yielding a closed-form or efficient procedure that adds almost no computation beyond standard LoRA setup.
AI.result: On a variety of challenging PEFT benchmarks, models using TaRA initialization achieve better performance than those using standard random or PCA-based initializations and prior state-of-the-art LoRA init methods, with consistent gains across tasks and scales.
AI.conclusion: Aligning LoRA initialization with full-rank gradient behavior is an effective, simple, and scalable way to stabilize and improve PEFT. TaRA offers a robust default initialization that enhances gradient fidelity at training onset and yields superior empirical performance over existing LoRA initialization strategies.

title: Door-in-the-Face Requests and Refusal Behaviour in Large Language Models
comment: 28 pages (9 pages of content plus references and appendix), 5 figures, 9 tables. Preprint, under review
summary: Does the door-in-the-face technique work on language models? In humans, a large request that is refused makes a smaller follow-up request more likely to be granted. We test this on nine production models from three providers: each model refuses a large request, then receives a smaller version of the same request, and we compare its compliance with asking directly. The answer depends on the model. On Anthropic's frontier models the technique works: Opus 5 answers the smaller request 65.8% of the time after refusing the larger one, against 29.3% when asked directly. On the frontier models of OpenAI and Google, and on Haiku 4.5, it backfires, lowering compliance by 15.5 to 23.0 points. A control locates the effect: a refused large request on an unrelated topic does less than the related one on all nine models, so the concession itself matters everywhere, while the reaction to having just refused something differs by model family. The technique does not transfer to refusals drawn from public benchmarks. What decides whether a retreat can work is what the request asks for: rewriting 265 refused requests for usable instructions into requests for explanations of the same topic removed the refusal in 263 cases. Human influence techniques port to language models one model family at a time.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether the psychological door-in-the-face persuasion technique works on different LLM families and finds model-dependent effects.
AI.motivation: To investigate if a classic human persuasion strategy, where a refused large request increases compliance with a smaller follow-up request, also applies to modern language models, and to understand how safety/refusal behavior varies across model families.
AI.method: They evaluate nine production models from three providers. For each, they issue a large, policy-violating request that is refused, then follow with a smaller, related request and measure compliance, comparing it to the compliance rate when the smaller request is asked directly. They also run controls with unrelated large requests, test benchmark-style refusals, and systematically rewrite refused requests (e.g., from action instructions to explanations) to probe what kinds of reframing bypass refusals.
AI.result: Anthropic frontier models, especially Opus 5, show a strong door-in-the-face effect: compliance with the smaller request jumps from about 29% when asked directly to about 66% after refusing a larger related request. In contrast, frontier models from OpenAI and Google and Anthropic’s Haiku 4.5 exhibit a backfire effect, with compliance dropping by around 15–23 percentage points. Controls show that related large requests affect compliance more than unrelated ones across all models, but the direction and magnitude differ by model family. The door-in-the-face effect does not appear when using refusals from public benchmarks. Rewriting harmful instructions into explanation-style requests removes nearly all refusals (263 of 265).
AI.conclusion: Door-in-the-face is not a universal LLM persuasion effect; it is highly model-family specific. The perceived “concession” from a large to a smaller related request influences all models, but some become more permissive while others become more cautious. Standard benchmark refusals do not capture these dynamics, and framing (e.g., asking for explanations instead of instructions) is crucial in determining whether safety refusals occur. Human social influence techniques can apply to LLMs, but only in a model- and request-specific way, underscoring the need for nuanced, model-targeted safety evaluations.

title: WinoQueer-NL: Assessing Bias in Dutch Language Models toward LGBTQ+ Identities
summary: While English language models have been widely examined for anti-queer bias, Dutch models remain understudied. To address this gap, we developed a culturally and linguistically adapted Dutch dataset based on the English WinoQueer benchmark, containing pairs of stereotypical and counter-stereotypical sentences. To validate and expand it, we conducted an online survey with 43 Dutch queer participants, confirming 145 of 171 stereotypes as culturally relevant and identifying 22 new biases through free-text responses. The final released dataset, comprising 42,906 sentences, was evaluated using a range of Dutch-specific and multilingual models, including both masked language models (MLMs) and autoregressive language models (ARLMs), with bias measured via a score comparing log-likelihoods of stereotypical versus counter-stereotypical sentences. While the mean bias score across models appeared neutral (~50%), closer analysis revealed significant disparities: some models favored stereotypical sentences up to 97% of the time for transgender identities, but only 6% of the time for gay-related pairs, with transgender and non-binary identities consistently receiving the highest bias scores. Our findings highlight the importance of culturally grounded datasets for evaluating and mitigating biases that disproportionately impact marginalized groups in Dutch language models.

AI.tldr: This paper builds and validates a Dutch version of the WinoQueer benchmark to measure anti-queer bias in Dutch language models, showing strong, uneven bias especially against transgender and non-binary identities despite seemingly neutral average scores.
AI.motivation: Most work on bias in language models is English-centric, and particularly for queer-related bias, Dutch models are underexplored. Existing English benchmarks like WinoQueer are not directly transferable because bias is culturally and linguistically specific. The authors aim to create a culturally grounded resource to reveal and quantify anti-queer bias in Dutch language models, especially for marginalized identities such as transgender and non-binary people.
AI.method: They adapt the English WinoQueer benchmark into Dutch, producing sentence pairs where one variant reflects a stereotype and the other counters it. They run an online survey with 43 Dutch queer participants to validate which stereotypes are culturally relevant and to elicit additional biases via free-text responses. From this they confirm most original stereotypes and add new ones, constructing a large dataset of 42,906 Dutch sentences. They then evaluate multiple Dutch-specific and multilingual language models (both masked and autoregressive) by comparing the log-likelihood assigned to stereotypical vs. counter-stereotypical sentences, summarizing bias as the percentage of times models favor the stereotypical continuation.
AI.result: Of 171 initial stereotypes, 145 are confirmed as culturally relevant for the Dutch context, and 22 new bias patterns are identified from participants’ input. The resulting dataset totals 42,906 sentences. When evaluated, the overall mean bias score across models is close to neutral (around 50%), but disaggregated analysis uncovers substantial variation: some models choose stereotypical sentences as much as 97% of the time for transgender-related items, while for gay-related items they favor stereotypes only about 6% of the time. Transgender and non-binary identities systematically show the strongest measured bias.
AI.conclusion: Culturally adapted benchmarks are crucial: aggregate scores can misleadingly suggest neutrality while hiding severe, group-specific bias. Dutch language models exhibit pronounced and uneven anti-queer bias, particularly targeting transgender and non-binary identities. The released Dutch WinoQueer-style dataset provides a needed tool for more accurate evaluation and, ultimately, mitigation of such biases in Dutch NLP systems.

title: Repo-To-Skill: Distilling GitHub Repositories Into AI4AI Skills
summary:
Autonomous agents are beginning to carry out machine-learning (ML) research end to end. These agents combine a model backbone with a harness for planning, execution, memory, and verification, but this architecture still leaves domain-specific know-how outside the agent. We call this missing layer operational knowledge, the know-how that separates knowing a method from making it work. That knowledge is not absent from the field. It appears in repositories and papers, but in forms written for human readers and too large to load during a task. Once distilled into compact, verified skills, this knowledge can be reused across tasks rather than rediscovered during each run.
  We present DisCo, a skill-powered research agent that creates skills and uses them during research. Its distillation runs in two complementary forms: task-agnostic, condensing the field's widely used repositories into reusable skills, and task-oriented, producing the skills a concrete task calls for. The former, applied across the open ecosystem, yields the AREX-Skill Library, with 5,000+ verified skills distilled from 1,000 widely used ML repositories and organized into 20 areas and 178 capability families. With the GPT-5.5 backbone, research harness, and downstream execution budget held fixed, the skill-equipped research agent scores 134.3% higher on MLE-bench, 34.4% higher on PaperBench, 9.2% higher on FrontierCS, and 14.0% higher on PassNet than the same agent without skills. These gains come from adding distilled operating context under that fixed setup.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DisCo, a skill-powered autonomous research agent that distills and reuses operational ML know-how as reusable skills, significantly improving benchmark performance over a similar agent without skills.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous ML research agents have strong model backbones and planning/execution harnesses but lack embedded domain-specific operational knowledge—the practical know-how needed to make methods actually work. This knowledge exists scattered across repositories and papers, written for humans and too large to load directly, causing agents to repeatedly rediscover similar solutions instead of reusing them efficiently.
AI.method: The authors propose DisCo, an autonomous research agent that automatically distills and manages "skills"—compact, verified units of operational knowledge. Distillation runs in two modes: (1) task-agnostic, where the system mines ~1,000 popular ML repositories to extract, compress, and verify more than 5,000 reusable skills organized into 20 areas and 178 capability families, forming the AREX-Skill Library; and (2) task-oriented, where the agent derives new skills tailored to a specific research task. DisCo then integrates these skills into an otherwise fixed agent stack (same GPT-5.5 backbone, planning harness, and execution budget) to test the impact of skills alone.
AI.result: With the model backbone, research harness, and execution budget held constant, augmenting the agent with the skill library yields large performance gains on several benchmarks relative to the same agent without skills: +134.3% on MLE-bench, +34.4% on PaperBench, +9.2% on FrontierCS, and +14.0% on PassNet. These improvements are attributed specifically to the addition of distilled skills as operational context.
AI.conclusion: Encoding operational ML know-how into compact, verified, reusable skills and integrating them into autonomous research agents substantially boosts their effectiveness without changing the backbone model or resource budget. The DisCo framework and the AREX-Skill Library illustrate a practical path to leveraging the field’s accumulated implementation wisdom, enabling agents to reuse rather than rediscover operational knowledge across tasks.

title: oHC: Orthogonal Hyper-Connections on SO(4) via Quaternions
summary: Hyper-Connections (HC) replace the single residual stream of a Transformer with $n$ parallel ones, mixing them at every layer with a learned $n \times n$ residual matrix. Leaving that matrix unconstrained places no limit on the factor by which the mixing step rescales the residual streams, and that factor compounds across layers, which destabilizes training. Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) address this by restricting the matrix to the doubly stochastic matrices. That caps the factor at one, so the mixing can no longer amplify any direction, but nothing bounds it from below.
