We prove that inside this set the mixing step can reduce the norm of the residual streams only by shrinking the differences between the streams, while their mean is left unchanged; and since the reduction accumulates over layers, the streams grow more alike and their diversity is spent with depth. We therefore propose Orthogonal Hyper-Connections (oHC), restricting the residual matrix to the rotation group $SO(n)$, so that the mixing step can neither amplify nor attenuate the residual streams in any direction, which keeps training stable and no longer forces the differences between the streams to contract. Specifically, at the four streams used by recent HC models we parameterize the group in closed form by a pair of unit quaternions, which adds no parameters, replaces the iterative projection with a fixed pattern of signed additions, and can be constructed faster than mHC. We evaluate oHC across a comprehensive set of downstream tasks, where it outperforms the single-stream residual baseline, mHC and iHC, which fixes the residual matrix to the identity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Orthogonal Hyper-Connections (oHC), a way to stabilize and improve multi-stream residual connections in Transformers by constraining their mixing matrices to be orthogonal rotations, avoiding norm explosion or decay while preserving diversity across streams.
AI.motivation: Hyper-Connections use multiple parallel residual streams in Transformers mixed by a learned matrix, but unconstrained matrices can cause compounding rescaling across layers and destabilize training. A previous fix, manifold-constrained HC (mHC) with doubly stochastic matrices, prevents amplification but allows progressive norm shrinkage and loss of diversity between streams. The motivation is to design a constraint that ensures stability (no amplification or attenuation) while maintaining diversity between multiple residual streams, and to implement it efficiently for practical use.
AI.method: The authors analyze the effect of different constraints on the residual mixing matrix across layers. They show that doubly stochastic constraints (mHC) cap the spectral norm at 1, preventing amplification but allowing contraction that progressively collapses differences between streams while keeping their mean fixed. To address this, they propose Orthogonal Hyper-Connections (oHC), which constrain the residual mixing matrix to the rotation group SO(n), ensuring exact norm preservation in all directions and no forced contraction of inter-stream differences. For the practically relevant case of four residual streams, they derive a closed-form parameterization of SO(4) via a pair of unit quaternions, enabling efficient implementation: no extra parameters, no iterative projection, and mixing via a fixed pattern of signed additions. They replace previous projection-based manifold constraints with this algebraic construction and integrate oHC into Transformer models.
AI.result: Theoretical results: (1) For mHC, within the set of doubly stochastic matrices, the mixing step can only reduce the norm by shrinking differences between residual streams, leaving their mean unchanged; repeated application causes residual streams to become more similar, reducing diversity with depth. (2) For oHC, orthogonal constraints guarantee that the mixing step neither amplifies nor attenuates any direction, preserving norms and not forcing contraction of inter-stream differences. Empirical results: Across a wide range of downstream tasks, Transformers with oHC outperform models using a single residual stream, mHC, and iHC (identity mixing), and oHC is computationally more efficient than mHC due to its closed-form quaternion-based parameterization and elimination of iterative projections.
AI.conclusion: Constraining multi-stream residual mixing in Transformers to orthogonal rotations (SO(n)) yields stable training, preserves diversity between residual streams, and improves performance across tasks compared to existing Hyper-Connection variants and standard single-stream residuals. The quaternion-based parameterization for four streams offers a practical, efficient implementation that removes the need for projection-based manifold optimization while maintaining strict norm preservation. Orthogonal Hyper-Connections thus provide a principled and empirically strong design for multi-stream residual architectures.

title: Bilevel Coordinated Reflection: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems commonly use an orchestrator to decompose a task for a team of workers and then improve through textual reflection. Despite strong empirical results, these systems lack a unified account of coordination, memory improvement, and the role of external verification. We model orchestrator-worker interaction as a bilevel coordination game: under bounded coupling, the workers' local-update game is an approximate potential game whose equilibrium slack is controlled by decomposition quality. We then analyse reflection as stochastic movement over semantic memory states. For free-form reflection, we derive a finite-time upper bound, prove worst-case tightness, and give a positive lower bound under a falsifiable persistent-harm condition. We further prove an information-theoretic impossibility result: no gate that observes only the generated transcript can improve uniformly over text-indistinguishable environments, whereas an environment-grounded gate can. Motivated by this separation, we introduce Stochastic Reflective Memory Ascent (SRMA), which accepts a candidate memory only after a grounded evaluation risk strictly decreases. Under calibration and non-degenerate corrective mass, SRMA converges exactly, geometrically or polynomially; matching constructions show that both rate regimes are order-tight. We also provide confidence gating for stochastic evaluation and re-anchoring guarantees for piecewise-stationary environments. Experiments instantiate these objects with environment-grounded metrics and test the predicted coordination and drift laws. On 500 SWE-bench instances, the complete Kimi-based system resolves 72.2% versus a 70.8% public mini-SWE-agent reference. Code: https://github.com/YihangChen9/Bilevel-Coordinated-Reflection

AI.tldr: The paper provides a theoretical framework for how an orchestrator and workers in multi-agent LLM systems coordinate, how reflection updates shared memory, and when grounded evaluation can reliably improve system performance, introducing an algorithm (SRMA) with provable convergence and empirical gains on SWE-bench.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM systems use heuristics: an orchestrator decomposes tasks, workers solve subtasks, and textual reflection updates shared memory. Despite good empirical performance, there is no unified theoretical account of (1) how task decomposition quality affects coordination, (2) how reflection dynamics over memory lead to improvement or drift, and (3) what external, environment-grounded verification adds beyond transcript-only signals. The paper aims to formalize these aspects as games and stochastic processes and derive guarantees and limits.
AI.method: 1) Formalize orchestrator–worker interaction as a bilevel coordination game, showing the workers’ local update process forms an approximate potential game controlled by decomposition quality. 2) Model reflection as a stochastic process over semantic memory states and derive finite-time bounds for free-form reflection, including worst-case tightness and conditions for positive progress. 3) Prove an information-theoretic impossibility result for transcript-only gating and a separation showing that environment-grounded gates can uniformly improve. 4) Propose Stochastic Reflective Memory Ascent (SRMA), which only accepts memory updates that strictly reduce grounded evaluation risk; analyze its convergence rates (geometric or polynomial) under calibration and corrective-mass assumptions, with matching lower-bound constructions. 5) Extend with confidence-based gating for noisy evaluators and re-anchoring guarantees in piecewise-stationary environments. 6) Empirically instantiate these components with concrete environment-grounded metrics in a Kimi-based multi-agent coding system and test theoretical predictions on SWE-bench.
AI.result: Theoretical results: (a) workers’ local-update dynamics form an approximate potential game whose equilibrium slack is explicitly tied to orchestrator decomposition quality; (b) free-form reflection admits finite-time upper bounds that are worst-case tight, plus a non-trivial lower bound under a persistent-harm condition; (c) a formal impossibility theorem shows transcript-only gates cannot uniformly improve across text-indistinguishable environments, while grounded gates can; (d) SRMA is shown to converge exactly under stated assumptions, with convergence that is either geometric or polynomial, and both rate regimes are shown to be order-tight. Empirical results: implementing these ideas in a Kimi-based system on 500 SWE-bench instances yields 72.2% resolution rate, outperforming a 70.8% public mini-SWE-agent baseline, and experiments validate the predicted coordination and drift behaviors.
AI.conclusion: A principled, game-theoretic and stochastic framework can clarify how multi-agent LLM systems coordinate via task decomposition and reflection, and why purely transcript-based gating is fundamentally limited. By leveraging environment-grounded evaluation, the proposed SRMA procedure yields provable convergence of reflective memory updates and practical performance gains on code-repair benchmarks. This suggests that future multi-agent LLM systems should be designed around grounded, risk-reducing memory updates and theoretically informed coordination mechanisms rather than solely heuristic, text-only reflection loops.

title: From Tokens to Semantics: Leveraging Complementary Signals for Hallucination Detection in Black-Box LLMs
summary: When LLMs support public-facing or high-stakes workflows, missed fabrications can harm users and institutions, while false alarms consume limited human-review capacity. When no trusted context or reference document is available, we study two signals accessible through black-box model APIs: semantic entropy, which measures disagreement among sampled response meanings, and uncertainty derived from token log-probabilities. Their failure modes can be complementary: semantic entropy becomes uninformative when responses form one semantic cluster, while token uncertainty can miss consistently confident errors. We extend token-based uncertainty detection by aggregating token-level signals across sampled responses through our TopK method, evaluate the hybrid CoCoA method, which combines target-response uncertainty with semantic dissimilarity, and propose and study two supervised methods: Gated, which routes single-cluster cases to an aggregated-token-feature classifier, and Stacked, which learns jointly from semantic uncertainty and broader token features. We evaluate seven benchmarks, including five public benchmarks (four text datasets and multimodal handwritten-cheque extraction) and two constructed benchmarks (Financial Summaries and Long-Text QA), using four language models. In our evaluation across models and datasets, Stacked gave the best performance in nearly half of the cases, while TopK and CoCoA remain competitive without supervised training labels, although their thresholds require careful calibration. No method is universally strongest. We therefore evaluate performance at false-positive-rate budgets from 1% to 15%, assess their sensitivity to generation and calibration choices, and examine variation across dataset characteristics.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to detect hallucinations or fabrications from LLMs in black-box settings by using semantic entropy and token-level uncertainty, extends existing methods, and compares hybrid and supervised detectors across multiple benchmarks and models.
AI.motivation: LLMs used in public-facing or high-stakes applications can cause harm when they hallucinate or fabricate information. Existing automatic detectors either over-flag correct answers (wasting human review resources) or miss confident but wrong answers, especially when no external ground-truth context or reference document is available. There is a need for more reliable, black-box-accessible signals and methods to estimate when an LLM output is likely to be a fabrication, while keeping false-positive rates under tight control.
AI.method: The authors focus on two black-box-accessible uncertainty signals: (1) semantic entropy, which measures disagreement in meaning among multiple sampled responses, and (2) uncertainty from token log-probabilities. They analyze complementary failure modes of these signals and then extend token-based uncertainty detection with a TopK aggregation over token-level features across samples. They also analyze a hybrid CoCoA method combining response-level uncertainty with semantic dissimilarity. Finally, they propose two supervised approaches: Gated, which detects single-cluster (low semantic entropy) cases using an aggregated-token-feature classifier, and Stacked, which learns on top of both semantic uncertainty and richer token-based features. They evaluate these methods on seven benchmarks (five public, two constructed) and four LLMs, under varying false-positive-rate constraints and calibration settings.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks and four models, no single method dominates in all settings. The supervised Stacked method achieves the best detection performance in nearly half of the model–dataset combinations. Unsupervised or weakly supervised methods like TopK and CoCoA remain competitive when labels for training are unavailable, though they require careful threshold calibration. The study also documents how performance varies with allowable false-positive-rate budgets (1–15%), generation strategies, calibration choices, and dataset properties.
AI.conclusion: Reliable hallucination detection for LLMs in black-box, no-reference settings requires combining complementary uncertainty signals rather than relying on a single metric. Semantic entropy and token-level uncertainty each have distinct failure modes, and hybrid or supervised methods that integrate both—especially the Stacked approach—often perform best but are not universally superior. Careful threshold calibration and consideration of deployment-specific false-positive-rate constraints are critical, and practitioners should expect method performance to vary by model, task, and dataset characteristics.

title: Measurement-Driven Sub-Network Selection for On-Premise Retrieval-Augmented Factory Agents
summary: On-premise assistants can give factory workers conversational access to machine documentation, but models capable of the task rarely fit shop-floor hardware. We show that after structural compression and retrieval-grounded adaptation, model size is no longer a reliable predictor of adapted answer quality: general capability falls almost linearly with parameter count, while judged retrieval-augmented answer quality does not. We therefore treat deployment as a post-adaptation selection problem, committing one sub-network per device on judged answer quality and measured on-device throughput under a configurable general-capability floor and memory budget; rules that optimize size, speed, or quality alone each give up capability or throughput. A weight-shared supernetwork trained with sandwich-style in-place distillation keeps this selection inexpensive. In a manufacturing-manual case study, extraction costs 13.7 percent of the unpruned model's judged quality and retrieval-grounded distillation returns it to within 4.6 percent, recovering two thirds of the loss, and the same assistant runs across three heterogeneous edge tiers at 1.3 to 5 watts standby.

AI.tldr: Paper compresses and adapts language models for on-premise factory assistants, showing that after retrieval-grounded adaptation, model size poorly predicts answer quality, and proposes a supernetwork-based selection method to deploy tailored subnetworks across heterogeneous edge devices.
AI.motivation: Factory workers need conversational access to machine documentation on local, low-power hardware, but capable language models are usually too large and generic. Existing scaling laws link model size to general capability, yet in retrieval-augmented, domain-adapted settings these laws may not hold, and naive deployment choices that optimize only size, speed, or quality can be suboptimal under edge constraints.
AI.method: Apply structural compression (pruning / sub-network extraction) to a base model, then perform retrieval-grounded adaptation/distillation using domain manuals. Treat deployment as a post-adaptation selection problem over subnetworks of a weight-shared supernetwork, trained with sandwich-style in-place distillation so many subnetworks can be evaluated cheaply. Subnetworks are selected per device based on judged answer quality on retrieval-augmented tasks and on-device throughput, subject to a configurable general-capability floor and memory budget.
AI.result: Empirically, general capability degrades roughly linearly with parameter count, but judged answer quality on retrieval-augmented tasks does not track size. In a manufacturing-manual case study, structural extraction reduces judged quality by 13.7% relative to the full unpruned model; retrieval-grounded distillation recovers two-thirds of this loss, ending within 4.6% of original quality. A single assistant design is successfully deployed across three heterogeneous edge tiers, each running at 1.3–5 W standby.
AI.conclusion: After structural compression and retrieval-grounded adaptation, model size is no longer a reliable proxy for answer quality in retrieval-augmented industrial assistants; deployment should be framed as selecting subnetworks under quality, capability, and hardware constraints rather than simply picking the largest feasible model. Weight-shared supernetworks with sandwich-style in-place distillation enable inexpensive exploration of these trade-offs and practical deployment of conversational factory assistants on low-power, heterogeneous on-premise hardware.

title: DKL: Decoupled Knowledge Learning for Instruction-Tuned Language Models
summary: RAG has become the de facto method for incorporating new, corpus-specific knowledge into an instruction following LLM (Instruct LLM). Although RAG-based prompting improves factual grounding, it fails when retrieval is incorrect or incomplete, leading to hallucinations. Finetuning methods such as RAFT and PA-RAG enhance RAG by injecting new knowledge into the model's parameters, but require generating a massive amount of synthetic QA that covers the entire corpus. Extended Pre-Training (EPT) on the text corpus avoids the need for comprehensive synthetic data generation but compromises an Instruct LLM's instruction-following capabilities, necessitating instruction fine-tuning (IFT) after pre-training. However, IFT is costly and may be infeasible due to the unavailability of an instruction-tuning corpus. In this work, we propose DKL-Decoupled Knowledge Learning for Instruction-Tuned Language Models. Instead of doing EPT on the Instruct LLM, DKL performs EPT on its corresponding base LLM to infuse new knowledge. These knowledge infused weights are then merged with the Instruct LLM, imparting new knowledge without affecting their instruction-following capabilities. DKL is a lightweight method that avoids expensive instruction fine-tuning and relies on model merging to infuse the new knowledge into the Instruct LLM without destroying its instruction following capabilities. Empirical results show that DKL improves RAG accuracy from 54.17 to 79.26 on retrieval failure cases, while outperforming prior approaches with substantially less training data.

AI.tldr: They propose DKL, a method that injects new corpus-specific knowledge into instruction-tuned LLMs by pre-training only the base model and then merging weights, improving RAG reliability without re-doing costly instruction fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: RAG improves factual grounding but fails when retrieval is wrong or incomplete, causing hallucinations. Existing fixes either need massive synthetic QA (RAFT, PA-RAG) or extended pre-training that destroys instruction-following, requiring expensive instruction fine-tuning with data that may not exist. The authors want a way to add new knowledge to an instruct model without large synthetic datasets or re-doing instruction tuning.
AI.method: Perform extended pre-training (EPT) on the domain corpus using the base LLM (the model before instruction tuning), producing a knowledge-enriched base model. Then merge these updated base-model weights with the existing instruction-tuned model’s weights, so that the instruction behavior is preserved while the underlying knowledge is updated. Use this merged model in a RAG setup and evaluate especially on retrieval-failure cases.
AI.result: DKL significantly boosts RAG performance in cases where retrieval fails, increasing accuracy from 54.17 to 79.26. It also beats previous approaches like RAFT/PA-RAG while using much less training data, demonstrating better data efficiency and robustness to retrieval errors.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling knowledge learning from instruction tuning via weight merging allows efficient infusion of new corpus-specific knowledge into instruction LLMs without costly instruction fine-tuning or huge synthetic QA datasets. DKL preserves instruction-following capabilities while substantially improving RAG robustness and accuracy, especially under retrieval failure conditions.

title: SafeEvolve: Harness-Policy Co-Evolution from Agent Experience for Safety Alignment
summary: The performance of LLM-based agents is jointly shaped by the base model and the harness used when interacting with the environment. This exposes them to safety risks in both harmful final responses and multi-step execution trajectories. Existing safety alignment mechanisms often rely on either external harness updates or policy optimization, yet applying either paradigm in isolation fails to bridge runtime control with intrinsic safety. We propose SafeEvolve, an experience-driven self-evolving framework for agent safety alignment. SafeEvolve leverages safety experience from completed on-policy trajectories to drive a continual loop of harness-policy co-evolution. On the harness side, SafeEvolve converts trajectory-level safety evidence into bounded, component-level updates across safety prompt and hierarchical skills, yielding auditable and reversible harness artifacts. On the policy side, SafeEvolve follows a two-stage SFT-RL paradigm, where harness-use SFT bootstraps the policy to actively leverage evolved harness artifacts, and harness-augmented RL further shapes autonomous safety behaviors during multi-step exploration via verifier-decomposed rewards. Through harness-policy co-evolution, SafeEvolve converts safety experience into an evolved runtime harness and improved policy behavior. Experiments on agentic safety benchmarks show that SafeEvolve achieves a stronger safety-utility tradeoff than existing baselines. For Qwen3.5-4B, SafeEvolve achieves a $3\times$ ASR reduction on AgentDojo while improving benign utility from 59.79% to 61.86%.

AI.tldr: SafeEvolve is a self-evolving safety framework that jointly improves both the agent’s harness (prompts, skills) and its policy, using safety feedback from its own trajectories to reduce harmful behavior while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents’ safety depends not only on the base model but also on the interaction harness (prompts, tools, skills). Current alignment approaches typically adjust either the external harness or the model policy alone, which cannot reliably ensure safe behavior over multi-step trajectories at runtime. There is a need for a method that tightly couples runtime control mechanisms with intrinsic safety behaviors and can continually improve from experience.
AI.method: SafeEvolve introduces an experience-driven, continual co-evolution loop between the agent harness and the policy. From completed on-policy trajectories, it collects safety evidence and converts it into bounded, auditable updates to the safety prompt and hierarchical skills (harness side). On the policy side, it uses a two-stage paradigm: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on data showing how to use the evolved harness, so the policy learns to leverage these safety artifacts; (2) harness-augmented reinforcement learning (RL), where multi-step exploration is guided by rewards decomposed by a verifier that evaluates safety, further shaping autonomous safety behavior. This loop iteratively refines both harness and policy based on accumulated safety experience.
AI.result: On agentic safety benchmarks, SafeEvolve demonstrates better safety-utility trade-offs than baselines. For example, with the Qwen3.5-4B model on the AgentDojo benchmark, SafeEvolve reduces the attack success rate (ASR) by a factor of 3 while slightly improving benign task success (utility) from 59.79% to 61.86%.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving the harness and policy using safety experience enables more robust and auditable safety alignment for LLM-based agents, improving both runtime safety control and intrinsic safe behavior. SafeEvolve shows that this joint, continual alignment process can significantly lower harmful outcomes without sacrificing, and even slightly improving, benign utility.

title: Trace as State: Reasoning Traces as Conditional States for Long-Context Transformers
summary:
Transformers process information causally, but long-context reasoning may depend on task state discovered only later. We formalize this mismatch through conditional state update tasks. For causal state update processors, providing the condition first can require exponentially less memory in the worst case than providing it last.
  Motivated by this principle, we introduce Trace as State. We use collected reasoning traces as a textual proxy for task state and place it before the long-context block on a fresh pass, allowing information derived previously to guide rereading.
  We conduct extensive experiments on Trace as State and Trace Append, a matched control that uses the same task state proxy but put it after the context. Across three models and three long-context datasets, Trace as State outperforms Trace Append in 26 of 27 reported combinations of model, task, and metric. On GraphWalks Parents, exact match lifts DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview from 29.2% on the initial pass and 43.0% with Trace Appendto 81.8% with Trace as State, and from 66.4% and 83.2% to 100.0% for GLM-5.2. These results show that placing traces before the context can improve long-context reasoning while retaining the causal transformer structure.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that putting reasoning traces before the long context (Trace as State) significantly improves long-context reasoning in causal transformers compared to putting the same traces after (Trace Append).
AI.motivation: Causal transformers read text left-to-right, but for many long-context tasks, important task-specific state is only determined after reading much of the context. This creates a mismatch: the model would benefit from knowing that state earlier so it can attend to relevant parts of the context efficiently. The authors want to formalize this limitation and explore how to inject task state information in a way that respects the causal structure but still improves long-context reasoning.
AI.method:
1) They formalize ":conditional state update" tasks to capture cases where having the condition early vs late in the input provably changes the memory demands for any causal state-update processor. They show that giving the condition first can reduce required memory exponentially in the worst case.
2) Inspired by this, they propose "Trace as State": run the model once to obtain a reasoning trace, then feed a second pass where this trace is prepended (placed before) the long context as a textual proxy for task state. This lets the model reread the context using the previously discovered information.
3) As a control, they define "Trace Append", which uses the same trace but appends it after the context, preserving the same content but not giving the model early access to it.
4) They evaluate both strategies across three transformer models and three long-context datasets, including tasks like GraphWalks Parents, and compare metrics such as exact match accuracy across initial pass, Trace Append, and Trace as State.
AI.result: Across 27 combinations of model, task, and metric, Trace as State beats Trace Append in 26 cases. The improvements are often very large. For example, on the GraphWalks Parents dataset, DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview improves from 29.2% exact match on the first pass and 43.0% with Trace Append to 81.8% with Trace as State. Similarly, GLM-5.2 goes from 66.4% (initial) and 83.2% (Trace Append) up to 100.0% exact match with Trace as State. These results empirically confirm that placing the reasoning trace before the long context is much more effective for long-context reasoning than placing it after, even though both use the same trace content.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates both theoretically and empirically that, for causal transformers, the position of task state information (here, reasoning traces) within the input sequence matters crucially for long-context reasoning. Providing the state first can drastically reduce effective memory requirements and yields substantial performance gains. The proposed Trace as State method offers a practical way to improve long-context reasoning while keeping the causal transformer architecture unchanged, simply by prepending reasoning traces before rereading the context.

title: Large Language Models (LLMs) for Telecom Root Cause Analysis (RCA): A Structured Reasoning Framework for Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis
summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) is a critical task in telecom network operations, but diagnosing performance degradations in modern 5G and emerging 6G networks remains challenging due to complex cross-layer dependencies. While large language models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for reasoning and knowledge integration, directly applying vanilla LLMs to telecom RCA often leads to hallucination, unstable reasoning, and poor alignment with structured network evidence. This work first reviews the evolution of telecom RCA from rule-based and machine learning (ML) approaches to emerging LLM-enabled techniques, and provides an overview of recent paradigms, including structured reasoning, retrieval-augmented knowledge grounding, agentic orchestration, and verifiable reasoning. Building upon these insights, we propose a structured reasoning framework for LLM-enabled telecom RCA that aligns diagnostic reasoning with telecom-specific evidence and domain knowledge. The proposed approach first organizes heterogeneous network telemetry into canonical contexts, and then enforces decision-path reasoning during diagnosis, and finally generates evidence-grounded explanations for reliable fault identification. Experimental results on two 5G RCA datasets, TeleLogs and TelecomTS, demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves diagnostic accuracy and decision consistency compared with baseline techniques. These cross-dataset results highlight the importance of structured reasoning design for practical LLM-based RCA systems in next-generation telecom networks.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys telecom root cause analysis (RCA) methods and proposes a structured reasoning LLM framework that grounds diagnostics in 5G/6G network evidence, improving accuracy and consistency over baselines on two datasets.
AI.motivation: Telecom RCA in 5G/6G networks is hard because of complex cross-layer dependencies. Traditional rule-based and ML methods struggle with this complexity, and vanilla LLMs hallucinate, reason unstably, and misalign with structured network data, so a more robust, evidence-grounded LLM approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors first review prior RCA approaches, then design a structured reasoning framework for LLM-based RCA. Their method: (1) organize heterogeneous network telemetry into canonical context representations, (2) constrain the LLM to follow explicit decision-path reasoning during diagnosis, and (3) generate explanations that are explicitly grounded in telecom evidence and domain knowledge. They evaluate on two 5G RCA datasets, TeleLogs and TelecomTS, against baseline techniques.
AI.result: On both TeleLogs and TelecomTS datasets, the proposed structured reasoning framework yields higher diagnostic accuracy and more consistent decision paths than existing baselines, demonstrating better reliability and robustness of RCA in 5G networks.
AI.conclusion: Structured, evidence-aligned reasoning is crucial for deploying LLMs in practical telecom RCA. By organizing telemetry into canonical contexts and enforcing decision-path reasoning with verifiable, evidence-grounded explanations, LLM-based RCA systems can more reliably diagnose faults in next-generation 5G/6G networks.

title: CORAL: An LLM-Native Harness for Production Recommender Systems
summary: Production recommender systems shape what billions of people see, and sustaining their performance requires continual optimization: as content, user behavior, and upstream models shift, the choices governing retrieval, ranking, and serving must be revisited. Traditionally, human engineers test such changes through online experiments--a slow, reactive process limited by engineering effort, leaving parts of the system unrevised as conditions change. Although large language models have been applied to ranking, user modeling, and offline model development, few systems place an agent in a continual closed loop that acts on a live recommender and learns from the measured effects of its decisions. We present CORAL (Constraint-Optimized Recommender via an Agentic Loop), an LLM-native harness that closes this loop: each cycle, the agent observes operating signals, reasons over a memory of past decisions and outcomes, and invokes tools--including a numerical optimizer that keeps changes within a fixed operating budget--to reconfigure the recommender, with measured outcomes informing the next cycle. We formulate this as a partially observed, non-stationary, constrained optimization problem in which the policy improves in context, without parameter updates, from its prior actions. Across two large-scale social platforms, evaluated with A/B experiments, the same harness improves engagement at no additional serving cost on one and reduces serving cost without degrading engagement on the other, spanning the engagement-efficiency frontier. Performance improves as the loop iterates, suggesting that a single agentic loop can automate continual optimization work traditionally performed by human algorithm engineers under explicit guardrails.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CORAL, an LLM-driven agentic loop that continuously optimizes production recommender systems by automatically reconfiguring them based on live feedback, improving engagement and/or serving cost under strict constraints.
AI.motivation: Production recommender systems constantly face distribution shifts in content, user behavior, and upstream models. Maintaining strong performance requires continuous retuning of retrieval, ranking, and serving parameters. Currently this is largely done manually by engineers via A/B tests, which is slow, reactive, and limited by human bandwidth, leading to stale configurations and suboptimal trade-offs between engagement and serving cost. Existing uses of LLMs in recommendation focus on ranking or offline modeling rather than closing a full live optimization loop. The authors aim to automate this continual optimization work safely and efficiently.
AI.method: The authors design CORAL (Constraint-Optimized Recommender via an Agentic Loop), an LLM-native control harness that operates in repeated cycles on a live recommender. In each cycle, an LLM-based agent: (1) observes operational signals and metrics from the recommender, (2) consults a memory of past configuration changes and their measured outcomes, (3) reasons about potential adjustments, and (4) invokes tools, notably a numerical optimizer that enforces a fixed change budget and other constraints, to modify retrieval/ranking/serving settings. The problem is framed as a partially observed, non-stationary constrained optimization task, where the policy adapts based on feedback from prior actions without updating model parameters. The system is deployed on two large-scale social platforms and evaluated through real A/B tests.
AI.result: When deployed in production on two large social platforms, the same CORAL harness achieves different but complementary wins: on one platform it increases user engagement without increasing serving cost, and on the other it lowers serving cost while maintaining engagement. These outcomes show that the system can traverse the engagement-efficiency frontier depending on context. Furthermore, performance continues to improve over successive optimization cycles, indicating that the agentic loop learns effective configuration policies from its own history of interventions and measured impacts, even without gradient-based model updates.
AI.conclusion: CORAL demonstrates that an LLM-based agentic loop can safely and effectively automate continual optimization of large-scale recommender systems under explicit operational constraints. By treating configuration tuning as a partially observed, non-stationary constrained optimization problem and using tools such as numerical optimizers within the loop, the system can replace a significant portion of repetitive manual tuning by human engineers while respecting guardrails on cost and performance. The positive A/B test results on two distinct platforms suggest that such agentic harnesses are a practical way to keep production recommenders aligned with shifting conditions along the engagement–efficiency frontier.

title: AI Contextual Measurement for Recovering Individual and Group-Level Effects: Validation Against Survey Measures and an Occupational Application
summary:
Researchers increasingly use artificial intelligence to construct measures of social, organizational, and occupational characteristics that are absent from conventional surveys. We propose AICOME, AI COntextual MEasurement, a framework for evaluating whether AI-derived respondent-level measures can recover individual and group-level effects in contextual models. The key idea is that an AI measure constructed at the respondent level can be used to derive its group-level aggregate and its individual deviation, allowing researchers to estimate both between-group and within-group associations rather than treating AI measurement as response prediction alone.
  We validate the framework using the 2022 China Family Panel Studies (CFPS), where occupations provide the empirical grouping structure and several job-related survey variables provide validation benchmarks. For computer use, foreign-language use, weekly hours, and management responsibilities, we compare survey measures with AI-derived measures in response-level, model-level, contextual, and boundary-condition validations. The results show that AI contextual measurement can recover much of the contextual-model information contained in observed survey variables when rich respondent and job characteristics are available. Weekly hours provides the strongest validation case, with AI-derived measures reproducing the large negative between- and within-occupation associations with satisfaction observed in CFPS. The framework also identifies clear boundary conditions: performance deteriorates when information is restricted to occupation and basic demographics, and recovery is weaker when several related concepts are treated as simultaneously unobserved. The findings suggest that AICOME is most useful for recovering a limited number of theoretically important constructs from rich existing datasets.

AI.tldr: AICOME is a framework to test whether AI-generated, respondent-level measures can validly recover both individual and group-level effects in contextual models, using occupations in the CFPS 2022 as a validation case.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly used to construct measures of social and organizational characteristics that are missing from standard surveys, but it is unclear whether such AI-derived measures can validly capture both within-group (individual) and between-group (contextual) effects used in contextual models, rather than just predict missing responses.
AI.method: The authors propose AICOME, which treats AI-generated respondent-level scores as building blocks to compute group-level aggregates and individual deviations, enabling full contextual modeling. They validate this using the 2022 China Family Panel Studies, defining occupations as groups and comparing AI-derived measures of job characteristics (computer use, foreign-language use, weekly hours, management responsibilities) against their survey-based counterparts through multiple validation exercises: response-level accuracy, model-level fit, ability to recover contextual (between/within-occupation) associations, and tests under restricted-information and multi-construct conditions.
AI.result: AI-derived contextual measures recover a large portion of the information in observed survey variables when rich respondent and job covariates are available. For weekly work hours in particular, the AI measures closely replicate both the strong negative between-occupation and within-occupation relationships with job satisfaction found using survey data. However, performance declines markedly when inputs are limited to basic demographics and occupation, and when multiple related unobserved constructs are simultaneously inferred.
AI.conclusion: AICOME can validly reconstruct both individual- and group-level relationships for a small number of key constructs, provided rich input data are available. It is less reliable in sparse-information settings or when many correlated latent concepts must be inferred at once. Thus, AICOME is best used to recover a limited set of theoretically central, missing variables in well-measured datasets, enabling AI-based contextual analysis beyond simple response imputation.

title: Choosing a PEFT Variant for Per-Patient Dysarthric ASR: A Single-Speaker Case Study on Two ASR Bases
summary: Per-patient adapters are the preferred production architecture for dysarthric automatic speech recognition (ASR), yet parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) variants have not been compared in the speaker-dependent, per-patient regime. We present a single-speaker case study comparing seven LoRA-family methods (LoRA, QLoRA, AdaLoRA, DoRA, LoHA, VeRA, VB-LoRA) on two production bases (Whisper-large-v3 with Hungarian fine-tuning, and a multilingual Qwen3-ASR-1.7B checkpoint) for one post-stroke Hungarian male speaker (S1, 409 utterances; severe dysarthria on auditory-perceptual clinical assessment). Attention-projection adapters substantially improve CER on both bases. Across three seeds, a paired bootstrap detects no significant LoRA-DoRA difference (p>0.5; 13.86/13.90 % CER on Whisper, 28.10/28.33 % on Qwen3-ASR), so we adopt the simpler, cheaper LoRA. Real 4-bit (NF4) QLoRA is worse on every seed and both bases (14.56/30.09 % CER) with no memory saving at this scale, and LoHA, VeRA, VB-LoRA and AdaLoRA do not reach the LoRA family, though LoHA still gives an 18.6 % relative CER reduction on Whisper. On the same base, full fine-tuning is more accurate (11.43 % CER), but a 115 MB LoRA that also adapts the feed-forward blocks reaches within 0.66 pp of it at approximately 3.7 % of the per-patient storage. A 6-point enrollment grid shows about 5 min of patient audio captures 45.6 % of the zero-shot-to-30-min CER reduction, with further gains at 10 and 30 min (caveat: one speaker, one language, severe post-stroke dysarthria). Training scripts and recipes will be released, source-available under a research-use licence, on publication.

AI.tldr: The paper compares several parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapter methods for dysarthric ASR in a strict per-patient setting and finds that simple attention-projection LoRA adapters give most of the benefit close to full fine-tuning with far lower storage cost.
AI.motivation: In clinical and assistive settings for people with dysarthria, ASR systems often use per-patient models because speech patterns are highly individual. However, per-patient full fine-tuning is storage-heavy and computationally expensive when scaling to many users. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) with adapters is attractive but has not been systematically evaluated, especially across LoRA-family variants, in a speaker-dependent dysarthria regime. The authors want to know which adapter type is actually best in this realistic, production-like scenario and how much patient data is needed to achieve good gains.
AI.method: The authors perform a single-speaker, speaker-dependent case study on one Hungarian male post-stroke speaker with severe dysarthria and 409 utterances. They compare seven LoRA-family PEFT methods (LoRA, QLoRA with 4-bit NF4, AdaLoRA, DoRA, LoHA, VeRA, VB-LoRA) attached to the attention projections, on two strong ASR bases: Whisper-large-v3 that has been fine-tuned for Hungarian, and a multilingual Qwen3-ASR-1.7B checkpoint. They run multiple random seeds and use paired bootstrap testing to check for significant differences. They also test variants that extend LoRA adaptation to feed-forward blocks and compare against full fine-tuning. Finally they explore an enrollment-time grid (varying amount of per-patient audio, up to 30 minutes) to quantify how accuracy improves as more patient data is used.
AI.result: Attention-projection adapters significantly improve character error rate (CER) on both Whisper-large-v3 and Qwen3-ASR-1.7B bases. LoRA and DoRA perform similarly: across three seeds, CER differences are statistically non-significant (p>0.5), with LoRA/DoRA achieving around 13.86/13.90% CER on Whisper and 28.10/28.33% on Qwen3-ASR. Real 4-bit QLoRA (NF4) performs worse than LoRA on every seed and both bases (about 14.56% and 30.09% CER) and does not yield memory savings at this model scale. LoHA, VeRA, VB-LoRA, and AdaLoRA also underperform LoRA, although LoHA still delivers an 18.6% relative CER reduction on Whisper compared to the unadapted base. Full fine-tuning on Whisper is best at 11.43% CER, but a larger LoRA configuration that also adapts feed-forward layers comes within 0.66 percentage points of this while using only about 3.7% of the per-patient storage (115 MB adapter vs full model copy). Enrollment analysis shows that with about 5 minutes of patient audio, the system already captures ~45.6% of the total CER reduction achievable between zero-shot and 30 minutes, with further incremental gains at 10 and 30 minutes.
AI.conclusion: For per-patient dysarthric ASR, simple attention-projection LoRA adapters are a strong and practical baseline: they offer large CER improvements across two production ASR bases and approach full fine-tuning performance when extended to feed-forward blocks, while using a small fraction of per-patient storage. More complex LoRA-family variants (QLoRA, AdaLoRA, DoRA, LoHA, VeRA, VB-LoRA) do not deliver consistent advantages in this small-scale, per-patient setting; quantized QLoRA in particular underperforms without memory savings. Roughly 5 minutes of patient-specific audio already yields a substantial portion of the possible accuracy gains, though more data continues to help. The findings are limited to one severely dysarthric Hungarian speaker and one language, but suggest that lightweight LoRA adapters are an efficient and scalable choice for per-patient clinical ASR deployments.

title: Discriminative World Models for Web Agents
summary: Recent web agents use world models for test-time action selection by sampling candidate actions, predicting the resulting web states, and ranking them with a ranker model or a Process Reward Model (PRM). These world models are typically trained via supervised next-state prediction to generate fixed representations like HTML or AXTree snapshots. However, this objective is misaligned with the downstream ranker, which relies on predicted states being discriminative across candidates to accurately score them. To address this, we introduce predicted-state matching, a training objective where the predicted representation must distinguish the true resulting state from those reached by alternative actions. We train these models using a branching web-agent dataset derived from WebArena Go-Browse trajectories, where every decision point contains multiple alternative actions and their resulting states. Experiments on our held-out predicted-state matching benchmark show that our approach outperforms world models trained with supervised next-state prediction. We further show that our approach improves PRM-style action ranking on WebPRMBench compared with action-only PRMs and PRMs augmented with supervised-next-state world models. Finally, on WebArena-Lite, using our world model for test-time action selection improves end-to-end task success. Our project page is available at: https://dhruvpendharkar.github.io/dwm/.

AI.tldr: They propose a new training objective for web-world models where predicted next states must distinguish the true next state from states of alternative actions, leading to better action ranking and higher task success for web agents.
AI.motivation: Existing world models for web agents are trained with supervised next-state prediction (e.g., predicting HTML/AXTree snapshots). This produces generic representations that are not necessarily useful for ranking candidate actions, because the ranker or PRM needs predicted states that are discriminative across alternative actions. The mismatch between world-model training (reconstruction) and downstream use (discrimination for ranking) limits performance in web-agent decision making.
AI.method: They introduce a predicted-state matching objective: the world model is trained so that its predicted next-state representation for an action is closer to the true resulting state and distinguishable from states reached by alternative actions at the same decision point. Training data comes from a branching dataset built from WebArena Go-Browse trajectories, where each decision point includes multiple alternative actions and their resulting states. The learned representations are then used in PRM-style pipelines for ranking candidate actions at test time.
AI.result: On a held-out predicted-state matching benchmark, world models trained with this new objective outperform standard supervised next-state prediction models. When integrated into PRM-style action ranking and evaluated on WebPRMBench, these models surpass both action-only PRMs and PRMs that are augmented with conventional supervised-next-state world models. Finally, on WebArena-Lite, using the proposed world model for test-time action selection yields higher end-to-end task success rates.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the world-model training objective with the discriminative needs of downstream action ranking—via predicted-state matching over branching trajectories—produces more useful predicted-state representations. This leads to better action ranking and improved overall performance of web agents on realistic web navigation and interaction benchmarks.

title: Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention
summary: Language models spend most of their attention on a small fraction of context, yet they read the entire KV cache to find the few tokens that matter. If the user asks about a previous detail in a 1M-token conversation, global attention layers must scan the full context to generate each token of the reply. A prominent approach mitigates this cost by pre-selecting relevant tokens via lightweight proxy scores, but this extrinsic scoring still incurs O(N) per step. We take an intrinsic approach motivated by the simple question: wouldn't the model already know which parts of the context are relevant? To this end, we introduce Declarative Attention (DA), a protocol that elicits the model to declare where it needs to attend within its chain-of-thought, partitioning generation into three modes: <global> (full context), <focus> (a specific region), and <local> (recent output only). The inference engine parses these declarations like tool calls and skips most of the KV cache read. Under zero-shot evaluation across 15 long-context tasks, DA on off-the-shelf models (Gemma-4-31B, Qwen-3.6-27B) significantly reduces total attended tokens during decoding (52.0%, 31.1%) with modest accuracy drops (1.27pp, 2.75pp) that shrink with model scale. DA unlocks a new axis of sparse attention, with further potential under training-based methods that future work can explore.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Declarative Attention, a way for language models to explicitly declare which parts of long context they need to read, cutting KV-cache reads and total attended tokens by about one‑third to one‑half with only small accuracy drops.
AI.motivation: Long‑context language models are computationally expensive at inference because global attention layers must scan the full key–value (KV) cache at every decoding step, even though the model only needs information from a small subset of tokens. Existing methods that pre-select relevant tokens rely on external, lightweight scoring mechanisms but still require O(N) operations per step over the full context. The authors aim to reduce the effective attention cost by leveraging the model’s own internal knowledge of which context regions are relevant, without additional external scoring passes.
AI.method: They introduce Declarative Attention (DA), a protocol in which the model, within its chain-of-thought, emits explicit declarations of where it wants to attend. Generation is partitioned into three modes: <global>, in which the full context is accessible; <focus>, in which the model specifies a particular region of the context to attend to; and <local>, which restricts attention to the recent output only. The inference engine parses these declarations similarly to tool calls and uses them to determine which segments of the KV cache to read or skip, thereby implementing a form of intrinsically guided sparse attention on top of standard long-context models, without retraining.
AI.result: Using DA on off‑the‑shelf long‑context models (Gemma‑4‑31B and Qwen‑3.6‑27B), evaluated zero-shot on 15 long‑context tasks, the method reduces the total number of attended tokens during decoding by 52.0% and 31.1%, respectively. These computational savings come with only modest drops in task accuracy of 1.27 percentage points for Gemma‑4‑31B and 2.75 percentage points for Qwen‑3.6‑27B, with evidence that the accuracy gap shrinks as model size increases.
AI.conclusion: Declarative Attention demonstrates that language models can be prompted to explicitly declare which parts of long contexts are relevant and that these declarations can be used at inference time to implement efficient sparse attention over the KV cache. This intrinsic, model-driven approach provides a new axis for scaling long-context inference efficiency, complementing or potentially replacing extrinsic proxy-scoring methods, and suggests that training-based refinements could further improve both efficiency gains and accuracy in future work.

title: Untangling the Mechanisms of Misleading Context in Medical Question Answering
summary: Large language models now answer medical questions with expert-level performance. However, the context these systems act on can be misleading, and misleading context can corrupt a model's medical judgment. To understand how misleading context corrupts this judgment, we examine the model's susceptibility to the context, disclosure of it, mechanism of corrupted reasoning, and monitorability of the decision. On the medical reasoning subset of MedMisBench, a clinician-reviewed question-answering benchmark of 8,627 questions, we inject two types of misleading context cues, fabricated evidence and a bare assertion. We test three reasoning models, two that expose their full reasoning trace and one frontier model that exposes only its response. All three are more susceptible to the assertion than to the fabricated evidence, adopting the asserted answer 10 to 27 points more often. The misleading cues are disclosed in 81 to 98% of traces but only 7 to 90% of responses, and the assertion is disclosed less often than evidence based cues. Resampling from reasoning traces without disclosure shows the two cues corrupt reasoning differently, evidence entering early and accumulating while the assertion redirects the conclusion near its end. An LLM monitor catches 78% of corrupted decisions at 5% false positives when reading an open model's trace with guidance, against at most 32% from any response. The misleading context that models are most susceptible to is disclosed least, and was caught reliably only from an open reasoning trace, which frontier providers withhold.

AI.tldr: Study of how misleading context corrupts medical reasoning in LLMs and how well we can detect it.
AI.motivation: LLMs now achieve expert-level medical QA, but real-world inputs can contain misleading or incorrect contextual information. It is crucial to understand when and how such context corrupts model decisions, and whether this corruption can be detected and monitored, especially as powerful frontier models often hide their internal reasoning.
AI.method: Using the medical reasoning subset of MedMisBench (8,627 clinician-reviewed QA items), the authors inject two types of misleading context into prompts: (1) fabricated evidence and (2) a bare, unsupported assertion. They evaluate three models—two that expose full reasoning traces and one frontier model that only outputs final answers. They measure susceptibility (how often the model adopts the misleading answer), disclosure (whether the misleading cue appears in the reasoning or response), temporal dynamics of corruption via resampling from partial traces, and detectability using an LLM-based monitor that reads either full traces or only final responses.
AI.result: All models are more easily swayed by bare assertions than by fabricated evidence, adopting the asserted incorrect answer 10–27 percentage points more often. Misleading cues are mentioned in 81–98% of internal reasoning traces but only 7–90% of final responses, and assertions are disclosed less than evidence. Trace resampling reveals distinct mechanisms: fabricated evidence influences reasoning early and accumulatively, whereas assertions shift the final conclusion late in the chain. An LLM monitor, when given full traces plus guidance, detects about 78% of corrupted decisions at a 5% false positive rate; when limited to final answers or short responses, detection tops out at ~32%.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are most vulnerable to misleading contextual assertions, yet those cues are the least likely to appear in final outputs, making them harder to audit from responses alone. Effective detection of corrupted medical decisions requires access to full reasoning traces, which current frontier models typically do not provide. This raises safety and transparency concerns for deploying such systems in high-stakes medical settings.

title: From Reweighting to Rewriting: Unlocking the Intervention Effects of Influential Samples in Training Data Attribution
summary: Training data attribution (TDA) aims to identify training examples that shape model behavior, but its intervention value depends on both which examples are selected and how they are modified. Influence functions (IF) estimate behavioral changes under infinitesimal reweighting, yet IF-selected examples often show limited advantages over random selection under conventional weight-based interventions. This raises the question of whether influential examples lack intervention value or whether reweighting fails to realize their behavioral leverage.We introduce influence-guided response rewriting, which uses IF to identify intervention targets and replaces their responses with behavior-aligned or behavior-opposed supervision while keeping instructions fixed. Across four open-weight LLMs, we compare rewriting and reweighting on the same influence-selected examples using epistemic abstention as our primary testbed. Response rewriting produces stronger, more persistent, and bidirectional behavioral shifts, while reweighting the same examples yields weak and inconsistent effects. Further analyses show that influence-selected examples provide greater rewriting leverage than alternative selectors, with changes remaining concentrated on target-relevant behaviors. The same qualitative contrast extends to safety refusal. These results distinguish the local reweighting effects captured by influence estimates from the broader intervention leverage of the examples they identify, motivating intervention-aware evaluation of TDA methods.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how training data attribution via influence functions can be used not just to diagnose but to effectively intervene on large language model behavior, showing that rewriting influential examples’ responses is far more effective than simply reweighting them.
AI.motivation: Training data attribution aims to find which training examples most affect model behavior, but it is unclear whether these examples are truly useful for changing behavior. Prior work uses influence functions mainly with infinitesimal reweighting and finds limited gains over random selection, raising doubt about the intervention value of influential examples and the practical utility of TDA for steering LLMs.
AI.method: The authors use influence functions to select influential training examples and then compare two intervention strategies on those same examples: (1) standard weight-based reweighting and (2) a new approach, influence-guided response rewriting, which replaces the examples’ responses with behavior-aligned or behavior-opposed supervision while keeping the instructions unchanged. They test these interventions across four open-weight LLMs, using epistemic abstention and safety refusal as primary behavioral domains, and analyze the strength, persistence, directionality, and specificity of resulting behavioral shifts, as well as compare influence-based selection to alternative selectors.
AI.result: Influence-guided response rewriting induces strong, sustained, and bidirectional shifts in model behavior on epistemic abstention tasks, whereas reweighting the same influence-selected examples produces only weak and inconsistent changes. Influence-selected examples, when rewritten, yield larger and more behavior-targeted effects than alternative selection methods, with modifications remaining focused on the targeted behaviors. Similar qualitative patterns are observed for safety refusal.
AI.conclusion: Influential examples identified by influence functions do possess substantial leverage for changing model behavior, but this leverage is not well realized by traditional reweighting interventions. Instead, editing the supervision content of these influential examples is far more effective. This distinction between local reweighting effects and broader intervention leverage motivates evaluating TDA methods with respect to concrete intervention strategies, not just diagnostic influence estimates.

title: HyperStyler: Low-resource Authorship Style Transfer via Context-aware Style Navigation and Hypernetworks
summary: Low-resource authorship style transfer (LAST) aims to rewrite text into the style of an arbitrary target author using only a few reference examples while preserving the original meaning. Existing methods often struggle to achieve both high style fidelity and semantic preservation because they compress diverse references into a single static author embedding, which averages out context-dependent stylistic variation, and rely on hidden representations for style control, which entangle style with content. We propose HyperStyler, a novel architecture that decouples LAST into style selection and style realization. Stylo-navigator predicts style coordinates by jointly modeling the source context and target-author references, and Stylo-hypernet realizes them via dynamic parameter modulation instead of hidden-state injection. Our experiments on Reddit, Blog, and News datasets demonstrate that HyperStyler consistently outperforms prior methods including LLM-based approaches and generalizes robustly across domains. Notably, HyperStyler achieves superior performance with as few as 2.4% additional parameters over T5-large, while being over 1.8x faster than LLMs at inference.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces HyperStyler, a model that improves low-resource authorship style transfer by separating style selection from style realization, achieving better style fidelity, semantic preservation, and efficiency than prior methods and LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing low-resource authorship style transfer approaches struggle to balance style fidelity and semantic preservation. They typically compress multiple reference texts from a target author into one static embedding, which washes out fine-grained, context-dependent stylistic variations, and they control style via hidden representations that mix style with content. This leads to weak style control and content distortion, especially when only a few reference examples are available.
AI.method: The authors propose HyperStyler, which decomposes the task into two stages: (1) Stylo-navigator, which predicts style coordinates conditioned jointly on the source text and a small set of target-author reference texts, capturing context-aware stylistic choices; and (2) Stylo-hypernet, a hypernetwork that turns these style coordinates into dynamic parameter modulations of a base T5-large model, realizing style at the parameter level instead of injecting style vectors into hidden states. This design aims to disentangle style from content and to exploit dynamic, instance-wise style adaptation with minimal additional parameters.
AI.result: On Reddit, Blog, and News style-transfer benchmarks, HyperStyler consistently outperforms prior specialized models and large language model baselines in terms of style accuracy and semantic preservation metrics. It also shows strong cross-domain generalization, maintaining good performance when applied to new domains. Moreover, it requires only about 2.4% extra parameters over T5-large and delivers more than 1.8x faster inference compared to LLM baselines, indicating both parameter and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: HyperStyler demonstrates that explicitly separating style selection from style realization and using hypernetwork-based parameter modulation enables better low-resource authorship style transfer than existing embedding- or hidden-state-based control methods. The approach delivers improved style fidelity and semantic preservation, generalizes across domains, and remains lightweight and efficient, suggesting a promising direction for practical, low-resource stylistic rewriting systems.

title: EarlyEval: Cheaper Agent Evaluation via Early Outcome Prediction
comment: Code and data available at https://github.com/inphotoo/earlyeval
summary: Evaluating LLM agents is essential for guiding their development, yet it has grown prohibitively expensive: a single pass of a frontier model over an agentic benchmark can cost hundreds to thousands of dollars, a price paid repeatedly across iterative development cycles. Prior efforts, centered on benchmark distillation, reduce the number of evaluation tasks but leave the cost of executing each retained task untouched. In this work, we introduce early outcome prediction, a complementary axis of efficiency that instead cuts cost within each task. Our key insight is that an agent's final outcome is often evident from its intermediate behavior well before execution completes. We instantiate this idea in EarlyEval, a lightweight framework that trains a pair of LightGBM success and failure classifiers over behavioral, textual, and reference-solution features, and halts an agent run the moment either classifier crosses a calibrated confidence threshold, adding negligible per-step overhead. Across three benchmarks, SWE-bench Verified, TerminalBench, and Toolathlon, EarlyEval can eliminate 13%-26% of agent steps and up to 44.1% input tokens and 29.4% output tokens at 89%-97% prediction accuracy, while perturbing per-agent resolve rates by only one to two percentage points on average.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes EarlyEval, a framework that predicts an LLM agent’s final success or failure early from its intermediate behavior, allowing runs to be stopped early and thus cutting evaluation cost while preserving evaluation fidelity.
AI.motivation: Evaluating frontier LLM agents on complex agentic benchmarks is very expensive, often costing hundreds to thousands of dollars per full evaluation pass, and this must be repeated throughout iterative development. Existing cost-reduction methods focus on reducing the number of benchmark tasks (benchmark distillation), but they do not reduce the cost of executing each task that remains. There is a need for a complementary approach that reduces per-task evaluation cost without significantly harming the reliability of the evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce EarlyEval, a framework for early outcome prediction during agent runs. They train two LightGBM classifiers—one for predicting success and one for predicting failure—using features derived from the agent’s intermediate behavior, the textual content produced so far, and reference-solution information. During evaluation, EarlyEval monitors each step of the agent’s trajectory and stops the run as soon as either classifier’s confidence exceeds a calibrated threshold, thereby predicting the final outcome without running the agent to completion. The framework is designed to add negligible computational overhead per step.
AI.result: Applied to three agent benchmarks—SWE-bench Verified, TerminalBench, and Toolathlon—EarlyEval is able to cut 13%–26% of agent steps. This results in savings of up to 44.1% in input tokens and 29.4% in output tokens consumed during evaluation. These savings are achieved while maintaining high prediction accuracy (89%–97%) and only minimally affecting evaluation metrics, with per-agent resolve (success) rates deviating by roughly one to two percentage points on average compared to full-run evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Early outcome prediction is a viable and effective axis for improving the efficiency of LLM agent evaluation. By learning to infer final success or failure from intermediate behavior and terminating runs early, EarlyEval significantly reduces token and step costs at modest accuracy trade-offs and minimal perturbation to benchmark metrics. This suggests that future evaluation pipelines for agentic LLMs can incorporate such predictors to make large-scale, iterative benchmarking more affordable and scalable.

title: DiscoSign: Discourse-Aware Text to Sign Language Gloss Translation
summary: Sign language processing systems have traditionally operated at the sentence level, ignoring critical discourse phenomena fundamental to sign language comprehension. We introduce DiscoSign, a computational approach for discourse-aware text to sign language gloss translation grounded in linguistic research. We address three key phenomena within our modular Large Language Model (LLM)-based translation framework: (i) spatial coreference resolution, where entities maintain consistent spatial locations throughout discourse; (ii) Question-Answer Clauses (QACs), pseudocleft structures serving specific discourse functions; and (iii) concept-gloss consistency, ensuring stable mappings between English concepts and American Sign Language (ASL) signs. Traditional translation metrics fail to capture discourse-level quality, so we introduce a suite of novel evaluation metrics designed to assess each dimension of discourse coherence addressed by our framework. Experiments on sentence-level and discourse-level datasets show that our approach for discourse-aware processing significantly improves spatial consistency and entity tracking relative to sentence-only translation, while maintaining competitive single-sentence gloss translation quality. Our work establishes the first systematic framework for discourse-level text to sign language gloss translation with corresponding evaluation methodology.

AI.tldr: The paper presents DiscoSign, a discourse-aware text-to-ASL-gloss translation framework that models spatial coreference, question-answer clauses, and concept-gloss consistency, together with new evaluation metrics for discourse coherence.
AI.motivation: Existing sign language processing systems operate mostly at the sentence level and ignore discourse phenomena like spatial coreference and discourse-structural constructions, which are crucial for natural and coherent sign language communication. Moreover, current evaluation metrics focus on sentence-level accuracy and fail to measure discourse-level quality. The authors aim to bridge this gap by creating a translation framework and metrics that handle discourse-level aspects of sign language.
AI.method: The authors design DiscoSign, a modular LLM-based text-to-gloss translation pipeline that explicitly models three discourse phenomena: (i) spatial coreference resolution that assigns and maintains stable spatial locations for entities across discourse; (ii) recognition and treatment of Question-Answer Clauses (QACs), which have particular discourse functions and structural properties; and (iii) concept-gloss consistency to keep English concepts mapped consistently to ASL glosses. They then define specialized automatic evaluation metrics aligned with each of these discourse dimensions and conduct experiments on both sentence-level and discourse-level datasets.
AI.result: Experimental results show that DiscoSign yields substantially better spatial consistency and entity tracking compared to sentence-only translation baselines, without degrading standard single-sentence gloss translation performance. The proposed discourse-aware metrics effectively capture improvements in coherence that traditional metrics miss.
AI.conclusion: DiscoSign constitutes the first systematic framework for discourse-level text-to-sign-language-gloss translation and comes with dedicated evaluation methodology for discourse coherence. The work demonstrates that explicitly modeling discourse phenomena in sign language translation improves spatial and referential consistency while preserving strong sentence-level performance, laying groundwork for more natural and context-aware sign language technologies.

title: User Feedback Provides a Unique Signal that LLMs Can not Detect
summary: Harnessing naturally occurring feedback from user interactions offers a promising learning signal for Large Language Models (LLMs). However, recent studies suggest this feedback is inherently noisy and difficult to leverage effectively. We challenge this conception by demonstrating that user feedback is a highly actionable signal for improvement, and that its perceived ineffectiveness stems from a systematic bias in current evaluation paradigms. To isolate the usefulness of feedback, we construct synthetic data with a definitive ground truth, alongside naturalistic data to validate that our findings hold in real-world scenarios. By comparing model revisions generated with and without access to feedback across both settings, we show that feedback-informed revisions resolve targeted issues at significantly higher rates than baseline revisions. Finally, we expose the root of the evaluation bias: when a model successfully fixes an issue exclusively due to feedback, LLM judges frequently fail to identify the genuinely corrected response, systematically preferring inferior baseline outputs instead.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that user interaction feedback is a strong, underutilized signal for improving LLMs, and that its perceived weakness comes from biased evaluation setups.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats naturally occurring user feedback as too noisy and unreliable to effectively improve LLMs. Yet this feedback is abundant and cheap compared to expensive expert annotations. The authors want to rigorously test whether the issue is the feedback itself or the way we evaluate models that use it.
AI.method: They build two settings: (1) synthetic data with clear ground-truth so they can precisely measure whether feedback helps fix known issues, and (2) naturalistic user feedback data to confirm the results hold in realistic conditions. They then generate model revisions in two modes—one with access to feedback and one without—and compare how often each resolves the targeted problems. They also use LLM-based judges to evaluate outputs and probe where evaluation goes wrong.
AI.result: Revisions produced with access to feedback correct the targeted issues much more often than revisions produced without feedback, both in synthetic and real-world-like data. However, LLM judges frequently fail to recognize the genuinely improved response when the fix depends on the feedback, and instead often prefer the baseline (inferior) answer.
AI.conclusion: User feedback is in fact highly useful for improving LLM behavior; the main obstacle is not noisy feedback but biased evaluation procedures. Current LLM-judge setups systematically undervalue feedback-informed improvements by misranking them below inferior baselines, so better evaluation strategies are needed to unlock the full value of user interaction data.
